teile.einleitung: The Namib is a coastal desert in the south-west of Africa on the Atlantic. It is regarded as the oldest desert on Earth. Here there are huge red dunes, strange plants and animals that drink water from the fog.
wichtigste: The country of Namibia is named after the Namib Desert.
The Namib lies on the Atlantic coast and has been dry for at least 55 million years.
The cold Benguela Current brings a lot of fog but hardly any rain.
Welwitschia has only two leaves and can live to over 1,000 years old.
In the Sossusvlei stand some of the highest dunes in the world.
The Namib Sand Sea has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2013.

abschnitte.text: The **Namib** stretches along the **Atlantic coast** in the south-west of Africa. It is a **coastal desert** that borders directly on the sea. The Namib has been dry for at least 55 million years. That is why it is regarded as the **oldest desert in the world**. The country of **Namibia** was named after it. In some places almost no rain falls for years.

Off the coast flows the cold **Benguela Current**. It cools the air over the sea. In this way dense **fog** often forms, which drifts far inland but brings hardly any rain. For plants and animals this fog is often the most important source of water. Some **darkling beetles** stand head down on a dune in the fog. The droplets collect on their backs and run to their mouths.

**Welwitschia** is one of the strangest plants in the world. It grows only in the Namib and the neighbouring areas. All its life it grows only **two long leaves**, which keep growing and fray at the ends. Some plants are over **1,000 years** old. Welwitschia is so important that it is shown on the coat of arms of Namibia.

In the **Sossusvlei**, some of the highest dunes in the world surround a pale **salt and clay pan**. Some dunes are over 300 metres high. They glow red because the sand is coated with **iron oxide**, a kind of rust. A large part of the Namib became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2013 under the name **Namib Sand Sea**. It is the only coastal desert dune field whose dunes are so strongly shaped by fog.

abschnitte.titel: Skeleton Coast and a ghost town
abschnitte.text: In the north the coast of the Namib is called the **Skeleton Coast**. Fog and currents left many **ships stranded** there, and in the past many whale bones lay on the beach. In the south near Lüderitz lies **Kolmanskop**. The town was founded in 1908 after diamonds were found and later abandoned. Today sand dunes fill the old houses, and tourists visit the ghost town.

gewusst: Many animals of the Namib get their water almost only from the fog.
Namibia was a German colony from 1884 to 1915, which is why places such as Lüderitz have German names.

teile.einleitung: Easter Island is a small island in the middle of the Pacific. It belongs to Chile and is famous for the moai, huge stone figures. It is one of the most remote inhabited islands in the world.
wichtigste: Easter Island lies in the Pacific and has belonged to Chile since 1888.
Its inhabitants call it Rapa Nui.
The first inhabitants came as seafarers from Polynesia.
The moai were carved from soft volcanic rock.
Most moai stand on the coast and look inland.
The island got its name because a European reached it at Easter 1722.

abschnitte.text: Easter Island lies in the middle of the **Pacific**, the biggest ocean in the world. It is about 3,500 kilometres to the coast of Chile. Since 1888 the island has belonged to **Chile**. In its own language it is called **Rapa Nui**. That is also what its inhabitants and their language are called.

The first people came about 800 to 1,000 years ago from **Polynesia**. These seafarers found their way across the open sea in big boats. They steered by stars, waves and birds. On Easter Sunday 1722 the Dutchman **Jacob Roggeveen** reached the island. That is why it is called Easter Island in English.

The **moai** are huge stone figures with big heads. There are hundreds of them. They were carved from soft **volcanic rock** that comes from the old crater **Rano Raraku**. Many stand on stone platforms, the **ahu**. Most stand on the coast, but look **inland**. They probably represented important ancestors and were meant to protect the villages.

A large part of the island is a **national park**. It has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since 1995. The inhabitants also had a script of their own, **rongorongo**. It has still not been deciphered with certainty. Today many tourists come to see the moai.

gewusst: Some moai are almost ten metres high and weigh many tonnes.
How the moai were brought from the quarry to their places is still being researched today.

teile.einleitung: Net zero means that a country does not emit more greenhouse gases than are permanently removed from the air again. In this way global warming is to be slowed. Switzerland, too, has set itself this goal.
wichtigste: With net zero, remaining emissions are balanced by removals from the air.
Switzerland wants to reach net zero by 2050.
The Climate and Innovation Act was adopted on 18 June 2023 with 59.1 per cent yes.
The revised CO2 Act had narrowly been rejected in 2021.
With methods such as DACCS and BECCS, CO2 can be taken from the air and stored.
China wants to become carbon neutral by 2060, Germany by 2045.

abschnitte.text: Greenhouse gases such as **CO2** warm the Earth. Doing without any emissions at all is hardly possible, for example in farming or in some industries. These **remaining emissions** have to be balanced by removing the same amount of CO2 from the air. The word **“net”** means: in the end everything is added up, and the result is zero. Forests and bogs take up CO2, and technical methods add to that.

On 13 June 2021 the voters rejected the revised **CO2 Act** with 51.6 per cent no. Among other things it provided for a levy on plane tickets. Later a group submitted the **Glacier Initiative**. Parliament set against it, as a counter-proposal, the **Climate and Innovation Act**. This was adopted on 18 June 2023 with 59.1 per cent yes, and then the initiative was finally withdrawn.

The Climate and Innovation Act states that Switzerland is to reach net zero by **2050**. It also contains **interim targets** for buildings, transport and industry. Supporters saw it as an important step for climate protection. Opponents feared higher costs and problems with the electricity supply. In the end the majority agreed.

With **DACCS**, plants draw in air, filter the CO2 out and store it underground. With **BECCS**, plants are burned to generate energy and the CO2 is captured. Because the plants took up the CO2 beforehand, **negative emissions** result. In Iceland the **Carbfix** method presses dissolved CO2 into **basalt**, where it turns into solid rock. The Zurich company Climeworks runs plants there that filter CO2 from the air.

Since the **Paris Agreement** of 2015, many countries have set themselves net targets. Germany wants to be climate neutral by **2045**. **China** announced in 2020 that it would become carbon neutral before 2060, and **India** names the year 2070. Whether the goals are reached depends on many measures.

gewusst: With the Carbfix method the CO2 turns to stone within a few years, whereas it used to be thought that this took centuries.
The Glacier Initiative wanted to ban fossil fuels such as heating oil and petrol from 2050.

teile.einleitung: Tropical rainforests are the habitats richest in species on Earth. But every year large areas are cut down. **Rainforest conservation** means preserving these forests with their animals, plants and people.
wichtigste: The rainforest is most threatened by the felling of trees.
On Borneo many forests are cleared for oil palm plantations.
In the Amazon region cattle pastures and soya fields often appear on cleared land.
In slash-and-burn farming forest is burnt down to gain fields.
Trees take carbon dioxide out of the air, which is important for the climate.
Bruno Manser from Basel campaigned for the rainforest on Borneo.
At Zurich Zoo you can visit the Masoala rainforest.

abschnitte.text: In the tropical rainforests live countless species of animals and plants, and many of them are found nowhere else. The trees take **carbon dioxide** out of the air and use it to build wood and leaves. In this way they help to protect the **climate**. Rainforests also influence how much it rains in a region. In addition, they are the home of many indigenous peoples.

The greatest danger is **felling**. On **Borneo** forests are cleared for **oil palm plantations**, from whose fruit **palm oil** is obtained. In the **Amazon region**, **cattle pastures** and **soya fields** often appear on cleared land. In **slash-and-burn farming** people set fire to the forest to make room for fields or pastures. Timber trading and mining also destroy forest.

**Bruno Manser** from Basel lived for several years in the 1980s with the **Penan** in the rainforest of Borneo. He learned their language and their way of life. When logging threatened their forest, he fought against it together with them and drew the world’s attention to it. In 2000 he vanished without trace on Borneo. An association in Basel continues his work.

At **Zurich Zoo** there is a large hall with the **Masoala rainforest**. Plants from **Madagascar** grow there, and animals such as lemurs, chameleons and flying foxes live in it. The zoo also supports the **Masoala National Park** in Madagascar. In a **national park** nature is especially protected. Switzerland also has a national park, in the **Engadine**.

You can help at home too. Anyone who **saves paper** and uses **recycled paper** spares forests. When shopping you can look out for wood and paper with the **FSC label**, which stands for responsible forestry. You can also look at how much palm oil is in products. And anyone who tells others about the rainforest is helping too.

gewusst: In a single tree in the rainforest, hundreds of different species of insect can live.
The Masoala Hall at Zurich Zoo is so big that it even has a damp, warm climate of its own.

teile.einleitung: A physical map shows the surface of the Earth with mountains, valleys, rivers and seas. With colours it shows how high the land is or how deep the water is. In contrast, a political map shows countries and borders.
wichtigste: A physical map uses colours to show how high the land is.
Green stands for low, flat land, yellow for land of medium height.
Brown shows high mountains: the darker, the higher.
White stands for glaciers and ice in high mountains.
Dark blue shows deep sea, light blue shallow water.
A political map, by contrast, shows countries and borders.
The Swiss national map shows mountains with shading.

abschnitte.text: The **physical map** shows what the Earth’s surface looks like: where mountains, valleys, plains, rivers and seas lie. With **colours** it shows the height of the land. A **political map**, by contrast, shows countries and borders. There, neighbouring countries have different colours so that they are easy to tell apart. Many atlases contain both kinds of map.

The colours follow a fixed series. **Green** shows low areas, usually plains and valleys. Above that comes **yellow** for land of medium height. **Brown** stands for high mountains: the higher the land, the darker the brown. That is why the Alps are drawn in brown. At the very top, **white** stands for snow, **glaciers** and ice. What each colour means exactly is explained in the map’s **key**.

Water also has different shades. **Light blue** shows shallow water, for example close to the coast. **Dark blue** shows deep water, for example in the middle of the oceans. Greenland usually appears **white** on physical maps, because most of it is covered by thick ice. So is Antarctica.

The **national map of Switzerland** is published by the Federal Office of Topography, **swisstopo**. Its mountains look almost real because they are **shaded**. The map behaves as if light were coming from the top left. As a result, slopes look light on one side and dark on the other, and the terrain looks three-dimensional. **Forests** are coloured green on the national map.

gewusst: A green area on a physical map does not necessarily mean that a lot grows there. A low-lying desert can also be drawn in green.
The shading on Swiss national maps is known around the world for its beauty and accuracy.

teile.einleitung: Pangaea was a huge supercontinent in which almost all the land masses of the Earth were united. It existed mainly in the Permian and the Triassic, about 300 to 200 million years ago. After that it broke up into the continents we know today.
wichtigste: Pangaea formed towards the end of the Carboniferous and existed in the Permian and the Triassic.
The name means roughly “the whole Earth”.
Around Pangaea lay a huge ocean, Panthalassa.
In the interior it was very dry, with big deserts.
Alfred Wegener recognised that the continents had once been joined.
Only plate tectonics explained why continents move.

abschnitte.text: About 300 million years ago, towards the end of the **Carboniferous**, several continents collided. In this way **Pangaea** arose, Greek for “the whole Earth”. Around this supercontinent lay a single huge ocean, **Panthalassa**. In the **Permian** and the **Triassic**, Pangaea was at its biggest. After that it gradually broke up into smaller continents, and the Atlantic opened.

Pangaea was so big that moist sea air hardly reached the interior. A **very dry climate** with wide deserts therefore prevailed there. Evidence of this today is red **sandstones** from the Permian and Triassic, which are also found in Europe. In this period the first **dinosaurs** also developed.

The German researcher **Alfred Wegener** noticed that the coasts of **West Africa** and **South America** fit together like pieces of a jigsaw. He collected further evidence and from 1912 presented his idea of **continental drift**. One proof is fossils of the small freshwater reptile **Mesosaurus**. They are found in South America and in southern Africa. The animal could not swim across the Atlantic, so the continents must once have been joined.

Many experts rejected Wegener's idea for a long time. He could not explain convincingly which **force** was supposed to move whole continents. Only in the 1960s did **plate tectonics** supply a mechanism: the Earth's crust consists of plates that move slowly on the viscous mantle, only a few centimetres a year.

The continents are still moving today. Researchers expect that in a few hundred million years they could unite again into a **supercontinent**. One proposed name is **Amasia**, because America and Asia would merge in it. Such predictions are only models, though, and not certain.

gewusst: The continents move about as fast as our fingernails grow.
Wegener was actually a meteorologist and also explored Greenland.

teile.einleitung: The New Silk Road is a huge building project that China announced in 2013. New ports, railway lines and roads are to link China with Asia, Africa and Europe. The name recalls the old Silk Road, along which silk and spices were once traded.
wichtigste: China's president Xi Jinping announced the New Silk Road in 2013.
In English it is called the Belt and Road Initiative.
It consists of an economic belt on land and a sea route.
China builds and finances ports and railways in many countries.
Critics warn of a possible debt trap.
Duisburg is an important end point of the freight trains from China.

abschnitte.titel: From the old to the new Silk Road
abschnitte.text: The old **Silk Road** was a network of trade routes between China and the Mediterranean. Along it, mainly **silk**, spices and porcelain were transported. In 2013 China's president **Xi Jinping** presented the idea of a **New Silk Road**. In English it is called the **Belt and Road Initiative**, BRI for short. With it China wants to promote trade and strengthen its influence in the world.

The project has two main parts. The **“Belt”** means the land routes with railways, roads and pipelines. The **“Road”** means the **Maritime Silk Road**, that is, the sea routes with ports. Freight trains now run from China all the way to Europe, for example to **Duisburg**, which has the biggest inland port in Europe. Because Kazakhstan and Russia have a wider **track gauge**, containers have to be reloaded onto other wagons at some borders.

China has built or bought ports in many countries. The state-owned company **COSCO** took over the majority of the port of **Piraeus** in Greece in 2016. In Pakistan the port of **Gwadar** on the Arabian Sea was expanded. In Kenya, since 2017 a railway has linked the port city of **Mombasa** with the capital Nairobi. It was largely paid for with loans from China.

Supporters say that many countries urgently need roads, railways and ports. Critics think some countries would take on too much **debt** to China. Often cited is **Hambantota** in Sri Lanka: because the country could hardly repay the loans, in 2017 it leased the port for 99 years to a Chinese company. People speak of a possible **“debt trap”**, but experts do not agree about this.

abschnitte.titel: Europe and the New Silk Road
abschnitte.text: In 2019 **Italy** joined the project as the only one of the seven big industrial countries (G7). In December 2023 it left again. In 2019 Switzerland, too, signed a declaration of intent on cooperation in third countries. Many European states like to trade with China, but look closely at who controls their ports and railways.

gewusst: A freight train from China to Europe takes about half as long as a container ship.
The term “Silk Road” was only made known in the 19th century by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen.

teile.einleitung: The name **Pygmies** is used for various peoples who live in the rainforests of Central Africa. What they have in common is a small body height and a traditional way of life as hunter-gatherers in the forest.
wichtigste: The word Pygmy comes from the Greek pygme, which means fist.
A shared feature is a small body height.
The Mbuti live in the Ituri rainforest of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The Baka live mainly in the south of Cameroon and in Gabon.
Traditionally these peoples live as hunter-gatherers.
The polyphonic songs of the Aka are part of UNESCO’s intangible cultural heritage.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Greek **pygme**, which means **fist**. In old Greek legends it referred to very small people. Today the term covers several different peoples who have their own names and languages. Some of them find the collective name unsuitable and prefer to be called by their own people’s name.

These peoples live in the rainforests of **Central Africa**. Well known are the **Mbuti** in the **Ituri rainforest** in the north-east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with the subgroup of the Efe. The **Baka** live in the forests in the south of Cameroon, in Gabon and in the Republic of the Congo. The **Aka** live in the Central African Republic and the Republic of the Congo. The men are on average usually only about 150 centimetres tall, which is largely inherited.

Traditionally these peoples live as **hunter-gatherers**. They gather fruit, nuts, roots and honey and hunt animals in the forest. The **Mbuti** often hunt together with **nets**: men and women stretch long nets through the forest and drive small antelopes into them. The people know the forest and its plants very well. Their camps move again and again to new places.

In the forest they build round **huts** from a frame of bendy **branches** covered with large **leaves**. A hut like this goes up quickly and is easily abandoned when the group moves on. For a long time many groups have traded forest products such as honey or meat with neighbouring farming peoples in exchange for crops and tools.

Famous is the **polyphonic singing** of the **Aka**. Many voices are skilfully woven together. **UNESCO** counts the oral traditions of the Aka as part of the **intangible cultural heritage of humanity**. Today the traditional way of life is under threat: forests are being cleared, protected areas and plantations push the people out, and many experience discrimination.

gewusst: The forest peoples know hundreds of plants of the rainforest by name and know what they can be used for.
When gathering honey, some men climb very high up rainforest trees.

teile.einleitung: A passport is an official document that shows who you are and which country you belong to. Anyone travelling to another country must be able to prove who they are with it at the border.
wichtigste: The passport shows name, date of birth and nationality, plus a photo.
The passport is checked at the border or at the airport.
Modern Swiss passports have a chip with a photo and fingerprints.
For travel to many countries in Europe, Swiss people can manage with the identity card.
Border officials sometimes press a stamp into the passport.
Children also need their own passport or identity card.

abschnitte.text: A passport is a small booklet with many pages. At the front are the most important **personal details**: surname, first name, date of birth, sex and nationality. There is also a **photo**, so that you can see that the passport really belongs to this person. In addition there are a passport number and an **expiry date**. After this date the passport is no longer valid.

Modern Swiss passports are **biometric passports**. They contain a small **chip**. The photo and the **fingerprints** are stored on it. In this way border control can use a device to check whether the passport is genuine. This makes it much harder to forge a passport.

Anyone entering another country shows the passport at the **border** or at **passport control** at the airport. Border officials look at it and compare the photo with the person. In some countries they press a **stamp** with the date into the passport. For some countries you also need a **visa**, that is, permission to enter.

Swiss people can travel to many countries in Europe with just the **identity card**. This is a card the size of a credit card. For travel to countries further away, however, you usually need the passport. The Swiss passport is applied for at the responsible office in your own **canton**. For adults it is valid for ten years, for children five years.

gewusst: The Swiss passport is red and bears the white Swiss cross.
The chip in the passport works without a battery; it is supplied with energy by the reader.

teile.einleitung: The Philippines is an island state in South-East Asia in the western Pacific. It is made up of more than 7,000 islands and has a long history as a Spanish and later American colony. The country is known for its nature, but also for frequent typhoons.
wichtigste: The Philippines is made up of more than 7,000 islands.
The capital is Manila on the island of Luzon.
Luzon is the largest island, Mindanao the second largest.
The name comes from the Spanish King Philip II.
In 1898 the Philippines passed from Spain to the USA, and in 1946 they became independent.
The great majority of people are Roman Catholic.
Every year several typhoons sweep across the country.

abschnitte.text: The Philippines is made up of **more than 7,000 islands**. Many of them are small and uninhabited. The largest and most populous island is **Luzon** in the north. The capital **Manila**, a very densely populated city, lies there. The second largest island is **Mindanao** in the south. In 2020 more than 100 million people lived in the Philippines.

In 1521 the navigator **Ferdinand Magellan** reached the islands. Later they were named after **Philip II**, who became King of Spain. Spain ruled the Philippines for more than 300 years. After the **Spanish-American War** of 1898 they became a colony of the **USA**. Only in 1946 did the Philippines become an **independent** state.

Many different languages are spoken in the Philippines. The national languages are **Filipino** and **English**. Because of the long Spanish colonial period, the great majority of the population is **Roman Catholic**. The Philippines is the largest Catholic country in Asia. In the south, especially on Mindanao, many Muslims also live.

In the Philippines live many animals that are found nowhere else. The **Philippine tarsier** is only as big as a hand but has huge eyes. On the island of **Bohol** stand more than 1,000 round hills, the **Chocolate Hills**. In the dry season their grass turns brown, and then they look like chocolate. The country lies on the Pacific Ring of Fire and therefore also has volcanoes.

A typical means of transport is the **jeepney**. These brightly painted shared taxis were originally built from old military jeeps. A great danger for the country is **typhoons**. A typhoon is a powerful tropical storm over the Pacific. Every year several typhoons sweep across the Philippines and bring storms and heavy rain.

gewusst: Ferdinand Magellan died in the Philippines in 1521, on the small island of Mactan. His fleet sailed on without him and was the first to sail around the world.
The Philippine tarsier can turn its head very far, almost like an owl.

teile.einleitung: In wet-rice cultivation, rice grows in fields flooded with water. This is how most of the world's rice is grown, above all in Asia. For billions of people, rice is the most important staple food.
wichtigste: In wet-rice cultivation the rice fields are flooded with water.
The water suppresses weeds, and does not bother the rice itself.
About 90 per cent of rice is grown in Asia.
Since 2012 India has been the world's biggest rice exporter.
In flooded rice fields the greenhouse gas methane forms.
In the tropics two or three harvests a year are possible.

abschnitte.text: In **wet-rice cultivation**, the rice plants stand in a layer of water while they grow. Rice has **air-conducting tissue** through which air reaches down to the roots. That is why it survives in standing water, but most **weeds** do not. The water also evens out the temperature and keeps nutrients available in the soil. To keep the water on the field, the fields are surrounded by small banks.

In the traditional method, the young rice plants are first raised in a **seedbed**. After a few weeks the seedlings are planted by hand in rows in the flooded field. This method is called **transplanting**. It takes a lot of labour. But it gives the plants a head start over the weeds. On steep slopes, **terraces** are built so that the water stays on the fields.

According to the Food and Agriculture Organization **FAO**, about **90 per cent** of rice is grown in Asia and also eaten there. The biggest producers are **China and India**. In 2012 India overtook Thailand and has been the world's biggest **rice exporter** ever since. It supplies about 40 per cent of world exports. If India restricts exports, prices on the world market therefore rise. In the tropics, where it never gets cold and the monsoon and irrigation provide enough water, **two or three harvests** a year are possible.

Some farmers use a small water fern as fertiliser, the algae fern **Azolla**. In its leaves live **cyanobacteria**, which fix nitrogen from the air. When the fern dies, this nitrogen is available to the rice. In this way less artificial fertiliser is needed. This method has been used in Asia for a long time.

In the low-oxygen mud of the flooded fields, **bacteria** break down plant remains. This produces **methane**, a strong greenhouse gas. Rice fields are therefore among the significant human-made sources of methane. One solution is the method **“Alternate Wetting and Drying”**: the water is allowed to drain away regularly before the field is flooded again. This saves water and clearly lowers methane emissions without greatly reducing the yield.

gewusst: Rice is also grown in Ticino, for example near Ascona.
The rice terraces on Bali and in the Philippines are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

teile.einleitung: A **rain shower** is a short, heavy fall of rain. It starts suddenly and soon stops again. Afterwards the sun is often shining again already.
wichtigste: A shower is a short, heavy fall of precipitation.
It starts suddenly and soon stops again.
Showers fall from individual towering clouds.
Steady rain, by contrast, falls for a long time and evenly from a closed layer of cloud.
Showers are typical in spring, in what is called April weather.

abschnitte.text: In a **shower** the rain suddenly starts pattering down, often in big drops. After a few minutes, or at most a few hours, it is all over. Between two showers the sky can be completely blue. Showers fall from individual, high-piled **cumulus clouds**. These clouds look like big, white or grey cauliflower heads.

**Steady rain** is quite different. It falls from a **closed, grey layer of cloud**. The rain is usually not so heavy, but lasts for many hours and sometimes a whole day. Showers form when warm, damp air rises quickly. Steady rain often forms when large air masses slowly slide over one another.

Showers are especially typical in spring. Then sun, rain and sometimes even snow or **soft hail** quickly take turns. This is called **April weather**. In summer, **thunderstorms** with lightning and thunder can also form from large cumulus clouds. After a shower, with the sun out, you often see a rainbow.

gewusst: A shower can be so narrowly limited that it rains on one side of the street and stays dry on the other.
Soft hail consists of small, soft pellets of ice that often fall in showers in spring.

teile.einleitung: The oriental city is a type of city found in North Africa and the Middle East. Its core is the old town, the medina, with mosque, market and narrow lanes. Its layout follows certain rules of religion, trade and family life.
wichtigste: The traditional old town is called the medina in North Africa.
In the centre there is usually the big Friday mosque.
Around the mosque lies the market, the souk or bazaar.
Valuable goods are sold near the mosque, noisy and smelly trades at the edge.
Dead ends and courtyard houses protect the privacy of families.
Fez el-Bali in Morocco is regarded as one of the biggest car-free urban areas in the world.

abschnitte.text: The **medina** is the traditional old town of an oriental city. In its middle there is usually the big **Friday mosque**, where the faithful meet for Friday prayer. Around it the market lanes are grouped. Often at the edge of the medina lies a fortified citadel, the **kasbah**. It was the seat of the ruler and his troops, an example is the Kasbah of the Udayas in **Rabat**.

The **souk** is a maze of market lanes with shops of traders and craftsmen. In Persia and Turkey people speak of the **bazaar**. The layout follows an order of rank. Fine, clean goods such as **gold**, **books** or fragrances are sold near the mosque. Noisy or foul-smelling trades lie further out, for example **tanneries**, which turn animal hides into leather.

In the residential quarters there are many **dead ends**. They keep strangers away from the houses and so protect the **privacy** of families. There is hardly any through traffic. Typical is the **courtyard house**: to the outside it has high walls with few windows. Family life takes place in the shady courtyard in the middle.

The old town **Fez el-Bali** in Morocco has thousands of narrow lanes. Cars cannot drive there, and loads are carried by **donkeys** and carts. It is regarded as one of the biggest car-free urban areas in the world and has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since 1981. In many Moroccan cities there is also a historic Jewish quarter, the **mellah**. The mellah of Fez arose in the 15th century near the ruler's palace.

Today the oriental cities are growing fast. Beside the medina, **new towns** arose with wide streets, often in the colonial period. Many old towns are popular destinations for **tourists**. At the same time it is a challenge to preserve the old houses and to live in them in a modern way.

gewusst: In the tanneries of Fez, leather is still dyed in open vats today.
The word medina simply means “city” in Arabic.

teile.einleitung: Nepal is a country in South Asia between India and China. In the north the Himalayas rise, with the highest mountains on Earth, among them Mount Everest.
wichtigste: The capital of Nepal is called Kathmandu.
In the north lie the Himalayas, the highest mountain range on Earth.
8 of the 14 eight-thousanders lie wholly or partly in Nepal.
The flag of Nepal is the only national flag that is not rectangular.
According to tradition, the Buddha was born in Lumbini.
Since 2008 Nepal has been a republic.

abschnitte.titel: The land of the highest mountains
abschnitte.text: In the north of Nepal lie the **Himalayas**. Here stand 8 of the 14 mountains higher than 8,000 metres, for example **Mount Everest**, Lhotse and Annapurna. In the south the land is flat and warm, and this plain is called the **Terai**. So on a small area there is both jungle and eternal ice. In a valley in the middle lies the capital **Kathmandu** with many old temples.

The **Sherpas** are a mountain people who live high in the mountains. Many work as porters and mountain guides and accompany climbers from all over the world. In the mountains people keep the **yak**, a bovine with long fur. It carries loads and gives milk and wool. Swiss people, too, wrote mountaineering history: in 1956 **Ernst Reiss** and **Fritz Luchsinger** were the first to climb Lhotse.

Most people in Nepal are **Hindus**, and many others are **Buddhists**. According to tradition, the Buddha was born in **Lumbini** in the south, and today the place is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. As a greeting people say **“Namaste”** and put their hands together in front of the chest. Everywhere you see colourful prayer flags and temples.

The flag of Nepal consists of two **triangles** on top of each other. It is the only national flag in the world that is not rectangular. For a long time Nepal was ruled by kings. In **2008** the monarchy was abolished and Nepal became a **republic**. Since the constitution of 2015 it has been a federal republic.

Nepal and Switzerland are both mountain countries. Since the 1950s Switzerland has worked with Nepal in **development cooperation**. This involves, for example, suspension bridges, roads and education. Many Swiss people travel to Nepal for hiking and climbing.

gewusst: Mount Everest is called Sagarmatha in Nepali.
In Nepal, besides the well-known peaks, there are hundreds of mountains higher than 6,000 metres.

teile.einleitung: The Northeast Passage is a sea route along the north coast of Europe and Asia. It connects the Atlantic with the Pacific and runs through the icy Arctic Ocean. Because the sea ice is shrinking, it is now used more and more often.
wichtigste: The Northeast Passage runs from the Barents Sea to the Bering Strait.
Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld was the first to sail through it, in 1878/79, with the Vega.
It is clearly shorter than the route through the Suez Canal.
Russia keeps it open with nuclear-powered icebreakers.
Thanks to warm Atlantic water, Murmansk is ice-free all year round.
Because of warming, the route can be sailed for longer in the year.

abschnitte.titel: The search for the sea route
abschnitte.text: As early as the 16th century, sailors were looking for a route to Asia in the north. The Dutchman **Willem Barents** got stuck in the ice in 1596 and spent the winter on **Novaya Zemlya** in a hut made of driftwood. He died on the way back, and the **Barents Sea** is named after him. Only in 1878/79 did **Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld** sail through the whole passage with the ship **Vega**. Shortly before the goal he too had to spend the winter in the ice.

abschnitte.titel: The route through the Arctic Ocean
abschnitte.text: The Northeast Passage runs from the **Barents Sea** along the north coast of Russia to the **Bering Strait**. On the way it crosses the Kara Sea, the Laptev Sea and the East Siberian Sea. A difficult point is **Cape Chelyuskin**, the northernmost point of the Eurasian mainland. There the ice is often especially stubborn. The section from the Kara Sea to the Bering Strait is administered by Russia as the **Northern Sea Route**.

Russia is the only country that runs a fleet of **nuclear-powered icebreakers**. They can travel a long time without refuelling and break thick pack ice. The western starting point is **Murmansk** on the Kola Peninsula. Thanks to offshoots of the **Gulf Stream**, the port does not freeze despite lying north of the Arctic Circle. On the Yamal Peninsula lies the port of **Sabetta**, from which tankers carry **liquefied natural gas** as far as Asia too.

Between Northern Europe and East Asia, the Northeast Passage is, depending on the destination, about a third shorter than the route through the **Suez Canal**. This saves time and fuel. But **ice**, costly **icebreaker** escorts and few ports make the route risky. That is why far fewer ships have so far used it than the Suez Canal.

Because of the warming of the **Arctic**, the area of sea ice in summer has fallen sharply. As a result the route can be sailed for **longer in the year**. This pleases shipping companies, but brings risks for the environment and climate. An oil accident in the icy sea would be almost impossible to deal with. Experts therefore watch developments closely.

gewusst: The counterpart on the other side of the Arctic is called the Northwest Passage, and it runs along the coast of Canada.
Murmansk is the biggest city in the world north of the Arctic Circle.

teile.einleitung: The Murray is the longest river in Australia. It flows about 2,500 kilometres from the Australian Alps to the sea in South Australia. Together with the Darling it forms the biggest river system on the continent.
wichtigste: At about 2,500 kilometres, the Murray is the longest river in Australia.
It rises in the Australian Alps in the south-east.
Over a long stretch it forms the border between New South Wales and Victoria.
In South Australia it flows through Lake Alexandrina into the sea.
Its longest tributary is the Darling.
In the river's basin there is a lot of farming with irrigation.

abschnitte.titel: From the mountains to the lowlands
abschnitte.text: The **Murray** rises in the **Australian Alps** in the south-east of the continent. This range is part of the Great Dividing Range, and the highest mountain in Australia is also there. From the mountains the river flows west through flat, often dry land. At about **2,500 kilometres**, it is the longest river in Australia. That makes it about twice as long as the Rhine.

In its upper reaches the Murray separates the state of **New South Wales** in the north from **Victoria** in the south. In this way the river forms a border over a long stretch, much as the Rhine in part forms the border of Switzerland. After that it flows into **South Australia**. There it crosses **Lake Alexandrina** and reaches the sea. The mouth is called **Murray Mouth**.

The longest tributary is the **Darling**. It joins the Murray near the town of **Wentworth**. Other important tributaries are the Murrumbidgee and the Goulburn. Together these rivers form the biggest river system in Australia. The area from which they get their water is called the **Murray-Darling Basin**.

The Murray-Darling Basin is very important for Australia. **Grain, fruit, wine** and livestock are produced here. Because it often rains little, a lot of river water is used for **irrigation**. Big reservoirs store the water, for example Lake Hume. Cities such as Adelaide also get part of their drinking water from the Murray.

In the 19th century many **paddle steamers** sailed on the Murray. They carried mainly wool and other goods to the ports. Today a few old steamers still run for tourists. In the river lives the **Murray cod**, one of the biggest freshwater fish in Australia. On the banks grow big eucalyptus trees.

gewusst: When very little water flows, the mouth of the Murray sometimes has to be dredged so that it does not close up.
For Aboriginal people the Murray has had great importance for thousands of years.

teile.einleitung: The Murray-Darling Basin is the biggest river system in Australia. It is one of the most important farming regions in the country. At the same time it shows how hard it is to share scarce water fairly.
wichtigste: The basin covers about one million square kilometres, roughly 14 per cent of the area of Australia.
It is about 25 times as big as Switzerland.
Clearing of land and intensive irrigation led to salinisation of soils and rivers.
From about 1997 to 2009 the Millennium Drought hit the region.
The Murray-Darling Basin Plan of 2012 regulates how much water may be taken.
The Murrumbidgee irrigates, among other things, rice fields in the Riverina.

abschnitte.text: The **Murray-Darling Basin** is the area from which the Murray and its tributaries get their water. It covers about **one million square kilometres**, roughly one seventh of the area of Australia. That is about 25 times the area of Switzerland. The basin stretches across several states, mainly New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland and South Australia. Large parts of it are dry and flat.

The **Darling** is very long, but often carries only a little water. It flows through **semi-arid** regions, that is, half-dry land where hardly any rain falls and a lot of water evaporates. In addition, a lot of water is taken for irrigation. That is why the Darling at times almost dries up. The **Murrumbidgee**, by contrast, rises in the Snowy Mountains and supplies irrigation areas around Wagga Wagga and Griffith.

In the basin, grain, fruit, wine, rice, cotton and livestock are produced. In the **Riverina** region, rice among other crops is grown with water from the Murrumbidgee. So that water flows even in the dry summer, big dams were built. The **Hume Dam** near Albury was completed in 1936 and raised several times. Its reservoir, **Lake Hume**, regulates the flow of the Murray for farming and cities.

In the past many deep-rooted trees were cleared and large areas were irrigated. As a result, **salty groundwater** rose. The salt reached soils and rivers and harmed farming and nature. This **salinisation** is still a problem today. From about 1997 to 2009 the **Millennium Drought** also hit south-eastern Australia. Flows and reservoirs sank to record lows, and the Murray mouth had to be dredged.

The drought led to reforms of water policy. Since 2012 the **Murray-Darling Basin Plan** has applied. It sets sustainable limits on how much water may be taken. In this way rivers and wetlands are to keep enough water. To do this the state buys back, among other things, **water rights** from farmers. How much water should be left for nature and how much for farming is hotly debated in Australia.

gewusst: In Australia, water rights can be bought and sold, much like a commodity.
The wetlands in the basin are important breeding grounds for many waterbirds.

teile.einleitung: Popocatépetl is one of the best-known volcanoes in the world. It lies in Mexico, not far from the huge capital Mexico City, and still sends out smoke and ash again and again.
wichtigste: Popocatépetl lies in Mexico, about 70 kilometres from Mexico City.
Its name comes from the Nahuatl language and means “smoking mountain”.
Many people in Mexico call it “El Popo” for short.
It is over 5,000 metres high and so the second highest mountain in Mexico.
Only Pico de Orizaba, also called Citlaltépetl, is higher in Mexico.
Since December 1994 Popocatépetl has been active again.
It is a steep stratovolcano made of lava and ash.

abschnitte.text: Popocatépetl rises over 5,000 metres into the sky. That makes it higher than any mountain in Switzerland, including the Dufourspitze. In Mexico only **Pico de Orizaba** is higher. The summit is often covered with snow, although the mountain lies in a warm country. Clouds of steam and ash often rise from its crater.

The name comes from **Nahuatl**, the language of the Aztecs. This language is still spoken by many people in Mexico today. Popocatépetl means “smoking mountain”, because smoke often rises from it. Because the name is long, many Mexicans simply say **“El Popo”**.

North of Popocatépetl lies the volcano **Iztaccíhuatl**. Its name means “white woman”. From far away its snow-covered mountain ridge looks like a woman lying down. There is an old legend about the two mountains, about a warrior and a princess. A high pass leads between the two volcanoes.

Popocatépetl is a **stratovolcano**. Over a very long time it has grown from many layers of lava and ash. That is why it has the typical steep cone shape. Volcanoes like this often erupt with explosions. Ash and lumps of rock are hurled high into the air.

For almost 50 years the volcano was quiet. In **December 1994** it erupted again. Since then it has sent out ash and smoke again and again. Because millions of people live in the surrounding area, it is closely **monitored** by experts. In strong eruptions the airport of Mexico City is sometimes even closed because of the ash.

gewusst: Popocatépetl is higher than all the mountains of the Alps, even higher than Mont Blanc.
On the slopes of Popocatépetl stand old monasteries from the 16th century that are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
The volcano even has a nickname of its own that almost every child in Mexico knows: El Popo.

teile.einleitung: The East African Rift System is a zone in which a continent is tearing apart. It stretches for thousands of kilometres through East Africa. Here you can watch how plates drift apart, volcanoes arise and perhaps one day a new sea.
wichtigste: At the rift the African Plate is being split into the Nubian and the Somali plates.
In the Afar Triangle the rift, the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden meet.
Lake Tanganyika in the western branch is the second deepest lake on Earth.
Nyiragongo in the Congo is known for its lava lake.
Kilimanjaro is a volcano linked to the rift.
In 1974 the famous fossil Lucy was discovered in the Afar region.
In 2005 a crack about 60 kilometres long opened in Ethiopia in a short time.

abschnitte.text: West of the rift lies the **Nubian Plate**, to the east the **Somali Plate**. Both are slowly moving away from each other. In the process the Earth's crust is stretched, becomes thinner and sinks in the middle. If the stretching goes on, the crust can tear apart completely and sea water can flow in. In this way a new **ocean basin** could arise, as happened with the **Red Sea**.

In the **Afar Triangle** in Ethiopia, Eritrea and Djibouti, three fracture systems meet: the East African Rift, the **Red Sea** and the **Gulf of Aden**. Such a point is called a **triple junction**. The region lies partly below sea level and is very volcanically active. In September 2005, near **Dabbahu**, magma pushed into the crust and tore it open over a length of about 60 kilometres, mostly within about a week. This showed that a rift can also open **suddenly**.

**Nyiragongo** in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo lies near the city of **Goma**. It is known for its **lava lake** in the crater. Its very runny lava can drain away quickly, as in the eruptions of 1977, 2002 and 2021. **Ol Doinyo Lengai** in Tanzania produces **natrocarbonatite**, a lava made of carbonates instead of silicates. **Kilimanjaro**, too, at about 5,895 metres the highest mountain in Africa, is a volcano whose origin is linked to the rift.

In the western branch lies **Lake Tanganyika**, about 1,470 metres deep and so the second deepest lake on Earth. The big **Lake Victoria**, by contrast, lies in a shallow basin between the two branches of the rift. The **Rwenzori Mountains** are not a volcano, but a raised **block of crust**. Their highest peaks even carry glaciers, although they lie close to the equator.

In 1974 the skeleton **Lucy** was discovered in the Afar region. It is about 3.2 million years old and belongs to the species **Australopithecus afarensis**, an early human ancestor. In the rift, fossils are found especially often. The edges of the rift are worn away by **erosion**, so old layers with bones come to the surface.

gewusst: Lucy got her name from a Beatles song that the researchers heard in camp.
In the Afar Triangle lie some of the hottest inhabited places on Earth.

teile.einleitung: Polynesia is a huge world of islands in the Pacific Ocean. The name comes from Greek and means “many islands”. Polynesia forms a large triangle between Hawaii, New Zealand and Easter Island.
wichtigste: Polynesia forms a triangle between Hawaii, New Zealand and Easter Island.
Hawaii has been a state of the USA since 1959.
The capital of Samoa is Apia, and that of French Polynesia is Papeete on Tahiti.
The Cook Islands and Niue are linked to New Zealand in free association.
Polynesian navigators found their way by stars, waves, birds and clouds.
The word “taboo” comes from Polynesian languages.
In January 2022 the volcano Hunga Tonga-Hunga Haʻapai exploded.

abschnitte.text: Polynesia is one of the great island regions of **Oceania**, alongside Melanesia and Micronesia. It forms a huge triangle: **Hawaii** in the north, **New Zealand** in the south-west and **Easter Island** in the east. In between lie thousands of islands, such as Samoa, Tonga, the Cook Islands and Tahiti. Hawaii forms the northern tip and has been a state of the **USA** since **1959**.

Some islands are states in their own right. **Samoa** has been independent since 1962, and its capital **Apia** lies on the island of Upolu. The **Cook Islands** govern themselves but are linked to New Zealand in **free association**. Their inhabitants hold New Zealand citizenship. The same is true of **Niue**, one of the largest raised coral islands in the world. **French Polynesia** is an overseas country of France with the capital **Papeete** on Tahiti. In the territory of **Wallis and Futuna**, three traditional kings still rule alongside the French administration.

The Polynesians settled their islands by sailing large **canoes** across thousands of kilometres of open sea. They had no compass. They read their way from **star risings**, from the **swell**, the long waves of the ocean, from **bird migrations** and from clouds that form over islands. In 1976 the canoe **Hōkūleʻa** sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti in the traditional way and proved that this works.

The British navigator **James Cook** came across the word “tapu” in Tonga. It means something sacred or forbidden. Through English it passed into German as **“Tabu”**, and into English as **“taboo”**. The French painter **Paul Gauguin** lived in French Polynesia from 1891. On Tahiti and later in the Marquesas he painted glowing pictures of island life, and he died in 1903 on the island of Hiva Oa.

Many islands of Polynesia are **volcanic islands** or **atolls**, ring-shaped coral islands. In **January 2022** the undersea volcano **Hunga Tonga-Hunga Haʻapai** near Tonga exploded with enormous force. It set off a **tsunami** and a **pressure wave** that travelled around the Earth. Even in Switzerland barometers recorded this wave.

gewusst: The pressure wave of the volcano at Tonga travelled several times around the whole Earth in January 2022.
Niue is also called the “Rock of Polynesia” because of its steep limestone coasts.

teile.einleitung: Canaima National Park lies in the south-east of Venezuela. It is famous for its huge table mountains, the tepuis, and for Angel Falls, the highest waterfall in the world. The park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wichtigste: Canaima National Park lies in the south-east of Venezuela.
In the park lies Angel Falls, the highest waterfall in the world.
Typical are the tepuis, table mountains with steep walls and a flat top.
The park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site because of its table mountains.
It is one of the biggest national parks in the world.

abschnitte.text: **Canaima National Park** was founded in 1962 and covers about 30,000 square kilometres, almost three quarters the size of Switzerland. Typical are the **tepuis**: table mountains with almost vertical walls and a flat top. They are made of very old sandstone and rise far above the rainforest and the savanna. On their summits grow plants that exist nowhere else. Because of this special landscape the park has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since 1994.

From the table mountain **Auyán-tepui** plunges **Angel Falls**, the highest waterfall in the world. The water falls about 979 metres. With so much height, part of the water turns into fine mist before it arrives at the bottom. The waterfall is named after the American pilot **Jimmie Angel**, who flew over it in the 1930s. In the language of the Pemón it is called Kerepakupai Merú.

In the park live the **Pemón**, an Indigenous people. For them the table mountains have a special meaning. Angel Falls is usually reached by plane and then by boat on rivers. In the park also lies the wide high plain of the **Gran Sabana**, with many more waterfalls.

gewusst: Angel Falls is over 40 times as high as the Rhine Falls.
On some tepuis grow carnivorous plants that catch insects.

teile.einleitung: Rhinoceroses are big, heavy plant eaters with thick skin and one or two horns on the nose. They live in Africa and Asia. Many rhinos are strongly threatened because poachers kill them for their horns.
wichtigste: Rhinos are plant eaters that eat grass or leaves and twigs.
In Africa live the white rhino and the black rhino.
African rhinos have two horns, one behind the other.
The white rhino is the biggest rhino.
Rhinos see rather badly, but smell and hear very well.
A young rhino is called a calf.

abschnitte.text: Today there are five species of rhino. In **Africa** live the **white rhino** and the **black rhino**. Both have two horns, one behind the other, and the front one is usually longer. In **Asia** live the Indian rhino, the Javan rhino and the Sumatran rhino. The white rhino is the biggest rhino and, after the elephant, one of the biggest land animals. It can weigh several tonnes.

Rhinos are **plant eaters**. The white rhino has a wide mouth and uses it to crop grass from the ground, like a lawn mower. The black rhino has a pointed, mobile upper lip. With it, it picks **leaves and twigs** from bushes. So the names of the two species describe their mouths.

The **skin** of a rhino is very thick, in some places up to about 5 centimetres. It acts like armour. Even so, it can get sunburnt, which is why rhinos like to wallow in **mud**. Rhinos **see rather badly**. In return they can **smell and hear** very well. Their horns are made of **keratin**, the same substance as our hair and fingernails.

A young rhino is called a **calf**. It stays with its mother for some years and learns from her. Often birds sit on the backs of rhinos, the **oxpeckers**. They pick ticks and other small animals from the skin. When danger threatens, they fly up calling loudly and so warn the rhino too.

Rhinos are strongly threatened. **Poachers** kill them illegally in order to sell the horns at a high price. In some countries people wrongly believe the horn is a medicine. That is why rhinos in protected areas are guarded by **rangers**. Some animals even have their horn cut off so that they are of no interest to poachers. Zoos also help to preserve the species.

gewusst: Of the northern white rhino, only two females are left (as of 2023).
Despite their weight, rhinos can run for a short time at up to about 40 kilometres an hour.

teile.einleitung: The polar circles are two imaginary lines on the Earth, one in the north and one in the south. They lie at about 66.5 degrees latitude. Beyond them there is at least one day a year on which the sun does not set, and one on which it does not rise.
wichtigste: The northern polar circle lies at about 66.5 degrees north.
The value comes from 90 degrees minus the tilt of the Earth’s axis of about 23.5 degrees.
North of it there is at least one day without a sunset.
The polar circle crosses Norway, Sweden and Finland, but not Estonia.
Rovaniemi in Finland lies right on the polar circle.
In Iceland the polar circle touches only the small island of Grimsey.
Antarctica lies almost entirely south of the southern polar circle.

abschnitte.text: The **polar circles** are **circles of latitude**, that is, lines that run around the Earth parallel to the equator. The **northern polar circle** lies at about **66.5 degrees north**, the **southern polar circle** at about 66.5 degrees south. The number comes from a simple calculation: 90 degrees minus the **tilt of the Earth’s axis** of about 23.5 degrees.

The polar circle is defined exactly like this: north of it, in summer, the sun stays completely above the horizon on **at least one day**. This is called the **midnight sun**. In winter there is at least one day there on which the sun does not rise at all, the **polar night**. The closer you get to the pole, the longer these periods last. In the south the same applies the other way round.

The northern polar circle passes through **Norway**, **Sweden**, **Finland**, Russia, the USA with Alaska, Canada and Greenland. **Estonia**, by contrast, lies at about 58 to 60 degrees north and so well to the south. The main island of **Iceland** lies just south of the polar circle. Only the small island of **Grimsey** off the north coast is touched by it.

The Finnish city of **Rovaniemi** is the capital of Lapland. A few kilometres north of the centre the polar circle runs. There is also a well-known **Santa Claus village** there, which many tourists visit. In the south the continent of **Antarctica** lies almost entirely south of the southern polar circle. Only a narrow part reaches north beyond it.

The tilt of the Earth’s axis does not stay the same for ever. Over many thousands of years it varies slightly back and forth. That is why the polar circles also **shift** slowly. At the moment they move by a few metres every year. On the island of Grimsey a work of art has therefore been put up, a large stone ball that is moved regularly.

gewusst: Switzerland lies at about 46 to 48 degrees north, roughly 2,000 kilometres south of the polar circle.
If you cross the polar circle in Rovaniemi, you can have a certificate made out for it.

teile.einleitung: The Orinoco is one of the biggest rivers in South America. It flows mainly through Venezuela and in part forms the border with Colombia. It flows into the Atlantic with a huge delta.
wichtigste: The Orinoco is over 2,000 kilometres long.
It flows through Venezuela and Colombia.
It flows into the Atlantic with a broad delta.
Its source lies in a remote upland on the border with Brazil.
Only in 1951 did an expedition reach the source.
Through the Casiquiare it is connected with the Amazon.

abschnitte.titel: From the source to the sea
abschnitte.text: The Orinoco rises in the uplands of the **Sierra Parima** on the border with **Brazil**. The area is so remote that only in 1951 did a **French-Venezuelan expedition** reach the source. The river flows in a big curve through **Venezuela**. Part of its course forms the border with **Colombia**. It crosses the wide grass plains of the **Llanos**.

The Orinoco flows into the **Atlantic** with a broad **delta**. The delta consists of many **channels** and islands with swamps and mangroves. Here lives the Indigenous people of the **Warao**. Many of them live in houses on stilts by the water and get about by boat.

A special feature is the **Casiquiare**. This natural waterway branches off the Orinoco and flows into the **Amazon** river system. In this way two big river systems are connected with each other. This is called a **bifurcation**. The German explorer **Alexander von Humboldt** explored this link in the year 1800.

In the area of the Orinoco live rare animals such as the critically endangered **Orinoco crocodile** and river dolphins. The highest waterfall in the world, **Angel Falls**, also lies in the river's catchment area. North of the river lies the **Orinoco Belt** with huge deposits of viscous **crude oil**.

gewusst: The Orinoco and the Amazon are connected with each other by a natural river.
Christopher Columbus reached the mouth of the Orinoco in 1498.

teile.einleitung: Petra is an ancient city in the south of Jordan whose houses, tombs and temples were carved straight into the rock walls. The Nabataeans built it more than 2,000 years ago. Today Petra is one of the most famous sights in the world.
wichtigste: Petra is a city carved into the rock in Jordan.
The sandstone glows red and pink, which is why Petra is also called the rose-red city.
Most people enter Petra through a narrow gorge, the Siq.
The most famous building is the Treasury with its magnificent façade.
The Nabataeans grew rich through trade in frankincense and spices.
In AD 106 the area became part of the Roman Empire.
Petra has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985.

abschnitte.text: Petra lies in a valley between mountains of **sandstone**. The inhabitants did not build their houses and tombs up from stones, but cut them straight into the rock walls. The stone glows in red, pink and orange, especially beautifully at sunset. That is why Petra is also called the **rose-red city**. The name Petra comes from Greek and means “rock”.

Petra was founded by the **Nabataeans**, an Arab people. Their city lay on important trade routes. Through Petra passed **caravans** of camels bringing frankincense from southern Arabia and spices to the Mediterranean. The Nabataeans charged customs duties and grew rich as a result. In AD 106 the Emperor **Trajan** made their kingdom the Roman province of Arabia.

The way into the city leads through the **Siq**, a narrow gorge with high rock walls. At its end the **Treasury** suddenly appears, a façade with columns about 2,000 years old, carved into the rock. High above the city lies the **Monastery**, in Arabic ad-Deir. About 800 steps lead up to it. It is one of the largest rock-cut buildings in Petra.

In the area around Petra it rarely rains. Even so, many people lived here. The Nabataeans were masters at handling water. They collected rainwater in **channels** and **conduits** and led it into large **cisterns**, which are underground water stores. This meant they had enough to drink even in the dry season.

After the Middle Ages Petra was forgotten in Europe. In 1812 **Johann Ludwig Burckhardt** came there, a traveller from a Basel family. He travelled through the Middle East in Arab clothing and was the first European of his time to report on the rock city. Since 1985 Petra has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** and is visited by very many people every year.

gewusst: The Treasury of Petra can be seen in the 1989 film “Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade”.
In 2007 Petra was chosen in a worldwide vote as one of the “New Seven Wonders of the World”.

teile.einleitung: The outback is the big, dry interior of Australia. There you find red earth, wide plains and only a few people. Many special animals such as kangaroos, emus and dingoes live here.
wichtigste: The outback is the wide, dry interior of Australia.
The earth is red because there is a lot of iron in the soil.
Kangaroos, emus and dingoes live in the outback.
Aboriginal people have lived there for tens of thousands of years.
Doctors often come to the sick by plane.
Children on remote farms learn with lessons by radio or internet.

abschnitte.text: The **outback** is not a precisely defined area, but the big, dry **interior of Australia**. Only a few people live there, and the houses lie far apart. The ground is often **red**. There is a lot of **iron** in the soil, which rusts and colours the earth red. Well known is the huge rock **Uluru**, which is sacred to Aboriginal people.

**Kangaroos** are at home in the outback, and you often see them in the morning and the evening. The **emu** is, after the ostrich, the biggest bird in the world. It cannot fly, but can run very fast. The **dingo** is a wild dog with mostly yellowish-brown fur. To keep dingoes away from the sheep, there is the **Dingo Fence**, about 5,600 kilometres long. It is regarded as one of the longest structures in the world.

The **Aboriginal people** are the first inhabitants of Australia. They have lived in the land for **tens of thousands of years**, in the outback too. They know the waterholes, plants and animals very well. Their stories, songs and rock paintings are very old and important for their culture.

The nearest school or hospital is often hundreds of kilometres away. That is why the **flying doctors** come to the sick in small aeroplanes. Children on remote farms learn with the **School of the Air**, that is, with lessons by radio or today over the internet. In the mining town of **Coober Pedy**, where people search for **opals**, it becomes extremely hot in summer. Many people therefore live there **underground**, where it stays pleasantly cool.

gewusst: In Coober Pedy there are even underground churches.
A single farm in the outback can be bigger than a Swiss canton.

teile.einleitung: The economy is often divided into sectors: agriculture, industry and services. In an extended division there is also the **quaternary sector**. It covers activities whose most important raw material is **knowledge and information**.
wichtigste: The quaternary sector covers activities based on information and knowledge.
It was split off from the tertiary sector, the services.
Typical examples are software development, research and consulting.
Highly qualified workers are especially important.
Digitalisation made the sector grow strongly from the 1990s.
Its growth is often linked with the knowledge society.
The dividing line from the tertiary sector is disputed.

abschnitte.text: The **primary sector** obtains raw materials, for example in agriculture, forestry or mining. The **secondary sector** processes them in industry and trades, for example in a cheese dairy or a sawmill. The **tertiary sector** covers services such as retail, banking or administration. Because this sector became very large and varied, the knowledge-intensive services were separated off as a **quaternary sector** of their own.

The quaternary sector includes activities in which knowledge and information are at the centre. Typical examples are **software development**, **research**, **consulting**, data processing and high-level education. A research institute of **ETH Zurich** is a good Swiss example: it produces new knowledge. Someone who sells goods in **retail**, on the other hand, belongs more to the tertiary sector.

Knowledge-intensive firms need above all **highly qualified workers**. That is why they like to settle near **universities** and in big cities. There they find well-trained specialists and can work together with other firms and researchers. In Switzerland these are, for example, the regions of Zurich, Basel, Geneva and Lausanne.

Since the **1990s** the quaternary sector has grown especially strongly. The reason is **digitalisation**: computers, the internet and data processing created many new jobs. People therefore speak of the **knowledge society**, in which knowledge becomes the most important resource. Some models even distinguish a **quinary sector**: it covers top positions in politics, business and science, where important decisions are made.

The dividing line between the tertiary and quaternary sectors is **disputed**. Almost all services use information and computers today, including banks, retail and administration. So it is hard to say where simple service ends and knowledge work begins. Many statistics therefore still work with only three sectors.

gewusst: The word quaternary comes from the Latin quartus, which means “the fourth”.
In Switzerland the great majority of employees work in service jobs, and only a small part in agriculture.

teile.einleitung: Plate tectonics explains why the Earth’s surface is constantly changing. The Earth’s outer shell is broken into large plates that move slowly. Where they push together or drift apart, mountains, volcanoes, earthquakes and new seas are formed.
wichtigste: The solid outer shell of the Earth is made up of several large plates and many small ones.
At the Mid-Atlantic Ridge lies a divergent plate boundary, where plates move away from each other.
The San Andreas Fault in California is a transform fault, where plates slide past each other.
In a collision, the denser oceanic plate usually dives under the continental plate.
This diving down, called subduction, creates deep-sea trenches such as the Mariana Trench.
The Himalayas were formed by the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates.
The Alps were formed mainly by the collision of Africa and Europe.
The Pacific Ring of Fire is a belt of volcanoes and earthquake zones around the Pacific.

abschnitte.text: The Earth is built like a peach: a core inside, then the thick mantle and a thin skin outside. This skin, the **lithosphere**, is broken into about a dozen large plates and many small ones. The plates float on a thick, hot layer of the mantle. Driven by heat from inside the Earth, they move a few centimetres a year.

At **divergent plate boundaries** two plates move away from each other. In the middle of the Atlantic, hot rock rises there and forms the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, a mountain range under the water. New sea floor is created as this happens. In Iceland this ridge lies above the sea, which is why there are many volcanoes and fissures there.

At **convergent plate boundaries** plates move towards each other. When an oceanic plate meets a continental plate, the heavier oceanic plate dives down, which is called **subduction**. This creates deep trenches in the sea, such as the Mariana Trench, and chains of volcanoes such as in the Andes. When two continents collide, the rock is folded up into high mountains, which is how the Himalayas and the Alps were formed.

At **transform faults** two plates slide sideways past each other. The best-known example is the San Andreas Fault in California. There the plates often catch on each other and build up tension. When the tension is suddenly released, there is a strong earthquake, like the one in San Francisco in 1906.

abschnitte.titel: Hotspots and the Ring of Fire
abschnitte.text: Some volcanoes do not lie on plate boundaries but above a **hotspot**, a hot place deep in the Earth’s mantle. The Pacific Plate moves over such a hotspot, which is why the chain of islands of Hawaii formed one after another. Around the Pacific lies the **Pacific Ring of Fire**, where many subduction zones line up. There are especially many volcanoes and earthquakes there, for example in Japan, Indonesia and Chile.

The **Alps** were formed because over many millions of years the African Plate pressed northwards against Europe. Layers of rock were folded, pushed over one another and lifted high up. That is why fossilised sea creatures can be found on some Swiss mountains. There are earthquakes in Switzerland today too, and the strongest known one destroyed the city of Basel in 1356.

begriffe.erklaerung: The solid outer shell of rock of the Earth, which is broken into plates.
The diving down of one plate of the Earth under another.
The place where two plates of the Earth meet.
A particularly hot place in the Earth’s mantle, above which volcanoes form.
A break in the rock along which two parts have moved against each other.

gewusst: The pressure of the Indian Plate still lifts Mount Everest a little every year.
On the summit of Mount Everest you can find rock that was once sea floor.
In Iceland you can dive in the Silfra fissure between two continental plates.

teile.einleitung: The East African Rift is a huge fracture in the Earth's crust. Here the African Plate is slowly breaking apart. Along the rift lie deep lakes, active volcanoes and famous sites where early humans were found.
wichtigste: At the East African Rift the Nubian and the Somali plates are drifting apart.
The ground in between sinks and forms long, deep valleys.
Lake Tanganyika is about 1,470 metres deep and the second deepest lake in the world.
Lake Kivu contains large amounts of dissolved methane gas.
The volcano Ol Doinyo Lengai produces a rare, cool black lava.
In Olduvai Gorge many traces of early humans have been found.
In many millions of years a new ocean could arise here.

abschnitte.text: At the East African Rift two parts of the African Plate are moving away from each other: the **Nubian Plate** in the west and the **Somali Plate** in the east. This happens very slowly, only a few millimetres a year. The ground in between **sinks**, so long valleys with steep edges arise. The rift has an **eastern** and a **western branch**.

In the basins, long, narrow and deep lakes have formed. **Lake Tanganyika** in the western branch is about 1,470 metres deep, and only Lake Baikal in Siberia is deeper. At the southern end lies **Lake Malawi**, famous for hundreds of colourful species of **cichlids**. In **Lake Kivu** between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, **methane** and carbon dioxide are dissolved in the deep water. Rwanda gets electricity from it. In the north of Kenya lies **Lake Turkana**, the biggest permanent desert lake in the world.

Where the Earth's crust becomes thin, **magma** rises. That is why there are many volcanoes along the rift. Special is **Ol Doinyo Lengai** in Tanzania. It produces a rare **carbonatite lava** that is only about 500 to 600 degrees hot. It is black at first and turns **white** in the air.

In **Olduvai Gorge** in Tanzania, researchers, above all the **Leakey** family, found many bones and **stone tools** of early humans. Important fossils were also discovered at other places along the rift. That is why East Africa is often called the **cradle of humankind**.

Many researchers believe that if the plates keep drifting apart, **sea water** could flow into the rift in many millions of years. Then a **new ocean** would arise. The **Red Sea** arose in a similar way in the past. The east of Africa would then be separated from the rest of the continent.

gewusst: The lava of Ol Doinyo Lengai is so runny that it sometimes flows almost like water.
Lake Tanganyika is about five times as deep as Lake Geneva.

teile.einleitung: A mushroom rock is a rock with a broad head and a narrow base that looks like a mushroom. Shapes like this form mainly in deserts, where the wind hurls grains of sand against the foot of the rock. Similar-looking shapes also exist in Switzerland, but they came about in a different way.
wichtigste: Mushroom rocks have a broad cap and a narrow stem.
The wind wears away mainly the foot of the rock with sand.
Most sand grains bounce close to the ground.
A hard cap layer above softer rock favours the mushroom shape.
Salt weathering can weaken the damp foot even more.
The White Desert in Egypt is known for its mushroom rocks.
The earth pyramids of Euseigne in the Valais were formed by rain.

abschnitte.titel: Like a mushroom made of stone
abschnitte.text: A **mushroom rock** has a broad **cap** at the top and a narrow **stem** below. Often there is a hard, resistant layer of rock on top. Underneath, the rock is softer. The soft layer is worn away faster than the hard one. Over time this produces the typical mushroom shape. Mushroom rocks are one of the forms of **wind erosion**, that is, wearing away by wind.

In deserts the wind carries **grains of sand** with it. Because they are heavy, it lifts them only a little way. Most grains bounce **close to the ground**. There they act like a sandblaster and wear away the foot of the rock more than the upper part. This is called **sand abrasion** or **corrasion**. Close to the ground the rock is also often damper and richer in salt. **Salt weathering** loosens it, and the wind carries it away more easily.

Famous mushroom rocks stand in the **White Desert** in Egypt, near the oasis of Farafra. There the wind has ground white **chalk and limestone rocks** into astonishing shapes. Many look like mushrooms, others remind you of animals. Other forms of wind erosion are **yardangs**, long streamlined rock ridges, and **ventifacts**, stones with sharp edges and smooth faces, for example three-edged stones (dreikanters).

In the Valais stand the **earth pyramids of Euseigne** in the Val d’Hérens. They look similar to mushroom rocks: tall pillars with a large stone as a cap. But they were not formed by wind. **Rain** has worn away soft **moraine material** that a glacier left behind. Pillars remained standing only where large capstones protected the material.

gewusst: The road into the Val d’Hérens passes through a short tunnel right through the earth pyramids at Euseigne.
If the capstone of an earth pyramid falls off, the pillar is quickly worn away by the rain.

teile.einleitung: Ottawa is the capital of Canada. The Canadian Parliament meets here. The city is known for its canal, which becomes a skating rink in winter, and for a big tulip festival.
wichtigste: Ottawa is the capital of Canada.
The city lies in the province of Ontario, right on the border with Québec.
It lies on the Ottawa River, and opposite lies the city of Gatineau.
Queen Victoria chose Ottawa as the capital in 1857.
Until 1855 the city was called Bytown.
In winter the Rideau Canal becomes a long skating rink and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: Ottawa is the **capital** of Canada. On the hill **Parliament Hill** stands the parliament building with its tall tower. The British **Queen Victoria** chose Ottawa as the capital in 1857. The city lay between the big cities of Toronto and Montréal and so between the English-speaking and the French-speaking parts of the country. In Ottawa you hear both languages.

The city lies in the province of **Ontario** on the **Ottawa River**. There the river forms the border with the province of **Québec**. On the other side lies the city of **Gatineau**. Many people live in Gatineau and work in Ottawa. The name Ottawa comes from the **Odawa** people, who used to trade in the area.

The settlement was first called **Bytown**, after Colonel **John By**, who led the building of the **Rideau Canal**. In 1855 it was given the name Ottawa. The canal connects Ottawa with Kingston on Lake Ontario and has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since 2007. In winter it freezes over. Then it becomes a **skating rink** many kilometres long in the middle of the city, where many people go **ice skating**.

In the **Second World War** Canada helped to liberate the **Netherlands**. The Dutch royal family lived partly in Ottawa during the war. As thanks, the Netherlands has sent **tulip bulbs** to Ottawa every year since the war. In spring the city celebrates a big **tulip festival**.

gewusst: Ottawa is one of the coldest capitals in the world.
The skating rink on the Rideau Canal is almost eight kilometres long.

teile.einleitung: Nomadism is a way of life and of making a living in which people move with their herds from pasture to pasture. There are different forms, from full nomads with no fixed home to seasonal movement with herders. Today this way of life is under threat in many regions.
wichtigste: Full nomads have no fixed home.
Semi-nomads have a permanent settlement and often do some farming.
In transhumance, herders move with the herds while the owners stay in the village.
Mobile livestock keeping is well adapted to dry regions.
Settling nomads often leads to overgrazing around wells.
A dzud is an extreme winter in Mongolia.

abschnitte.text: **Full nomads** have no fixed home and travel with their herds all year round.
