With **semi-nomads**, part of the family stays in a permanent settlement with fields, while others move on with the animals for part of the year. In **transhumance**, only herders move with the herds back and forth between **summer** and **winter pastures**. The owners of the animals live permanently in the village. A related form is **alpine farming** in Switzerland.

In **dry regions** rain falls very unevenly, sometimes here, sometimes there. It is often too dry there for crop farming. Someone who moves with the herds to where **grass** is growing can still use this land. That is why **mobile livestock keeping** is regarded as a well-adapted way of making a living. After the herds have moved on, the plants have time to grow back.

The **Tuareg** live in the central Sahara and in the Sahel, for example in Niger, Mali and Algeria. Traditionally they were camel nomads, and among them the men wear an **indigo-blue veil**. The **Maasai** in Kenya and Tanzania keep mainly **cattle**. In the north of Scandinavia the **Sami** move with their **reindeer** between forest and mountains. In Mongolia many families live with horses, sheep and goats.

In Mongolia the herders fear the **dzud**, an extreme winter. Deep snow, ice or great cold then prevent the animals from finding food. In the winter of 2009/10, **millions of livestock** died in this way. Droughts, too, can hit herds hard. Many families lose their whole livelihood as a result.

Many states wanted to make nomads **settle**. When big herds stay in the same place all the time, they eat the plants faster than they can grow back. Around settlements and **wells**, **overgrazing** and bare soils result. The Maasai lost large parts of their pastures in the colonial period and through protected areas such as the **Serengeti**. Today people debate how nature conservation and herding life can fit together.

gewusst: The blue veil of the Tuareg is called a tagelmust.
The dye of the Tuareg veil sometimes rubs off on the skin, which is why they were also called “blue men”.

teile.einleitung: The Øresund is a strait between Denmark and Sweden. It connects the Baltic Sea with the Kattegat and so with the North Sea. Since 2000 a famous link of bridge and tunnel has crossed it.
wichtigste: The Øresund separates the Danish island of Zealand from southern Sweden.
It is one of the entrances from the North Sea to the Baltic Sea.
Since 2000 the Øresund Link has connected Copenhagen and Malmö.
The link consists of a bridge, an artificial island and a tunnel.
Cars and trains travel across the bridge.

abschnitte.text: The **Øresund** lies between the Danish island of **Zealand** and the Swedish region of **Scania**. Besides the Great Belt and the Little Belt, it is one of the routes from the North Sea into the **Baltic Sea**. At its narrowest point, between Helsingør and Helsingborg, it is only about 4 kilometres wide. On its shores lie the capital **Copenhagen** and the Swedish city of **Malmö**.

In **2000** the **Øresund Link** was opened. It connects Copenhagen with Malmö. One part is a long **bridge**, on which cars run on top and trains below. In the middle lies the artificial island of **Peberholm**. From there a **tunnel** leads under the sea on to Denmark. In this way the route stays clear for big ships, and Copenhagen Airport is not disturbed.

Since the link has existed, many people commute every day between Denmark and Sweden. People speak of the **Øresund Region**. In the past you needed a **ferry** to cross. Between Helsingør and Helsingborg such ferries still run today.

gewusst: The Øresund Bridge became world famous through the television series “The Bridge”.
The artificial island of Peberholm has become a habitat for many plants and birds.

teile.einleitung: In the tropical rainforest huge trees grow even though the soil is very poor. The secret is a fast nutrient cycle. Almost all the nutrients are in the living plants and are reused straight away.
wichtigste: In the rainforest most of the nutrients are stored in the living biomass.
Warmth and moisture make leaves break down very fast, so the litter layer is thin.
Mycorrhizal fungi help the trees take up nutrients directly from the litter.
This is called a short-circuited cycle because the nutrients hardly reach the soil.
If the forest is cleared, heavy rain washes the nutrients out.
In the Central European broadleaf forest, a bigger share of the nutrients is stored in the soil.

abschnitte.text: The soil in the tropical rainforest is old and heavily **leached**. It can hardly hold on to nutrients. Even so, the most species-rich forest on Earth grows here. The reason: almost all the nutrients are in the **living biomass**, that is, in trees, leaves and animals. When something dies, the substances are taken up again at once.

Because it is always warm and humid, **decomposers** such as fungi, bacteria and **termites** work very fast. They break down fallen leaves in a few weeks to months. That is why the **litter layer** is thin and hardly any **humus** forms. The nutrients that are released are ready right at the top of the soil.

Many rainforest trees live in **symbiosis** with **mycorrhizal fungi**. These fungi wrap around the fine roots and fetch nutrients directly from the decomposed litter. The trees mostly root **very shallowly**, because the nutrients lie only in the top layer. In this way hardly any substances are lost. This is called a **short-circuited cycle**, because the mineral soil plays almost no role.

If the rainforest is **cleared** over a large area, the cycle is broken. The nutrients from ash and plant remains are washed out by **heavy rain**. Fields then often give good harvests for only a few years. That is why **replanting** forest is also very difficult.

In the **Central European broadleaf forest**, for example in Switzerland, decomposition is slower. **Humus** and **clay minerals** hold many nutrients in the soil, so the soils stay fertile even after clearing. In the Amazon region there is an exception: **terra preta**. Indigenous communities enriched the soil centuries ago with charcoal, bones and waste. This dark earth is still clearly more fertile than its surroundings today.

gewusst: Terra preta means “black earth” in Portuguese.
A leaf that falls to the ground in the rainforest can be almost gone after just a few weeks.

teile.einleitung: The plantation economy is a form of agriculture with large, capital-intensive farms that usually grow a single perennial crop for export. It arose in the colonial period and still shapes many tropical countries today. Its history is closely tied to slavery.
wichtigste: The plantation economy means large farms with monoculture for export.
From the 17th century sugar cane shaped the Caribbean and was linked to the slave trade.
In 2023 Côte d’Ivoire was the world’s largest cocoa producer.
In Sri Lanka in the 19th century tea replaced coffee.
The term “banana republic” goes back to the influence of foreign fruit companies.
The Cavendish banana variety is threatened by the fungal disease TR4.
Rubber comes from the Amazon region but is now grown mainly in South-East Asia.

abschnitte.text: Plantations are **capital-intensive** large farms. That means a lot of money is needed for land, machinery and facilities. They usually grow a single **perennial crop**. The harvest is often processed on site and then **exported**. Such products are called **cash crops**, that is, farm products grown not for the farmers’ own needs but for sale. Examples are coffee, cocoa, cotton and tea.

From the 17th century, **sugar cane plantations** shaped the Caribbean. There, millions of **enslaved people** from Africa had to work in harsh conditions. Sugar was one of the most important goods in the **triangular trade** between Europe, Africa and America. Merchants and firms from Switzerland also took part in this trade, as historical research shows.

In the British colony of **Ceylon**, today’s Sri Lanka, a fungus called **coffee rust** destroyed the coffee plantations in the 19th century. The planters switched to **tea**, and Ceylon tea is still famous today. **Rubber** comes from the Amazon region. In 1876 seeds were brought to London and from there to British colonies in Asia. Today most natural rubber comes from **South-East Asia**. For cocoa, **Côte d’Ivoire** was in the lead in 2023, followed by Ghana, grown mostly by smallholders.

In the early 20th century, US companies such as the **United Fruit Company** owned huge banana plantations in Central America. They had a strong influence on governments. In 1904 the writer O. Henry coined the scornful term **“banana republic”** for this. Today the **Cavendish** variety dominates world trade. From the 1950s it replaced the Gros Michel variety, which had been wiped out by **Panama disease**.

All Cavendish plants are almost genetically identical, because they are grown from cuttings. That is why the new pathogen **TR4**, a form of Panama disease, spreads easily. This shows a basic problem of the plantation economy: a single disease can threaten whole harvests. Other criticisms are deforestation, high water use and low wages. Supporters stress jobs and export earnings.

gewusst: The Gros Michel was regarded as especially full of flavour. Some banana flavourings in sweets still recall its taste today.
The first rubber trees of South-East Asia came from seeds that were first raised in Kew Gardens near London.

teile.einleitung: The Netherlands is a small, flat country in the north-west of Europe on the North Sea. About a quarter of the country lies below sea level and is protected by dykes.
wichtigste: The Netherlands lies on the North Sea between Germany and Belgium.
About a quarter of the country lies below sea level.
Dykes, dams and pumping stations protect the country from the water.
The capital is Amsterdam, and the government sits in The Hague.
Rotterdam has the biggest port in Europe.
The Rhine flows from Switzerland to the Netherlands.

abschnitte.text: Large parts of the Netherlands were won from the sea. **Dykes** were built and the water pumped out, and in this way new land arose, a **polder**. In the past **windmills** did this, today electric **pumping stations** do. About a quarter of the country lies lower than sea level. If the sea rises because of climate change, the dykes will have to be even higher.

In 1953 a severe **storm surge** flooded large areas in the south-west, and many people died. After that the Netherlands built the **Delta Works**, a huge system of dams and storm surge barriers. Some barriers can be closed in a storm. The Dutch are now regarded as experts in hydraulic engineering all over the world.

The capital is **Amsterdam**, with its many canals, but the government sits in **The Hague**. The country is a **kingdom**. Because it is so flat, many people ride **bicycles**. Also well known are **tulips**, cheeses such as Gouda and Edam, and windmills. People often say “Holland”, but that is really only two of the provinces.

The **Rhine** rises in Switzerland and flows into the North Sea in the Netherlands. Ships travel on it from **Basel** to **Rotterdam**. Rotterdam has the biggest port in Europe. Many goods that come to Switzerland are transferred there.

gewusst: The Netherlands has more bicycles than inhabitants.
The Afsluitdijk of 1932 is over 30 kilometres long and turned a sea bay into a lake.

teile.einleitung: Pachacuti Yupanqui (in Spanish spelling Pachacútec) was a ruler of the Inca in the 15th century. Under him a small kingdom in the Andes grew into a powerful state. Machu Picchu was probably built for him.
wichtigste: Pachacuti ruled the Inca in the 15th century.
He greatly expanded the Inca Empire through conquests.
He had the capital Cusco splendidly rebuilt.
Machu Picchu probably served as his country estate.
His name means roughly “he who changes the world”.

abschnitte.titel: From a small kingdom to an empire
abschnitte.text: Before Pachacuti, the Inca ruled only an area around **Cusco** in present-day Peru. After a victory over the neighbouring people of the **Chanka**, he became ruler around 1438. After that he conquered many regions in the Andes. His son **Túpac Yupanqui** continued the conquests. In this way arose the biggest empire in America at the time, which the Inca called **Tawantinsuyu**.

Pachacuti is regarded as a great builder. He had Cusco reorganised and equipped with temples and palaces of precisely cut stones. High above the valley of the Urubamba arose **Machu Picchu**. Researchers suspect that the site was his **country estate**. Today Machu Picchu is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** and one of the most famous destinations in South America.

Pachacuti is also credited with having organised the empire better. Roads connected the parts of the land, and storehouses secured supplies. Because the Inca had no writing in the modern sense, much of what we know about him comes from **accounts** that Spanish chroniclers wrote down later. Some details are therefore uncertain.

gewusst: Machu Picchu was never found by the Spanish conquerors and became known worldwide only in 1911.
The Inca built walls so precisely that between some stones not even a knife blade fits.

teile.einleitung: Permafrost is ground that stays frozen all the time. It is found in the polar regions and in high mountains, including the Swiss Alps. Because the Earth is warming, it is thawing in many places, with consequences for the landscape, the climate and safety.
wichtigste: About a quarter of the land area of the Northern Hemisphere lies above permafrost.
In Switzerland around 5 per cent of the country’s area is affected.
Permafrost soils store about twice as much carbon as the atmosphere.
When ice-rich ground thaws, it sinks and thermokarst forms.
Rock glaciers are a visible sign of permafrost.
The PERMOS network monitors permafrost in the Swiss Alps.

abschnitte.text: About **24 per cent** of the land area of the Northern Hemisphere lies above permafrost, so roughly a quarter. There are large areas in **Siberia**, Canada, Alaska and on the **Tibetan Plateau**. In high mountains too, the ground is often permanently frozen. In **Switzerland**, according to model calculations by the Federal Office for the Environment, this affects about **5 per cent** of the country’s area. That is more than the area of all Swiss glaciers put together.

In the Alps, permafrost is found mainly in rock faces and scree slopes at high altitude. A visible sign is **rock glaciers**: tongue-shaped masses of rock debris with ice inside, which creep slowly down the valley. Many of them now move much faster than they used to. The Swiss monitoring network **PERMOS** (Permafrost Monitoring Switzerland) measures, among other things, temperatures in boreholes. Above **Pontresina** in the Engadine, large protective dams against debris flows and avalanches were built on the Schafberg in 2003.

If frozen ground contains a lot of ice, it loses its support as it thaws. The surface sags unevenly. Hollows, pools and lakes form. This kind of landscape is called **thermokarst**. The water in the hollows stores heat and speeds up the thawing even more. A well-known example is the **Batagaika crater** in Yakutia in north-eastern Siberia. It is more than a kilometre long and has been growing for decades, because its edges thaw and break off.

In the northern permafrost soils an estimated **1,400 to 1,600 gigatonnes of carbon** are stored. That is about twice as much as in today’s atmosphere. The carbon is held in old, frozen plant remains. When the ground thaws, **microbes** can turn it into **CO2 and methane**. These gases strengthen the warming, which in turn makes more permafrost thaw.

Disease-causing germs can also survive for a long time in frozen ground. In 2016 **anthrax** broke out on the **Yamal** Peninsula in Siberia. During a heatwave, an infected, frozen reindeer carcass had thawed. The spores had survived in the ground and caused an outbreak among reindeer and people.

gewusst: There is more permafrost area in Switzerland than there is glacier area in the whole country.
In Siberia only the top layer of soil thaws in summer, and below it the ground stays frozen all year round.

teile.einleitung: Polar lights are glowing bands and curtains in the night sky. They appear when tiny particles from the sun hit the air of the Earth high up. They are seen most often near the poles, and very rarely even in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Polar lights are coloured lights in the night sky.
Most polar lights glow green.
In the north they are called the northern lights, in the south the southern lights.
The particles that make them glow come from the sun.
They are best seen on dark, clear nights.
They are most common near the poles.
In May 2024 polar lights could also be seen in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: **Polar lights** are glowing bands, arcs and curtains in the night sky. They often move like a **curtain** in the wind and can change shape quickly. Most often they glow **green**. **Red** or **violet** colours are seen more rarely. Polar lights are not very bright. That is why you can only see them when the sky is **dark and clear**.

The **sun** constantly hurls tiny, electrically charged particles into space. This stream is called the **solar wind**. The Earth’s **magnetic field** steers the particles mainly into the regions around the poles. There they hit the air high up, about 100 kilometres above the ground. In doing so, they make oxygen and nitrogen glow, rather as in a fluorescent tube.

Polar lights in the north are called the **northern lights** (aurora borealis). You can see them, for example, in **Norway**, **Iceland**, Finland or **Canada**. Polar lights around the South Pole are called the **southern lights** (aurora australis). You can see them, for example, in **Antarctica** or in the south of **New Zealand**. Polar lights are most common in a ring around the poles.

During very strong **solar storms** the sun hurls especially many particles into space. Then polar lights can appear far away from the poles. In Switzerland this is rare. In **May 2024**, however, it happened: many people saw red and violet lights in the sky. With mobile phone cameras the colours were often even clearer than with the naked eye.

gewusst: Polar lights often appear at the North and South Poles at the same time, almost like a mirror image.
Other planets such as Jupiter and Saturn also have polar lights.

teile.einleitung: The Peters projection is a way of showing the round Earth on a flat world map. It shows all countries at their correct size in relation to one another. In return, the shapes of the countries look badly distorted.
wichtigste: The Peters projection is equal-area.
Regions of the same size appear the same size on it.
In return, the shapes of the countries are badly distorted.
James Gall had already described the same projection in 1855.
That is why it is often called the Gall-Peters projection.
Arno Peters made it known from 1973.

abschnitte.titel: The problem of every world map
abschnitte.text: The Earth is a sphere. If you want to put it on a flat sheet, you have to distort it. The method for doing this is called a **map projection**. No map can show areas, shapes and angles correctly all at once. The widely used **Mercator map** is **conformal** (it keeps angles true) and is handy for sailing. But it greatly enlarges regions near the poles. On it Greenland looks almost as big as Africa, although Africa is about fourteen times bigger.

abschnitte.titel: True to area instead of true to shape
abschnitte.text: The Peters projection is an **equal-area cylindrical projection**. Regions of the same size also appear the same size on it. In return, the **shapes** are badly distorted. Countries near the equator, such as those in Africa, look stretched out lengthways. Regions near the poles look squashed flat.

The German **Arno Peters** presented the map from 1973. He argued that the Mercator map enlarges Europe and North America and makes the countries of the **global South** look too small. His map was therefore spread by **development organisations** and churches. But the same projection had already been described in 1855 by the Scottish clergyman **James Gall**. Peters did not mention him. That is why people often speak of the **Gall-Peters projection**.

Many **cartographers** criticise the Peters projection because of the strong distortion of shapes. They also point out that other equal-area maps existed before it. For world maps many prefer **compromise projections**, which show neither areas nor shapes quite exactly, but show both reasonably well. One example is the **Winkel tripel projection**, which many atlases also use.

gewusst: On the Mercator map Greenland looks about as big as Africa, but in reality Africa is about fourteen times bigger.
Only a globe shows areas, shapes and angles all correctly at the same time.

teile.einleitung: Trade winds are steady winds in the tropics. All year round they blow fairly evenly from the subtropics towards the equator. In the past they were very important for sailing ships.
wichtigste: Trade winds blow between the subtropics and the equator.
They flow from the subtropical high-pressure belt to the lower pressure at the equator.
In the Northern Hemisphere the north-east trade wind blows, in the Southern Hemisphere the south-east trade wind.
The Earth's rotation deflects the winds.
In German they are called “Passat”, in English “trade winds”.
In 1492 Columbus used the trade wind for his voyage across the Atlantic.

abschnitte.text: At the **equator** the Sun heats the air strongly. The warm air rises, and so **low air pressure** arises at the ground. In the **subtropics**, by contrast, air sinks, and a **high-pressure belt** forms. Wind always blows from high to low pressure. That is why the air at the ground flows from the subtropics to the equator: this is the trade wind.

Because the Earth rotates, the trade wind does not blow straight north or south. It is deflected. In the **Northern Hemisphere** it therefore comes from the north-east and is called the **north-east trade wind**. In the **Southern Hemisphere** the deflection works the other way round, and there the **south-east trade wind** blows. Where the two trade winds meet at the equator, the air rises, and it often rains heavily.

The steady trade winds were very important for **sea trade** with sailing ships. That is why they are called **“trade winds”** in English. In 1492 **Christopher Columbus** first sailed south to the **Canary Islands** in order to reach the zone of the trade wind. From there the north-east trade wind drove him westwards across the Atlantic. For the return journey he chose a more northerly route.

At about 1 to 2 kilometres up, there is often sinking, warmed air above cooler, moister air. This temperature inversion is called the **trade wind inversion**. It acts like a lid and limits cloud formation at height. That is why **trade wind clouds** mostly stay flat. Mountains can, however, lift the moist air above the lid.

When the trade wind meets mountains, the moist sea air rises, cools and rains out. On the **Hawaiian Islands** the **windward side**, facing the wind, is therefore mostly very rainy and green. The **leeward side**, turned away, is often dry. Something similar can be seen on the Canary Islands.

gewusst: Trade winds are among the most regular winds on Earth.
Sailors called the areas of weak wind in the subtropics the “horse latitudes”.

teile.einleitung: An offshore wind farm is a group of wind turbines that stand in the sea. The wind blows more strongly and more steadily there than on land. That is why such plants produce a lot of electricity.
wichtigste: Offshore means “off the coast”.
Over the sea, no hills, trees or houses slow the wind down.
The first offshore wind farm was built in 1991 in Denmark: Vindeby.
In shallow water most turbines stand on monopiles, big steel tubes.
Floating wind turbines make wind farms possible in deep water too.
The North Sea is regarded as Europe's most important offshore wind area.

abschnitte.text: Over the sea there are no hills, trees or houses to slow the wind down. That is why it blows **more strongly** and **more steadily** there. Offshore turbines therefore usually produce more electricity than plants on land. But building and maintenance cost more, because everything has to be done with ships and salt water attacks the plants.

The most common type of foundation in shallow water is the **monopile**. This is a single big steel tube that is driven into the sea floor. It suits water depths of up to about 30 to 40 metres. Where the sea is deeper, there are **floating wind turbines**. They are fixed to the sea bed with **anchor chains**, as in the park **Hywind Scotland** since 2017.

The electricity flows ashore through **sea cables**. With long cables, alternating current causes high losses. For wind farms far out, people therefore often use **high-voltage direct current transmission**, or **HVDC** for short. For this, big transformer platforms stand out at sea.

The first offshore wind farm in the world was **Vindeby**, off the Danish island of Lolland. It went online in 1991 with eleven turbines. In Germany the test field **alpha ventus**, north of Borkum, started in 2010 with twelve big turbines. Among the biggest wind farms is **Hornsea**, off the coast of Yorkshire in England. Since 2021 **China** has had the most offshore wind power installed in the world.

In many places the **North Sea** is only 20 to 50 metres deep and has strong westerly winds. These are ideal conditions for fixed foundations. Many countries around the North Sea are building big wind farms there. During construction, people take care of sea creatures, because driving in the foundations is very loud.

gewusst: The rotors of the biggest offshore turbines have a diameter of over 200 metres.
Vindeby was taken down again in 2017 after over 25 years of operation.

teile.einleitung: The Niger Delta is the huge mouth area of the River Niger in Nigeria. Here lie big oil deposits and one of the biggest mangrove areas in Africa. Oil production has brought wealth to the country, but to the region it has also brought severe environmental damage and conflicts.
wichtigste: In 1956 oil that could be produced was first found in Nigeria at Oloibiri.
Port Harcourt is the centre of the oil industry.
Oil pollution harms above all the mangrove forests.
In gas flaring, associated gas is simply burned off.
The environmental activist Ken Saro-Wiwa was executed in 1995.
Nigeria has been a member of OPEC since 1971.

abschnitte.text: In 1956 the company Shell-BP struck oil at **Oloibiri** in the Niger Delta, and in 1958 exports began. Nigeria became one of the biggest oil producers in Africa. In **1971** the country joined **OPEC**, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries. The centre of the oil industry is the port city of **Port Harcourt**. The village of Oloibiri hardly benefited and is seen as a symbol of the unequal sharing of wealth.

The Niger Delta has one of the biggest **mangrove areas** in Africa. Mangroves are trees that grow in salty water on the coast. Spilled oil clogs their roots and kills trees, **fish** and **crabs**. Many people in the delta live from fishing and so lose their livelihood. In **gas flaring**, the natural gas that comes out during oil production is simply burned, because pipelines are missing. This pollutes the air.

In **Ogoniland** in the delta, the writer **Ken Saro-Wiwa** campaigned non-violently against the destruction of the environment. In 1995 he was executed by the military regime of the time after a disputed trial. This set off protests worldwide. In 2011 the **UN Environment Programme** (UNEP) studied Ogoniland. It estimated that a complete clean-up could take up to **30 years**.

Many people in the delta felt that they got too little of the oil wealth. From 2006 the armed group **MEND** attacked production facilities and kidnapped oil workers. Another problem is **oil bunkering**: gangs tap pipelines and steal oil. This causes leaks, fires and new environmental damage.

After two big leaks in 2008, residents of the community of **Bodo** sued Shell in London. In 2015 the company agreed on compensation of **55 million pounds** and promised to clean up the waters. Such cases show that companies can be held responsible for damage.

gewusst: The Niger Delta is one of the biggest river deltas in the world.
Mangrove forests protect coasts from storm surges and are the nursery of many species of fish.

teile.einleitung: Nairobi is the capital and biggest city of Kenya in East Africa. The city lies in the highlands and has a national park with wild animals right on its edge. Nairobi is also one of the most important UN locations.
wichtigste: Nairobi is the capital and biggest city of Kenya.
In the 2019 census Nairobi had about 4.4 million inhabitants.
The city lies at about 1,700 metres.
The name means roughly “cool water”.
Nairobi arose at the end of the 19th century as a camp during the building of the Uganda Railway.
The UN Environment Programme UNEP and UN-Habitat have their headquarters in Nairobi.

abschnitte.titel: From a camp to a big city
abschnitte.text: From 1896 the British built the **Uganda Railway** from the coast near Mombasa into the interior. At a watering place, a **camp** for the railway building arose. This small camp soon became a city. The name comes from the **Maa** language of the Maasai: “Enkare Nairobi” means roughly “cool water”. Since Kenya's independence in 1963, Nairobi has been the capital of the country.

abschnitte.titel: A mild climate in the highlands
abschnitte.text: Nairobi lies in the highlands in the south of Kenya, depending on the district at about **1,600 to 1,800 metres** above sea level. Although the city is close to the equator, the climate is therefore quite **mild**. It is rarely very hot, and the nights can be cool. In the 2019 census, Nairobi counted about **4.4 million** people. The city is an important centre for business, trade and transport in East Africa.

Right next to the city lies **Nairobi National Park**. It was the first national park in Kenya. There you can see giraffes, zebras, lions and **rhinoceroses**, and in the background stand the city's high-rises. In the park there is also a well-known **orphanage for young elephants**. There, baby elephants whose mothers have died are raised and later returned to the wild.

In Nairobi the **United Nations Environment Programme**, **UNEP** for short, has its headquarters. **UN-Habitat**, the UN organisation for cities and housing, is also based here. Alongside New York, Geneva and Vienna, Nairobi is one of the most important UN locations in the world. It is the only big UN headquarters in the Global South. Many international organisations have offices here.

gewusst: Geneva and Nairobi are both important UN locations.
Kenyan runners are among the best in the world, and many train in the highlands.

teile.einleitung: The North-South divide refers to the big differences between rich industrial countries and poorer countries. The terms North and South are meant economically here, not exactly geographically. Since the 1950s countries have argued about what a fairer world economy could look like.
wichtigste: North and South are economic, not geographical terms.
Australia and New Zealand count as part of the global North.
The term “Third World” was coined in 1952 by Alfred Sauvy.
In 1964 developing countries founded the Group of 77 in Geneva.
In 1974 the UN called for a New International Economic Order.
There are also North-South gaps within countries, for example in Italy.

abschnitte.text: Most **industrial countries** lie in the Northern Hemisphere, and many **developing countries** in the South. That is why people speak of the **global North** and **global South**. But the terms are meant economically: **Australia** and **New Zealand** lie south of the equator and still count as part of the North. The French demographer **Alfred Sauvy** coined the term **“Third World”** in 1952. He compared the poor countries with the “Third Estate” before the French Revolution.

abschnitte.titel: The countries of the South join together
abschnitte.text: In 1955, 29 states from Asia and Africa met in **Bandung** in Indonesia. They wanted to ally themselves with neither the West nor the East. In 1961 this led in Belgrade to the **Non-Aligned Movement**. In 1964, at the first world trade conference, **UNCTAD**, in **Geneva**, developing countries founded the **Group of 77**. Today it has over 130 members.

The economist **Walt Rostow** described five stages of economic growth in 1960, with a **“take-off”**. He thought all countries would go through the same stages. The **Prebisch-Singer hypothesis**, by contrast, says that raw-material prices fall over the long term relative to industrial goods. Raw-material countries then have to sell more and more to buy the same amount. Which explanation is right is disputed in science.

In 1974 the **UN General Assembly** adopted a declaration on a **New International Economic Order**. Better raw-material prices and more control over a country's own natural resources were demanded. In the 1980s and 1990s the **IMF** and the **World Bank** gave indebted countries loans only with conditions. These **structural adjustment programmes** required saving, privatising and open markets. Supporters saw them as necessary reforms, and critics thought they had in part made poverty worse.

Within countries, too, there are differences between North and South. A well-known example is the **Mezzogiorno**, the south of Italy. There incomes are lower and unemployment higher than in the industrialised north. Switzerland supports projects in countries of the South through the **SDC**.

gewusst: The Group of 77 is still called that today, although it has long had many more members.
The world trade conference UNCTAD has its seat in Geneva.

teile.einleitung: North Korea is a state in the north of the Korean Peninsula in East Asia. Since the Korean War the country has been separated from South Korea by a strictly guarded border. North Korea is ruled as a dictatorship and is heavily cut off from the world.
wichtigste: The capital of North Korea is Pyongyang.
The Korean War lasted from 1950 to 1953 and ended with an armistice.
There is still no peace treaty today.
The Demilitarized Zone separates North and South Korea.
Switzerland has helped to monitor the armistice since 1953.
The Yalu River forms a large part of the border with China.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War, Korea was divided in 1945. The Soviet Union occupied the north, and the USA the south. In 1948 two states arose: in the north the **Democratic People's Republic of Korea**, in the south the Republic of Korea. The capital of the north is **Pyongyang**. In the north the country borders **China** and for a short stretch Russia.

In 1950 the **Korean War** between north and south began. Many countries intervened: China helped the north, and the USA and other states under the UN banner helped the south. In 1953 the fighting ended with an **armistice**. A **peace treaty** was never signed. That is why officially only a ceasefire has applied to this day.

Between the two states lies the **Demilitarized Zone**, a strip about 4 kilometres wide and about 250 kilometres long. No troops may be stationed there. Even so, the border is regarded as one of the most heavily guarded in the world. In the village of **Panmunjom**, representatives of both sides meet.

Since 1953 **Switzerland**, together with **Sweden**, has been a member of the **Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission**. Swiss officers are stationed in Panmunjom. They monitor whether the armistice is being observed. Switzerland was chosen because it is regarded as a **neutral** country.

Since its founding North Korea has been ruled by the **Kim** family, first by Kim Il-sung. Since the end of 2011 Kim Jong-un has been at the top. The government controls newspapers, television and the internet, and travel abroad is hardly possible. Because of its nuclear weapons tests the UN has imposed **sanctions**. The border with China is formed mainly by the rivers **Yalu** and **Tumen**.

gewusst: The Yalu rises on Paektu Mountain, the highest mountain in Korea, and flows into the Yellow Sea.
The Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission is one of the oldest peace missions of the Swiss Army.

teile.einleitung: Nigeria is a big country in West Africa on the Gulf of Guinea. It has more inhabitants than any other country in Africa and is named after the River Niger.
wichtigste: The capital of Nigeria has been Abuja since 1991.
The biggest city is Lagos.
Nigeria has more inhabitants than any other country in Africa.
The official language is English, and there are hundreds of other languages besides.
The biggest ethnic groups are the Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo.
Oil is the most important export.

abschnitte.text: Nigeria is named after the **Niger** River, which flows through the country and into the Atlantic. In the south there are rainforest and mangroves, in the north dry savanna. The country was a **British colony** and became independent in **1960**. That is why **English** is the official language. The flag has three vertical stripes: **green, white, green**.

The biggest city is **Lagos** on the coast, one of the biggest cities in Africa. In the past Lagos was also the capital. Since **1991** **Abuja** has been the capital. It was built specially for this purpose in the middle of the country. In this way it lies between the big parts of the country and is easy for everyone to reach.

In Nigeria live over **250 ethnic groups**. The biggest are the **Hausa** in the north, the **Yoruba** in the south-west and the **Igbo** in the south-east. Hundreds of languages are spoken. In the north live mainly Muslims, in the south mainly Christians. Nigeria is a **federal state** with **36** states and a capital territory of its own, similar to Switzerland with its cantons.

Nigeria has big **oil deposits**, and oil is the most important export. People pay with the **naira**, which replaced the Nigerian pound in 1973. Very well known is the film industry **Nollywood**. A great many films are made there every year. Nigerian music, too, is popular all over the world.

gewusst: Measured by the number of films, Nollywood is one of the biggest film industries in the world.
The name Nollywood is a mix of Nigeria and Hollywood.

teile.einleitung: Orangutans are big apes with reddish-brown fur. They live in the rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra. They spend almost their whole life high up in the trees.
wichtigste: Orangutan means “forest person” in Malay.
Their fur is long and reddish-brown to orange.
Wild orangutans live only on Borneo and Sumatra.
Every evening they build a sleeping nest in a tree.
They like eating ripe fruit best.
They are the biggest mammals that live mainly in trees.

abschnitte.text: The name comes from the **Malay language**: “orang” means person and “hutan” means forest. Orangutans belong to the **great apes**, like gorillas and chimpanzees. You can easily recognise them by their long, **reddish-brown** to orange hair. Adult males often have broad **cheek pads** on their faces. They can weigh over 80 kilograms.

Orangutans are the biggest mammals that live mainly in **trees**. Their **arms** are much longer than their legs. With them they skilfully reach from branch to branch. Every evening they bend branches and leaves together into a **sleeping nest**. In it they sleep high up in the tree.

Orangutans like eating ripe **fruit** such as figs best. In addition there are leaves, bark, flowers and **insects**. They are very clever and sometimes use sticks as **tools**, for example to get at honey or seeds. Young orangutans stay with their mother for several years and learn from her which fruits are good.

Wild orangutans exist only on **Borneo** and **Sumatra** in South-East Asia. Three species are distinguished: the Bornean, the Sumatran and the **Tapanuli orangutan**, which was described only in 2017. All three are **critically endangered**. Their rainforest is being cut down, often for **oil palm** plantations. Protected areas and rescue centres try to save the animals.

gewusst: The outstretched arms of a big orangutan can reach over two metres.
When it rains, orangutans sometimes hold big leaves over their heads like an umbrella.

teile.einleitung: Puerto Rico is a tropical island in the Caribbean. It has belonged to the USA since 1898, but is not a state. Its history has been shaped by both Spanish and American influence.
wichtigste: Puerto Rico is a territory of the USA with its own government.
The capital is called San Juan.
The official languages are Spanish and English, and in everyday life people mostly speak Spanish.
Since 1917 the people of Puerto Rico have held US citizenship.
In the east lies the El Yunque rainforest.
The little coquí frog is seen as a symbol of the island.
In September 2017 Hurricane Maria devastated the island.

abschnitte.text: Puerto Rico lies east of the Dominican Republic between the Atlantic and the Caribbean Sea. The climate is warm all year round. The Spanish name means **“rich port”**. Originally this was the name of the capital, later of the whole island. The original inhabitants, the **Taíno**, called the island Borinquen. In the 2020 census about 3.3 million people lived in Puerto Rico.

Christopher Columbus reached the island in 1493. After that Puerto Rico was **Spanish** for about 400 years. In **1898**, after a war between Spain and the USA, the island passed to the **United States**. The capital **San Juan** on the north coast has a colourful old town and the mighty fortress of **El Morro** from Spanish times. People pay with the US dollar.

Puerto Rico is a **territory of the USA** with its own government and its own constitution. Since **1917** the people from there have been US citizens. As long as they live on the island, however, they may not vote in the election of the US president. There is a lot of discussion about the future: some want Puerto Rico to become a state, others want to keep the present status, and still others wish for independence. There have already been several referendums on this.

In the east of the island, in the mountains, lies the **El Yunque** rainforest. It rains very often there, and the area is a protected area of the USA. All over the island at night you can hear the **coquí**, a tiny tree frog. Its name imitates its call, “ko-kee”. The coquí is a popular symbol of Puerto Rico.

Puerto Rico lies in an area where **hurricanes** often occur. In **September 2017** **Hurricane Maria** hit the island with great force. Houses, roads and power lines were badly damaged. Almost the whole island lost power, in many places for months. The rebuilding took many years.

gewusst: The coquí frog is only about as big as a fingertip, but its call is very loud.
North of Puerto Rico, in the Atlantic, lies the deepest point of the whole Atlantic, the Puerto Rico Trench.

teile.einleitung: Physical weathering, also called mechanical weathering, breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing its chemical make-up. The causes are mainly changes in temperature, frost, salts, release of pressure and plant roots. It prepares the ground for chemical weathering.
wichtigste: In physical weathering rock breaks up, but the minerals stay the same.
Insolation weathering is caused by strong temperature swings between day and night.
It is especially effective in deserts.
Exfoliation is the flaking off of rock in curved layers after pressure is released.
Root wedging is caused by roots growing in cracks.
Broken-up rock gives chemical weathering more surface to attack.
Granite often crumbles into grus or into rounded woolsack blocks.

abschnitte.text: In **physical weathering** rock is only broken into smaller pieces. Its **minerals** stay unchanged. In **chemical weathering**, by contrast, the minerals are changed or dissolved by water and dissolved substances. The two processes often work together. Physical weathering increases the **surface** of the rock, so that chemical weathering can attack in more places.

In **deserts** the surface of the rock heats up strongly by day and cools down at night, because there are no clouds or plants. The repeated expansion and shrinking creates stresses. This **insolation weathering** makes the rock crumbly. In the Alps **frost wedging** is especially important: water seeps into cracks, freezes and expands by about nine per cent as it does so. The large **scree slopes** beneath Swiss rock faces are formed mainly in this way.

In **salt weathering**, salt crystals grow in pores and cracks and push the rock apart. A related form is **hydration weathering**. In it, certain minerals, such as some salts, build water molecules into their **crystal lattice** and expand. The pressure loosens the rock. It must be clearly distinguished from **hydrolysis**, a kind of chemical weathering.

Deep underground, rock is under great pressure. When the rock above it is worn away, the rock expands. As it does so, layers come away parallel to the surface, rather like an onion. This is called **exfoliation**. Granite also often weathers along its joints. The edges are attacked most strongly, and rounded blocks form, which are called **woolsacks**.

Plants can also break up rock. Roots grow into joints and press on the rock as they get thicker. This **root wedging** counts as physical-biological weathering. When **granite** breaks up into its separate grains of quartz, feldspar and mica, a coarse, loose debris forms. This material is called **grus**.

gewusst: The force of freezing water in a closed crack is so great that it can split even hard granite.
Well-known woolsack blocks of granite can be found, for example, in the Fichtelgebirge and the Harz in Germany.

teile.einleitung: Oceans are the huge salt-water seas between the continents. There are five oceans, and together they cover about 71 per cent of the Earth's surface. That is why the Earth is also called the “Blue Planet”.
wichtigste: The five oceans are the Pacific, the Atlantic, the Indian Ocean, the Arctic Ocean and the Southern Ocean.
The Pacific is the biggest and deepest ocean.
Between Europe and America lies the Atlantic.
The water in the ocean tastes salty.
On maps oceans are mostly shown in blue.
On average the oceans are almost 4 kilometres deep.
The oceans store a lot of heat and so influence the climate all over the world.

abschnitte.text: The **Pacific**, or Pacific Ocean, lies between Asia, Australia and America. The **Atlantic** separates Europe and Africa from America. The Indian Ocean lies between Africa, Asia and Australia. Around the North Pole lies the Arctic Ocean and around Antarctica the Southern Ocean.

The Pacific is so big that all the continents together would fit into it. In the Pacific also lies the **Mariana Trench**, the deepest place on Earth at almost 11,000 metres. If you put Mount Everest into it, its summit would still be over two kilometres under water. The smallest ocean is the Arctic Ocean.

Ocean water contains on average about 3.5 per cent **salt**. That is why you cannot drink it without first desalinating it at great expense. Most of the salt is common salt, as we use for cooking. On maps oceans are blue, and the darker the blue, the deeper the water often is.

In the oceans huge **ocean currents** flow like rivers in the sea. The **Gulf Stream** brings warm water from the Caribbean into the North Atlantic. That is why it is much milder in Western Europe than in other regions at the same latitude, for example in Canada. The oceans also take up a lot of heat and carbon dioxide and so slow global warming.

The oceans are the biggest habitat on Earth. Here lives the **blue whale**, the biggest animal that has ever lived. Coral reefs in warm seas are like colourful underwater cities full of fish. Even in the dark **deep sea** there are strange animals that can glow themselves.

The oceans suffer from plastic waste, overfishing and the warming of the water. Because water needs more space when it warms and glaciers melt, the **sea level** is slowly rising. To protect the seas, protected areas are being set up. In 2023 the UN agreed a treaty to protect the high seas.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the five great seas of the world between the continents.
A big movement of water in the sea that carries heat over long distances.
The dark part of the sea at great depth, where no sunlight reaches any more.
The average height of the sea surface, from which heights are measured.

gewusst: The seafarer Magellan called the Pacific “peaceful ocean” because he sailed it in calm weather.
Less is known about the sea floor of the deep sea than about the surface of the Moon.
The Swiss Jacques Piccard dived into the Mariana Trench in 1960 with the bathyscaphe Trieste.

teile.einleitung: The Pacific Ring of Fire is a belt about 40,000 kilometres long around the Pacific Ocean. There are especially many volcanoes and earthquakes there. The reason lies deep below the Earth's surface, at the plates.
wichtigste: The Ring of Fire lies around the Pacific Ocean.
It has roughly the shape of a horseshoe.
About three quarters of the Earth's active and dormant volcanoes lie there.
About 90 out of 100 earthquakes happen on the Ring of Fire.
There plates collide or slide under one another.
Well-known volcanoes on the Ring of Fire are Mount Fuji and Mount St. Helens.

abschnitte.text: Around the **Pacific** lie very many volcanoes like a chain. That is why people speak of the **Pacific Ring of Fire**. It runs from New Zealand via Indonesia, Japan and Alaska to the west coast of America and down to Chile. The ring is not quite closed and has roughly the shape of a **horseshoe**.

The Earth's crust consists of big **plates** that move slowly. At the Ring of Fire they collide, or one plate slides under the other. This is called **subduction**. The sinking plate partly melts at depth, and the **magma** that forms rises. This is how volcanoes arise. When the plates shift suddenly, the Earth shakes.

On the Ring of Fire lie more than half of the Earth's active volcanoes. If you also count the dormant volcanoes, it is about **three quarters**. Also about **90 per cent of all earthquakes** happen there. Strong quakes under the sea can trigger **tsunamis**, that is, huge tidal waves.

**Mount Fuji** is a volcano and, at 3,776 metres, the highest mountain in **Japan**. It has a beautiful, even cone shape. In the west of the USA lies **Mount St. Helens**. In its violent eruption in 1980 a large part of the summit slid away, and the mountain lost its top. In Chile, Indonesia and the Philippines too there are many active volcanoes.

In many countries on the Ring of Fire, millions of people live near volcanoes. Experts watch the volcanoes with measuring instruments in order to spot eruptions early. In **Japan** houses are built to withstand earthquakes, and children practise at school what to do in an earthquake. Switzerland does not lie on the Ring of Fire, but here too there are sometimes earthquakes.

gewusst: The Ring of Fire is about as long as the circumference of the Earth at the equator.
Volcanic soils on the Ring of Fire are often very fertile.

teile.einleitung: Drizzle is a very fine rain made of tiny droplets. They are smaller than half a millimetre and almost float in the air. Drizzle often falls from low, grey clouds.
wichtigste: Drizzle consists of droplets smaller than half a millimetre.
The droplets fall very slowly.
Drizzle usually falls from low, grey stratus clouds or from fog.
Despite the small drops, you can get wet in it.
Freezing drizzle can make roads slippery.

abschnitte.text: In **drizzle**, the droplets are smaller than **half a millimetre**. Normal raindrops are bigger. Because the droplets are so light, they fall very slowly. They seem almost to **float** in the air. On a puddle you hardly see any rings, but clothes gradually become damp.

Drizzle usually falls from low, grey **stratus clouds**. It can also drizzle from dense **fog**. In these clouds the air is calm, so the drops do not grow big. In Switzerland this happens, for example, in autumn and winter when high fog lies over the Plateau.

If it is below zero, drizzle can freeze immediately on impact. It is then called **freezing drizzle**. On roads, pavements and cars a thin, transparent layer of ice forms, **black ice**. Because it is hardly visible, it is especially dangerous. Weather services therefore warn about it.

gewusst: In drizzle often only a few tenths of a millimetre fall per hour, yet in a long spell of drizzle you really do get wet.

teile.einleitung: The polar night is the time when, in areas near the poles, the sun does not rise all day. It then stays dark or dim even at midday. There is no polar night in Switzerland, but there is one every winter in the north of Norway.
wichtigste: In the polar night the sun does not rise for days or months.
Polar night occurs only close to the North and South Poles.
It begins beyond the polar circles.
At the North Pole the polar night is in winter and lasts about half a year.
In Switzerland there is never a polar night.
In Tromsø the sun does not rise from the end of November to mid-January.
In the polar night you often see polar lights.

abschnitte.titel: When the sun does not rise
abschnitte.text: In the **polar night** the sun stays below the **horizon** all day. So it is dark or only dim even at midday. Polar night occurs only in the areas around the **North Pole** and the **South Pole**. More precisely: north of the northern and south of the southern **polar circle**. The closer you get to the pole, the longer it lasts.

The **Earth’s axis** is tilted. In the winter of the Northern Hemisphere, the north of the Earth is **tilted away** from the sun. That is why sunlight no longer reaches the regions in the far north. Half a year later it is the other way round, and then it is polar night in the south. At the **North Pole** the sun rises only once a year and sets once. There the polar night lasts about **half a year**.

The Norwegian city of **Tromsø** lies far north of the polar circle. From the end of November to mid-January the sun does not rise there. During this time people need far more **lamps** than usual, in houses and on streets. Animals such as the **polar bear** in the Arctic also cope with the long darkness. On clear nights green **polar lights** often dance in the sky.

Switzerland lies far away from the poles. So even in winter the sun rises **every day** here. The days in December are short, but light enough. In some deep mountain valleys, however, the sun disappears behind the mountains for weeks in winter. But that is not a real polar night, because the sun still shines above the mountains.

gewusst: The opposite of the polar night is the polar day: then in summer the sun does not set for weeks.
Even during the polar night, near the polar circle it is often dimly light around midday, because the sun is only just below the horizon.

teile.einleitung: Ecotourism is a way of travelling in which you experience nature without harming it. The income is meant to help protect nature and give the local people an income. Costa Rica in Central America is regarded as a well-known model.
wichtigste: Ecotourism means nature-friendly and responsible travel.
The term was coined by the Mexican architect Héctor Ceballos-Lascuráin in the 1980s.
In Costa Rica about a quarter of the country's area is protected.
Costa Rica is home to about 5 per cent of the Earth's biodiversity.
Since 1997 Costa Rica has paid landowners to protect forest.
The forest area rose from about a fifth to over half of the country.

abschnitte.text: In **ecotourism**, people travel to nature-rich areas to experience animals, plants and landscapes. Nature should be disturbed as little as possible. Part of the money flows into **nature conservation** and to the **local people**. The term was coined by the Mexican architect **Héctor Ceballos-Lascuráin** in the 1980s. He is regarded as the originator of the term.

Costa Rica is a small country between two oceans with many **climate and altitude zones**. Although it makes up only about 0.03 per cent of the Earth's land area, about **5 per cent of all species** occur there. About a **quarter of the country's area** is protected as national park or reserve. This rich nature is the basis for ecotourism. With the **CST certificate**, the tourism institute rates how sustainably hotels and travel providers work. This is meant to make **greenwashing** harder, that is, false environmental promises.

In the past, much forest in Costa Rica was cut down for pasture. In the 1980s only about a fifth of the country was still forested. Since 1997 the programme **“Pago por Servicios Ambientales”** (payment for environmental services) has paid landowners to protect forest or plant new forest. It is financed, among other things, by a **fuel tax**. Today over half of the country is covered with forest again. Ecotourism too created an incentive to preserve the forest.

In the **Monteverde** reserve grows a **cloud forest**. Clouds drift almost constantly through the mountain forest and bring moisture. Visitors come for orchids, the colourful **quetzal** bird and the suspension bridges. In **Tortuguero** National Park on the Caribbean coast, tourists watch **sea turtles**, which come onto the beach at night and lay eggs. The tours are strictly regulated so that the animals are not disturbed.

gewusst: Tortuguero means roughly “place of the turtles”.
Costa Rica abolished its army in 1948.

teile.einleitung: Puerto Williams is a small settlement in the far south of Chile. It lies on Navarino Island on the Beagle Channel, not far from the famous Cape Horn. Puerto Williams disputes with the Argentine city of Ushuaia the title of the southernmost city in the world.
wichtigste: Puerto Williams lies on Navarino Island in Chile.
The settlement lies on the Beagle Channel, south of Ushuaia.
Because it is much smaller than Ushuaia, it is disputed whether it counts as a city.
It arose in the 1950s as a base of the Chilean navy.
In the area the Yaghan once lived, an indigenous people of seafarers.

abschnitte.titel: At the end of the world
abschnitte.text: Puerto Williams lies on the north coast of the island of **Navarino** in the far south of Chile. Opposite, on the other side of the **Beagle Channel**, lies Tierra del Fuego. The Argentine city of **Ushuaia** lies a little further north. The climate is cool, windy and damp, and even in summer it is rarely really warm. Around the settlement there are forests, mountains and a lot of untouched nature.

Ushuaia likes to call itself the southernmost city in the world. But Puerto Williams lies even further south. However, Puerto Williams is only a small settlement with a few thousand inhabitants. That is why it is **disputed** whether it can be called a city. Chile and Argentina, understandably, see the question differently.

Puerto Williams arose in the 1950s as a base of the **Chilean navy**. Today walkers and sailors also come here, for example on their way to **Cape Horn** or to Antarctica. Long before the settlement existed, the **Yaghan** lived here. They travelled through the channels in canoes and lived from fishing. Near Puerto Williams, descendants of the Yaghan still live today.

gewusst: The Beagle Channel is named after the ship Beagle, on which the scientist Charles Darwin also travelled.
From Puerto Williams it is not far to Cape Horn, the famous southern tip of South America.

teile.einleitung: Oruro is a city in the highlands of Bolivia. It lies on the Altiplano, a high plain in the Andes. It is world famous for its colourful carnival.
wichtigste: Oruro lies on the Bolivian Altiplano, about 3,700 metres above sea level.
The city grew big through mining, above all of silver and tin.
The carnival of Oruro combines Catholic festivals with Andean traditions.
Well known is the devil dance, the Diablada.
In 2001 UNESCO recognised the carnival as intangible cultural heritage.

abschnitte.text: Oruro lies on the **Altiplano**, a wide high plain in the **Andes**. The city is about 3,700 metres above sea level, much higher than any place in Switzerland. The air is thin, and the nights are cold. The city was founded at the start of the 17th century by the Spanish. It grew big through **mining**, above all of **silver** and later **tin**.

Every year before Lent, Oruro celebrates a huge **carnival**. Thousands of dancers move through the city in splendid costumes and masks. The festival combines **Catholic** celebrations with old **Andean traditions**. It is dedicated to the Virgin of the Mine, the **Virgen del Socavón**, the patron saint of miners.

The best-known dance is the **Diablada**, the devil dance. The dancers wear big, colourful devil masks with horns. The dance tells of the fight between good and evil. In 2001 **UNESCO** recognised the carnival of Oruro as a masterpiece of the **intangible cultural heritage** of humanity.

gewusst: The masks of the Diablada are made by hand in Oruro and are often very heavy.
Intangible cultural heritage means customs, dances and knowledge, that is, things you cannot touch.

teile.einleitung: The Okavango Delta in Botswana is an inland delta: the Okavango River ends here without reaching the sea. Geology, termites and plants shape a unique landscape of channels, islands and floodplains. In 2014 it was entered as the 1,000th UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wichtigste: The Okavango rises in the highlands of Angola, where it is called the Cubango.
The delta lies in a basin bounded by tectonic fault lines.
In the narrow Panhandle the river still flows in a tight valley.
Many islands arose from termite mounds.
Salts build up under the islands, which is why the channels stay fresh.
The Moremi Game Reserve protects a large part of the eastern delta.
The town of Maun is regarded as the gateway to the delta.

abschnitte.titel: From the Cubango to the delta
abschnitte.text: The river rises in the **highlands of Angola** and is called the **Cubango** there. Only at the border with **Namibia** does it bear the name Okavango. In Botswana it first flows in the **Panhandle**, literally “handle of a pan”. There it is squeezed into a narrow valley between two fault lines. After that it fans out into the actual **delta**.

The delta lies in a **basin** bounded by **faults**. These fault lines are regarded as south-western offshoots of the **East African Rift system**. Here the Earth's crust is slowly beginning to break apart. The town of **Maun** on the south-eastern edge also lies on such a fault line, which bounds the delta.

Many of the countless islands begin as **termite mounds**. Termites build their mounds above the water level. Trees grow on them, sand collects, and the island gets bigger over time. Trees at the edge of the island draw up **groundwater** and evaporate it. The dissolved **salts** stay behind in the middle of the island. There bare salt crusts form, while the channels stay **fresh**.

The **Moremi Game Reserve** protects a large part of the eastern delta. It was one of the first protected areas set up by the local people themselves. It is known for elephants, lions and **African wild dogs**. Very common is the **red lechwe**. With long hind legs and splayed hooves it runs well in shallow water and flees there when in danger.

**Maun** is the most important starting point for trips into the delta. From its airport many **light aircraft** fly to the camps in the middle of the wetland. There are hardly any roads in the delta. Tourism is an important source of income for Botswana. In 2014 UNESCO added the delta as the **1,000th World Heritage Site**.

gewusst: The water of the Okavango is so clear that you can often see right to the bottom in the channels.
Without the termites there would be far fewer islands in the delta.

teile.einleitung: Every river has a beginning and an end. It starts at the **source** and ends at the **mouth**, where it flows into another river, a lake or the sea. In between it changes a great deal.
wichtigste: A river is divided into an upper course, a middle course and a lower course.
In the upper course near the source it usually flows steeply and fast.
The left and right bank are always determined looking in the direction of flow.
The Vorderrhein flows out of Lake Toma near the Oberalp Pass.
The Brigach and the Breg form the Danube at Donaueschingen.
At Passau the Inn flows into the Danube.
At Koblenz in Aargau the Aare carries more water than the Rhine.

abschnitte.text: Near the source lies the **upper course**. There the gradient is steep and the water fast. It wears away a lot of rock and often cuts narrow, deep valleys. In the **middle course** the gradient becomes smaller, and the river becomes wider and calmer. In the **lower course** it flows slowly through flat country. There it deposits a lot of sand and mud and often forms wide loops, the **meanders**.

Which bank is the left one and which the right? You always look **in the direction of flow**, that is, downstream. What lies on the left then is the **left bank**. This makes the term clear everywhere in the world. In Basel, for example, Greater Basel lies on the left bank and Lesser Basel on the right bank of the Rhine.

**Lake Toma**, in Romansh Lai da Tuma, lies near the **Oberalp Pass** at over 2,300 metres. It is regarded as the source of the **Vorderrhein** and so of the Rhine. The **Danube** begins at **Donaueschingen** in Germany, where the two Black Forest streams **Brigach and Breg** flow together. A German saying goes: “Brigach und Breg bringen die Donau zuweg”, which means “Brigach and Breg make the Danube”.

The **Inn** rises in the Engadine and flows through the Tyrol and Bavaria. At **Passau**, the city of three rivers, it flows into the Danube. At **Koblenz** in the canton of Aargau the **Aare** flows into the Rhine. The special thing is that there the Aare carries on average **more water** than the Rhine, about 485 compared with 440 cubic metres per second. Even so, the river carries on afterwards under the name Rhine.

When a river flows into the sea, it can take different forms. In a **delta** it splits into many arms and deposits sand and mud. Well-known examples are the Nile Delta and the Camargue on the Rhone. In an **estuary** the river becomes wider and wider towards the sea, as with the Elbe. The Rhine flows into the **North Sea** in the Netherlands.

gewusst: At its mouth in Passau the Inn is often wider and carries more water than the Danube.
The Danube flows through more countries than any other river in the world.

teile.einleitung: New Zealand is an island state in the south-west of the Pacific Ocean. The country is known for its mountains, volcanoes and sheep, for the kiwi bird and for the culture of the Māori.
wichtigste: New Zealand consists mainly of the North Island and the South Island.
The capital is Wellington, the biggest city Auckland.
The Indigenous people are called Māori, and their language is an official language.
The kiwi is a bird that cannot fly, and is the national emblem.
In 1893 women in New Zealand were the first in the world to vote nationwide.
The highest mountain is Aoraki, also called Mount Cook.

abschnitte.text: New Zealand consists mainly of the **North Island** and the **South Island** as well as many smaller islands. On the South Island lie the **Southern Alps**. As in Switzerland, there are high mountains and glaciers there. The highest mountain is **Aoraki**, in English **Mount Cook**, at about 3,700 metres. The North Island has many volcanoes and hot springs.

The **Māori** came to New Zealand about 700 years ago in big boats from Polynesia. They call the country **Aotearoa**. Their language is today an **official language**. Well known is the **haka**, a dance with stamping, loud shouting and sticking out the tongue. The rugby team the **All Blacks** performs it before every match.

In 1840 Britain and Māori chiefs concluded the **Treaty of Waitangi**. It is regarded as the founding document of New Zealand, which is why **6 February** is the national holiday. New Zealand was a British colony and later became independent. In 1893 women here were the first in the world to **vote** nationwide. In Switzerland this was possible at federal level only in 1971.

The national emblem is the **kiwi**, a small bird that cannot fly. New Zealanders like to call themselves **“Kiwis”**. About 5.3 million people live in the country (2024), but over 20 million **sheep**. Sheep farming is very important, along with dairy farming and tourism. The biggest city is **Auckland**, where about a third of the population lives.

gewusst: Before humans arrived, no mammals except bats lived on land in New Zealand.
The films of “The Lord of the Rings” were shot in the landscapes of New Zealand.

teile.einleitung: Neodymium is a shiny, silvery metal and belongs to the rare earths. It is very important for technology because the strongest permanent magnets in the world are made from it.
wichtigste: Neodymium is a chemical element with the symbol Nd.
It belongs to the rare earth metals.
Very strong magnets are made from neodymium, iron and boron.
These magnets are found in electric motors, wind turbines and headphones.
Most of the rare earths are mined and processed in China.

abschnitte.text: Neodymium has the chemical symbol **Nd** and the atomic number 60. It is one of the **lanthanides**, a group of metals that are also called the **rare earths**. They are not really that rare, but they usually occur only scattered and mixed. That is why it is costly to extract them from rock. Pure neodymium tarnishes quickly in air and has to be protected.

If you mix neodymium with **iron** and **boron**, **neodymium magnets** result. They are the strongest permanent magnets there are. Even a small magnet can hold a lot of weight. That is why they are built into the **electric motors** of electric cars, **wind turbines**, loudspeakers and **headphones**. Because they are so strong, they can pinch fingers, so you have to handle them carefully.

For the energy transition, many electric motors and generators are needed, and so a lot of neodymium. Most of the rare earths are now mined and processed in **China**. Many countries therefore want to be less dependent and are looking for deposits of their own. Mining often causes environmental problems, such as toxic wastewater. That is why research is also being done on **reusing** neodymium from old devices.

gewusst: The name neodymium comes from Greek and means roughly “new twin”.
Neodymium was discovered in 1885 by the Austrian chemist Carl Auer von Welsbach.

teile.einleitung: North America is a continent in the Northern Hemisphere between the Atlantic and the Pacific. It includes Canada, the USA, Mexico, the countries of Central America and the islands of the Caribbean.
wichtigste: The biggest countries of North America are Canada, the USA and Mexico.
Canada is the biggest country in North America and the second biggest in the world.
Mexico borders the USA in the south.
Greenland counts geographically as part of North America, but politically belongs to Denmark.
The islands of the Caribbean, such as Cuba, also belong to North America.

abschnitte.text: The three biggest countries are **Canada**, the **USA** and **Mexico**. **Canada** lies right in the north and is the biggest country in North America and the second biggest in the world. The **USA**, the United States of America, lie in the middle. **Mexico** borders the USA in the south. Further south follow the smaller countries of **Central America** such as Guatemala, Costa Rica and Panama.

abschnitte.titel: Islands in the north and south
abschnitte.text: The huge island of **Greenland** lies geographically with North America. Politically, though, it belongs to the Kingdom of **Denmark**. In the south lie the islands of the **Caribbean**, for example **Cuba**, Jamaica and the Bahamas. They too count geographically as part of North America. It is warm there all year round.

In the west high mountain ranges such as the **Rocky Mountains** stretch from Canada into the USA. The highest mountain is **Denali** in Alaska, at over 6,000 metres. In the east lie the **Great Lakes**, and the long **Mississippi** flows into the Gulf of Mexico. In the north there is icy **tundra**, in the south deserts and rainforests.

In North America lie huge cities such as **New York**, Mexico City, Los Angeles and Toronto. For a long time only **Indigenous peoples** lived here. From about 1500 Europeans came and founded colonies. That is why today mainly **English**, **Spanish** and **French** are spoken. In Canada, English and French are official languages.

gewusst: Panama is the southernmost country of North America, and after it South America begins.
Lake Superior, between Canada and the USA, is the biggest freshwater lake on Earth by area.

teile.einleitung: The Persian Gulf is a marginal sea of the Indian Ocean between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula. On its coasts lie some of the largest oil deposits in the world. That is why it is very important for the world economy.
wichtigste: As a marginal sea, the Persian Gulf belongs to the Indian Ocean.
The Strait of Hormuz connects it with the Gulf of Oman.
Iran lies along the whole northern shore, Arab states along the southern shore.
Bahrain is an island state in the Gulf, Qatar a peninsula.
Before oil, many people lived from pearl fishing.
Ghawar in Saudi Arabia is the largest conventional oil field in the world.

abschnitte.text: The Persian Gulf is linked to the **Indian Ocean** by the **Gulf of Oman** and the Arabian Sea. **Iran** owns the whole of the northern coast. On the southern shore lie Arab states such as Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. **Bahrain** is an island state off the coast of Saudi Arabia with the capital Manama. **Qatar** juts into the Gulf as a small peninsula, and its capital is Doha.

The Gulf is connected to the open sea only by a narrow channel: the **Strait of Hormuz**. At its narrowest point it is only about 40 kilometres wide. Many **oil tankers** pass through here, which is why it is one of the most important shipping routes in the world. Saudi Arabia has built an **east-west pipeline** to the port of **Yanbu** on the Red Sea. This means part of the oil can still be exported even if the sea route through the Gulf is blocked.

Before oil was found, many people on the Gulf lived from **pearl fishing**. Divers brought up oysters with pearls from the sea bed. Cultured pearls and oil later replaced this trade. In 1908, at **Masjed Soleyman** in Persia, today’s Iran, the first commercially important oil in the Middle East was found. From this grew the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, the forerunner of **BP**.

On the Gulf lie some of the largest oil deposits on Earth. The **Ghawar field** in eastern Saudi Arabia is the largest conventional oil field in the world and about 280 kilometres long. In the **United Arab Emirates**, about 95 per cent of the oil reserves lie in the emirate of **Abu Dhabi**. **Dubai** produced comparatively little oil and turned early to trade, tourism and finance.

The name “Persian Gulf” comes from Persia, the old name of Iran. In Arab countries the name **“Arabian Gulf”** is often used. There has long been a dispute between the neighbouring countries over the correct name. In English “Persian Gulf” is the usual name.

gewusst: The Persian Gulf is quite shallow, less than 50 metres deep in many places.
The water in the Gulf is especially salty, because a lot of water evaporates in the heat.

teile.einleitung: Myanmar, formerly called Burma, is a country in Southeast Asia. It is the biggest country on the Southeast Asian mainland. It is known for golden pagodas, thousands of temples and a long Buddhist tradition.
wichtigste: Myanmar covers about 677,000 square kilometres.
The biggest city is Yangon, formerly Rangoon.
The Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon is the most important Buddhist shrine.
The most important river is the Irrawaddy.
Until 1948 Myanmar was a British colony.
In Bagan there are over 2,000 temples and pagodas.

abschnitte.text: Myanmar lies between India, China, Thailand, Laos and Bangladesh. At about **677,000 square kilometres**, it is bigger than Thailand or Vietnam. The most important river is the **Irrawaddy**. It flows from north to south through almost the whole country and empties into the **Andaman Sea** in a big delta. A lot of rice is grown in the delta. Since 2005, **Naypyidaw** has been the capital.

**Yangon**, formerly Rangoon, is the biggest city and the economic centre of Myanmar. Until 2005 it was also the capital. Its landmark is the **Shwedagon Pagoda**, which is covered in gold. **Mandalay** was founded in 1857 and was the last royal city until 1885, before the British conquered the whole country. Today it is the second biggest city.

Most people in Myanmar are **Buddhists**. Everywhere in the country there are pagodas and monasteries, and many boys live for a time as monks. Especially famous is the old royal city of **Bagan**. On its plain stand over 2,000 temples and pagodas from the 11th to 13th centuries. Bagan is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

In the 19th century **Britain** conquered the country in several wars. Myanmar was for a long time part of British India and afterwards a British colony of its own. In **1948** it became independent. After that the military ruled for many decades. The politician Aung San Suu Kyi received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1991 for her work for democracy. In 2021 the military seized power again, and since then there have been serious conflicts in the country.

Many people smear **thanaka** on their faces, a yellowish paste. It is made by rubbing the bark of the thanaka tree with a little water on a stone. The paste cools and protects against the Sun. On **Lake Inle**, the fishermen row in a special way: they stand on one leg at the end of the boat and row with the other leg. This leaves their hands free for the net and the trap.

gewusst: Very many different ethnic groups with their own languages live in Myanmar.
In 1989 the country changed its official English name from Burma to Myanmar.

teile.einleitung: The Nile Delta is the mouth area of the Nile in Egypt. North of Cairo the river splits and flows through fertile, flat land into the Mediterranean. Its triangular shape gave all river deltas their name.
wichtigste: The Nile Delta begins north of Cairo and reaches to the Mediterranean.
The two main arms are called Rosetta and Damietta.
Alexandria lies on the western edge of the delta.
The Rosetta Stone helped to decipher the hieroglyphs.
Since the Aswan High Dam was built, hardly any mud reaches the sea.
The rising sea level threatens the flat delta.

abschnitte.text: North of **Cairo** the **Nile** splits into several arms. Today there are two main arms: the western one flows into the **Mediterranean** at **Rosetta**, the eastern one at **Damietta**. In between lies flat, fan-shaped land. The Greek historian **Herodotus** is said to have compared it with the capital letter **delta** (Δ). Since then such river mouths have been called deltas.

In the past the Nile flooded the land every year and brought fertile **mud**. That is why the soil in the delta is very good for farming.
