Since the 19th century a lot of **cotton** has been grown here. **Egyptian cotton** has especially long fibres and is regarded as very high quality. A large part of the population of Egypt lives in the delta.

At Rosetta, French soldiers found a special stone in 1799. On the **Rosetta Stone** the same text is written in three scripts: in **hieroglyphs**, in Demotic script and in **Greek**. Because Greek could be read, the text could be compared. In 1822 **Jean-François Champollion** succeeded in deciphering the hieroglyphs with it. Today the stone stands in the British Museum in London.

On the western edge of the delta lies **Alexandria**. The city was founded by **Alexander the Great**. In antiquity it was famous for its lighthouse and a great library. Today it is the second biggest city in Egypt and an important port.

Since the **Aswan High Dam** was built, the mud stays behind in the reservoir. Without new mud, the sea wears away the coast in many places. On top of that comes **climate change**: large parts of the delta lie only a few metres above the sea. If the **sea level** rises, floods and salty groundwater in the fields threaten.

gewusst: In the past the Nile had seven arms in the delta, and today only two big ones are left.
From space you can clearly see the green Nile Delta in the yellow desert.

teile.einleitung: Papua New Guinea is a country in the Pacific, north of Australia. It lies on the eastern half of the island of New Guinea and on many smaller islands. No other country in the world has so many languages.
wichtigste: Papua New Guinea lies in the east of the island of New Guinea.
The west of the island belongs to Indonesia.
After Greenland, New Guinea is the second biggest island in the world.
Over 800 languages are spoken in the country.
The capital is Port Moresby.
In 1975 the country became independent from Australia.

abschnitte.text: **New Guinea** is the second biggest island in the world, and only **Greenland** is bigger. The island is divided: the east is **Papua New Guinea**, the west belongs to **Indonesia**. The country also includes many smaller islands. The capital **Port Moresby** lies on the south coast and is the biggest city.

In Papua New Guinea **over 800 languages** are spoken, more than in any other country. By comparison: Switzerland has four national languages. So that people with different mother tongues can understand each other, there is **Tok Pisin**. This is a **creole language** that contains many words from English. English is also used.

Large parts of the country are covered with dense tropical **rainforest**. In the interior lies a **highland** with steep mountains. The highest mountain is **Mount Wilhelm**, at about 4,509 metres. Because the terrain is so difficult, many communities lived separately from each other for a long time. That is one reason for the large number of languages.

On the flag of Papua New Guinea you can see a yellow **bird of paradise**. These birds have splendid, long feathers and live in the forests of the country. The flag is divided diagonally: one part is red with the bird, the other black with the stars of the **Southern Cross**.

Before independence the territory was administered by **Australia**. On **16 September 1975** Papua New Guinea became an independent state. Today it belongs to the **Commonwealth**. Many people live in the countryside, grow vegetables and keep pigs.

gewusst: About one in ten of the world's languages is spoken in Papua New Guinea.
Switzerland is more than ten times smaller than Papua New Guinea.

teile.einleitung: The Niger is a big river in West Africa and the third longest river in Africa. It makes a great bend to the edge of the Sahara before it flows into the Atlantic.
wichtigste: The Niger is about 4,180 kilometres long.
Only the Nile and the Congo are longer in Africa.
It rises in the highlands of Guinea.
At first it flows away from the sea into the interior.
In Mali it forms a big inland delta.
It flows into the Gulf of Guinea in Nigeria.

abschnitte.text: The Niger rises in the **highlands of Guinea** near the border with Sierra Leone. The source lies only about 240 kilometres from the **Atlantic**. Even so, the river first flows **north-east**, towards the Sahara. Only then does it make a great bend to the south. In all it is about **4,180 kilometres** long and so the **third longest** river in Africa.

In the middle of **Mali** the Niger branches into many arms and lakes. This area is called an **inland delta** because it does not lie on the sea. In the rainy season it is flooded over a wide area. It is important for **fishermen**, **farmers** and herders. In winter many **migratory birds** from Europe also rest here. Nearby lies the old trading city of **Timbuktu**.

abschnitte.titel: Cities and countries on the Niger
abschnitte.text: The Niger flows through **Guinea**, **Mali**, **Niger** and **Nigeria** and for a stretch forms the border with Benin. **Bamako**, the capital of Mali, lies on both banks of the river. **Niamey**, the capital of the state of Niger, also lies on the river. Two countries are even named after it. For many people the river is the most important source of water in a dry region.

The biggest tributary is the **Benue**. It comes from Cameroon and joins the Niger in Nigeria. After that the Niger forms the big **Niger Delta**. There it flows into the **Gulf of Guinea**, a part of the Atlantic. In the delta there are mangrove forests and big oil deposits.

For a long time Europeans did not know where the Niger flows. The Scottish explorer **Mungo Park** reached it in 1796 at **Ségou** in present-day Mali. He established that the river flows **east**. Where it flows into the sea, explorers found out only a few decades later.

gewusst: The Niger flows through the Sahel, where it does not rain for months.
Because the river makes such a great bend, this part is often called the “Niger Bend”.

teile.einleitung: During the last Ice Age, huge ice sheets lay on North America and northern Europe. Their enormous weight pressed the Earth’s crust downwards. Since the ice melted, the land has been slowly rising again: this is called **post-glacial uplift**.
wichtigste: Post-glacial means “after the Ice Age”.
Thick ice sheets pressed the Earth’s crust down during the Ice Age.
Since the ice has gone, the crust has been springing back very slowly.
Around Hudson Bay in Canada the land is still rising today.
In Scandinavia too, for example on the Gulf of Bothnia, the land rises a little every year.
That is why old shorelines now lie far above the sea.

abschnitte.text: In the last Ice Age large parts of Canada and Scandinavia were buried under ice. In some places the ice sheet was several kilometres thick. This enormous weight pressed the **Earth’s crust** into the thick, slow-flowing mantle below. You can picture it like a board floating on water that is pushed down by a heavy stone.

When the ice melted about 10,000 to 20,000 years ago, the load was gone. The Earth’s crust began to rise again. Because the mantle is very thick and slow, this happens extremely slowly and takes many thousands of years. Experts call this striving for balance **isostasy**. Around **Hudson Bay** and on the **Gulf of Bothnia** between Sweden and Finland, the land still rises today by up to about one centimetre a year.

Because of the uplift, old **shorelines** now lie far above sea level. On the coast of Sweden, the **High Coast** (Höga Kusten), you can find former shores almost 300 metres above today’s sea. This landscape is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In some places harbours that used to lie on the water are now cut off from the sea, and new islands are rising out of the sea.

gewusst: In Finland and Sweden the land grows because of the uplift: year after year new land is added from the sea.
In the Alps too, researchers explain part of the uplift by the melting of the great glaciers of the Ice Age.

teile.einleitung: Why do people leave their homeland and move to another country? Migration research distinguishes **push factors**, which drive people away, and **pull factors**, which draw them to a new place. There are various theories about this.
wichtigste: Push factors drive people out of the region they come from.
Pull factors draw people to a destination, for example a shortage of workers.
Ernst Georg Ravenstein published the “Laws of Migration” in 1885.
Everett S. Lee added intervening obstacles in 1966.
Neoclassical theory puts differences in wages at the centre.
In chain migration, people who have already emigrated help those who follow.
In 1948 Switzerland concluded an agreement with Italy to recruit workers.

abschnitte.text: **Push** means to shove, and **pull** means to draw. Typical push factors are war, persecution, poverty, unemployment or natural disasters. Pull factors are attractive conditions at the destination, for example job vacancies, higher wages, safety or good schools. If a country is short of workers, that is a classic pull factor.

The German-born geographer **Ernst Georg Ravenstein** published the “Laws of Migration” in **1885**. He derived them from British censuses. They are seen as the starting point of modern migration research. **Everett S. Lee** developed the model further in **1966**. He stressed that between origin and destination lie **intervening obstacles**, such as distance, cost or immigration laws. Personal factors such as age or family also play a part.

The **neoclassical theory of migration** sees **wage differences** as the most important cause: workers move from regions with low wages to regions with high wages. The **dual labour market theory** of Michael Piore (1979) stresses that rich countries permanently need workers for insecure, poorly paid jobs. The **new economics of labour migration**, put forward by Oded Stark among others, sees migration as a strategy of whole households: a family member who has emigrated insures the family against risks.

Many people move to where relatives or acquaintances already live. These help with information, housing and work. This is called **chain migration**. In this way communities from the same region of origin form at the destination. The thesis of the **migration hump** says: when incomes begin to rise in poor countries, emigration at first increases, because more people can afford the journey. Only at higher prosperity does it fall again.

After the Second World War the Swiss economy needed many workers. In **1948** Switzerland concluded an **agreement with Italy** on recruiting workers. Many Italians afterwards worked in construction, in factories and in hotels and restaurants. In **1961** a similar agreement followed with **Spain**. Here push factors such as unemployment in the country of origin and pull factors such as job vacancies in Switzerland worked together.

gewusst: Ravenstein’s laws of 1885 are still cited in migration research today.
Many Italians who came as workers stayed in Switzerland, and their descendants still shape the country today.

teile.einleitung: The prime meridian is an imaginary line from the North Pole to the South Pole. From it, geographic longitude is counted east and west. It runs through the observatory at Greenwich near London.
wichtigste: The prime meridian has the geographic longitude 0 degrees.
It runs through the Royal Observatory in Greenwich.
In 1884 it was set at an international conference in Washington.
In Europe it runs through Great Britain, France and Spain.
In Africa it crosses, among others, Algeria, Mali, Burkina Faso, Togo and Ghana.
After that it leads across the South Atlantic to Antarctica and the South Pole.

abschnitte.text: A **meridian** is a line on the globe that runs from the North Pole to the South Pole. All places on a meridian have the same **geographic longitude**. To be able to count longitude, you need a starting point: the **prime meridian**. From there you count up to 180 degrees east and up to 180 degrees west. Switzerland lies east of it, at roughly 6 to 10 degrees east longitude.

The prime meridian runs through the **Royal Observatory** in Greenwich near London. A line in the ground marks it there, and visitors like to stand with one foot on each side. In 1884, at the **International Meridian Conference** in Washington, representatives of 25 states chose Greenwich as the starting point. Many sea charts were already using Greenwich at that time.

Not all countries followed at once. **France** counted longitude for a long time from the meridian through the **Paris Observatory**. Only in 1911 did it switch its legal time to Greenwich, and shipping followed in 1914. Other countries, too, used to have prime meridians of their own through their capitals.

From England the prime meridian runs across the **English Channel** through western France and eastern Spain into the **Mediterranean**. In Africa it crosses **Algeria, Mali, Burkina Faso, Togo** and **Ghana**. Then it goes across the South Atlantic to **Antarctica**. On the other side of the Earth lies the 180th meridian, which the **International Date Line** roughly follows.

Modern satellite systems such as **GPS** use the **IERS Reference Meridian**. In Greenwich it lies about 100 metres east of the historic line. Anyone standing on the old line with a phone therefore does not see exactly 0 degrees. The reason is more precise measurements of the Earth's shape.

gewusst: The prime meridian and the equator cross in the Gulf of Guinea, in the middle of the sea.
World time was also named after Greenwich: GMT stands for Greenwich Mean Time.

teile.einleitung: The polar zone is the coldest climate zone on Earth. It begins roughly at the polar circles and reaches to the poles. There are two of them: in the far north around the Arctic and in the south around the Antarctic.
wichtigste: The polar zone begins roughly at the polar circles, at about 66.5 degrees latitude.
It is the coldest climate zone on Earth.
There is a northern and a southern polar zone.
The sun stands low there, so it gives little warmth.
There is polar night in winter and polar day in summer.
Plants grow very little, and trees are mostly missing altogether.

abschnitte.text: The Earth is divided into several **climate zones**, for example the tropics, the subtropics, the temperate zone and the **polar zone**. The polar zone begins roughly at the **polar circles**, which lie at about **66.5 degrees** latitude. Beyond them it is cold almost all year round. In the north the Arctic with Greenland and northern parts of Canada, Russia and Scandinavia belong to it, in the south the Antarctic.

In the polar zone sunlight hits the Earth at a very **slanting angle** and so gives little warmth. Snow and ice also reflect a lot of light. In winter there is the **polar night**, when the sun does not rise for a long time. In summer there is the **polar day**, when it does not set for a long time. Despite all the light, it stays cool even in summer.

Near the edge of the polar zone the **tundra** grows. There are mosses, lichens, grasses and dwarf shrubs, but hardly any trees. The ground is often frozen deep down, which is called **permafrost**. Closer to the poles comes the **ice desert**, where almost nothing grows. At great heights in the high Alps of Switzerland there is also a similarly harsh climate, although they do not lie in the polar zone.

gewusst: Despite all the ice, very little precipitation falls in large parts of the polar zone. Some areas are as dry as deserts.
In the tundra many small flowers bloom all at once in the short summer.

teile.einleitung: The rock city of Petra lies in the south of Jordan, in a valley near the town of Wadi Musa. It has a long and exciting history: from the Nabataeans through a severe earthquake to the Bedouins, who were still living in its caves only a few decades ago.
wichtigste: At the entrance to Petra lies the town of Wadi Musa, which means “Valley of Moses”.
The Siq is a narrow rock gorge more than a kilometre long.
In AD 363 an earthquake badly damaged many buildings.
Johann Ludwig Burckhardt travelled to Petra disguised as Sheikh Ibrahim.
The Arabic script developed from the script of the Nabataeans.
Until the 1980s Bedouins lived in the caves of Petra.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who visits Petra usually stays the night in the town of **Wadi Musa**. The name means “Valley of Moses”. From there you walk through the **Siq**. This gorge is more than a kilometre long and in some places only a few metres wide. The rock walls tower high into the sky on the left and right. At the end the view opens up onto the famous Treasury.

The **Nabataeans** developed Petra into their capital. They had their own **script**, which is found on inscriptions all over the area. Over time the letters changed more and more. The **Arabic script**, which very many people in the world use today, eventually developed from the Nabataean script.

In AD 363 a strong **earthquake** shook the region. Many free-standing buildings and water pipes were destroyed. After that Petra lost more and more importance, also because the trade routes had shifted. The façades cut into the rock survived the quake much better than the houses built of masonry.

In Europe, people long knew hardly anything about Petra. **Johann Ludwig Burckhardt**, a traveller from a Basel family, learned Arabic and passed himself off as a Muslim scholar, **Sheikh Ibrahim**. This way he was able to reach Petra unrecognised in 1812. His reports made the rock city known in Europe.

For a long time a **Bedouin tribe** lived in the old rock caves of Petra. Bedouins are people who traditionally travel through the desert with their animals. When Petra became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985, the families moved to a new village nearby. Many of them now work in tourism, for example with donkeys, camels or sales stalls.

gewusst: At the top of the Treasury façade stands a stone urn. Bedouins thought it held gold and shot at it. You can still see the bullet holes today, but the urn is made of solid stone.
In Arabic the Treasury is called al-Khazneh. But no treasure was ever found there.

teile.einleitung: The North Island is one of the two main islands of New Zealand. It is smaller than the South Island, but most of the population lives here. The island is known for volcanoes, geysers and hot springs.
wichtigste: About three quarters of New Zealanders live on the North Island.
On the North Island lie Auckland and the capital Wellington.
Lake Taupo is the biggest lake in New Zealand.
The highest mountain is the volcano Ruapehu at about 2,800 metres.
Rotorua is known for geysers and hot springs.

abschnitte.text: On the North Island live about **three quarters** of the population of New Zealand. Here lies **Auckland**, the biggest city in the country. Right in the south of the island lies **Wellington**, the **capital**. The climate in the north is mild, almost subtropical. Many Māori live on the North Island.

In the middle of the island lies a chain of **volcanoes**. The highest is **Ruapehu**, at about 2,800 metres. It is an active volcano, and on its slopes there are even **ski areas**. Not far away lies **Lake Taupo**, the biggest lake in New Zealand. It fills the crater of a huge volcano that erupted long ago.

The area around **Rotorua** is very active volcanically. Here **geysers** shoot hot water into the air, and **mud pools** bubble. It often smells of **sulphur**, a bit like rotten eggs. The Māori have used the heat for centuries for cooking and bathing. Today many tourists come here.

Around the volcanoes Ruapehu, Ngauruhoe and Tongariro lies **Tongariro National Park**. It is the oldest national park in New Zealand and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The mountains are sacred to the Māori. Well known is a long hike across the volcanic landscape with coloured crater lakes.

gewusst: New Zealand also uses the heat from the ground of the North Island to generate electricity.
Wellington is regarded as the southernmost capital of a state in the world.

teile.einleitung: Nomads are people who have no fixed place to live. They move with their animals from place to place to find food and water. They take their home, for example a tent, with them.
wichtigste: Nomads have no fixed place of residence and move around.
They keep looking for new pastures and water for their animals.
Many nomads live from their animals.
The yurt is a tent covered with felt on the outside.
The Bedouin live in the deserts of Arabia and North Africa.
Many Sami in the north of Scandinavia keep reindeer.

abschnitte.text: Many nomads live mainly from their **animals**. The animals give **milk**, **meat**, **wool** and **leather**. When the herds have eaten the grass in one place, new pastures are needed. That is why the nomads move on, to find **fodder** and **water**. Their herds are very valuable to them.

abschnitte.titel: A home to take with you
abschnitte.text: Nomads need a home that can be carried. When they move on, they take down their **tent** and load it onto animals or carts. In Mongolia many live in a **yurt**, a round tent. It is covered on the outside with **felt** made from sheep's wool and keeps out cold and wind well. The Indigenous peoples of the prairie in North America used to live in the **tipi**, a pointed tent made of poles and animal hides.

In **Mongolia** **horses** are especially important. Even small children learn to ride there. Besides horses the nomads also keep **sheep**, **goats** and **cattle**, and some keep camels. The winters are very cold and the summers short. That is why the families have to plan well where to move to with their animals.

In the deserts of Arabia and North Africa live the **Bedouin**. In the past they lived in tents made of **goat hair** and moved around with camels, sheep and goats. In the far north of Norway, Sweden and Finland live the **Sami**. Many of them breed **reindeer** and move with the herds. Today many nomads spend only part of the year on the move.

In Switzerland there are no herding nomads. But here too, farmers move up to the **alp** with their cattle in summer, where fresh grass grows. In autumn they return to the valley in the **Alpabzug**. Unlike nomads, though, they have a fixed house in the village.

gewusst: A yurt can be put up and taken down again by one family in a few hours.
The word nomad comes from Greek and means roughly “moving about with herds”.

teile.einleitung: Pompeii was a Roman city on the Bay of Naples in Italy. When Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, it was buried under ash and pumice. Today it is one of the most important excavation sites in the world.
wichtigste: Pompeii lay at the foot of Vesuvius near Naples.
In AD 79 the city was buried under several metres of pumice and ash.
Pompeii has been excavated since the 18th century, starting in 1748.
The plaster casts were made by pouring plaster into hollows in the ash.
Pompeii shows Roman everyday life as if frozen in time.
Pompeii has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997.

abschnitte.text: **Pompeii** lay in the region of **Campania** in the south of Italy, near the sea and at the foot of **Vesuvius**. The city had streets of stone slabs, shops, bakeries, baths, temples and an **amphitheatre**. Many rich families lived in beautiful houses with inner courtyards and colourful **wall paintings**. No one suspected that the nearby mountain was a dangerous volcano.

In **AD 79** **Vesuvius** erupted. At first pumice, small, light stones, rained down on the city for hours. Later glowing clouds of ash and gas raced down the mountain. Pompeii was buried under several metres of **pumice and ash**. The neighbouring town of **Herculaneum** was also buried. The Roman **Pliny the Younger** later described the eruption in letters.

Beneath the ash Pompeii stayed hidden for many centuries. The **excavations** began in **1748** under the Bourbon kings of Naples. To this day the whole city has not yet been uncovered. From 1863 the archaeologist **Giuseppe Fiorelli** had a special idea: the bodies of the victims had decayed in the hardened ash and had left **hollows**. Fiorelli filled them with **plaster**. This is how the famous **plaster casts** came about.

Pompeii is very valuable for historical research. Houses, shops, wall paintings and even **inscriptions** on the walls survived. You can find election slogans, price lists and scribbles. This shows how people lived almost 2,000 years ago, almost as if **frozen**. Since **1997** Pompeii, together with Herculaneum, has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** and is visited by very many people every year.

gewusst: In a bakery in Pompeii, charred loaves of bread were found that are almost 2,000 years old.
Vesuvius is still an active volcano today. Its last eruption was in 1944.

teile.einleitung: Pakistan is a big country in South Asia between India, Afghanistan, Iran and China. It was founded in 1947 and stretches from the Arabian Sea to the highest mountains in the world.
wichtigste: The capital is Islamabad, the biggest city is Karachi.
Lahore is the second biggest city and lies near the border with India.
The official languages are Urdu and English.
Muhammad Ali Jinnah is regarded as the founder of the state.
In the north stand several eight-thousanders, among them Nanga Parbat.
The Khyber Pass connects Pakistan with Afghanistan.

abschnitte.text: Until 1947 the area belonged to British India. At independence the country was divided: **India** and **Pakistan** arose, where the majority of people are Muslim. **Muhammad Ali Jinnah**, the leader of the Muslim League, is regarded as the founder of Pakistan. He became the first Governor-General. In Pakistan he is called “Quaid-e-Azam”, which means great leader.

**Islamabad** was planned and built in the 1960s as the new capital. **Karachi** on the Arabian Sea is the biggest city and the most important port. It was the capital until 1959. **Lahore** is the second biggest city and the capital of the province of Punjab. It is known for splendid buildings from the **Mughal period**.

**Urdu** is the national language, and English is also an official language. In everyday life, though, many people speak other languages, most often **Punjabi**. In addition there are, among others, Pashto, Sindhi and Balochi. Much as in Switzerland, people with different mother tongues live together in Pakistan.

In the north the mountain ranges **Himalaya**, **Karakoram** and Hindu Kush meet. There stands **K2**, the second highest mountain on Earth. **Nanga Parbat** (8,125 m) is called “Germany's Mountain of Destiny”, because many climbers died on German expeditions in the 1930s. In 1953 the Austrian **Hermann Buhl** made the first ascent. In the west the **Khyber Pass** leads to Afghanistan, centuries ago already an important trade and military route.

Through Pakistan flows the **Indus**, one of the great rivers of Asia. It comes from the highlands of Tibet and flows into the Arabian Sea near Karachi. Its water makes a lot of **agriculture** possible in the dry plain, for example the growing of wheat, rice and cotton. On the Indus, over 4,000 years ago, lay one of the oldest advanced civilisations in the world.

gewusst: K2 on the border with China, at 8,611 metres, is the second highest mountain on Earth.
Islamabad is a planned city and was built only after the founding of Pakistan.

teile.einleitung: A permafrost soil is ground that stays frozen for a long time. It is found in cold regions such as Siberia, Canada and the high mountains. When it thaws, it becomes soft and unstable.
wichtigste: Permafrost stays below 0 °C without a break for at least two years.
The top layer thaws in summer and is called the active layer.
Permafrost lies beneath about a quarter of the land area of the Northern Hemisphere.
In Switzerland it occurs on about 5 per cent of the country’s area.
When it thaws in the Alps, rockfalls and rockslides increase.
When it thaws, greenhouse gases such as methane are released.

abschnitte.text: We speak of **permafrost** when ground or rock stays colder than 0 °C **for at least two years** without a break. The word is made up of “permanent”, meaning lasting, and “frost”. Above the frozen ground lies the **active layer**. It thaws every summer and freezes again in winter. It is often only a few decimetres to a few metres thick.

Permafrost lies beneath about a quarter of the land area of the Northern Hemisphere. It is most widespread in **Siberia**, Alaska, Canada and on the Tibetan Plateau. In eastern Siberia the ground is frozen in some places to a depth of about **1,500 metres**. Some of this frost dates from the **Ice Ages**. In Switzerland permafrost occurs on about 5 per cent of the country’s area, mainly in scree slopes and rock faces above about 2,500 metres.

Frozen water in cracks in the rock acts like **cement** and holds the stone together. When it gets warmer and the ice thaws, the rock loses this hold. Then **rockfalls** and **rockslides** increase, and debris can slip away. That is why experts in Switzerland keep a close watch on endangered mountain slopes. Mountain railways and huts built on permafrost also have to be well secured.

In **Siberia** many houses stand on **stilts**. A heated house built directly on the ground would thaw the permafrost beneath it. The ground would turn soft, and the house could sink or crack. This way cold air can flow underneath the house. Roads and pipelines are also hard to build in such areas.

Huge amounts of **dead plant remains** are frozen in permafrost. When they thaw, **microorganisms** break them down. This produces **carbon dioxide** and **methane**. These greenhouse gases strengthen the warming of the Earth. Experts speak of a feedback loop: warmth makes permafrost thaw, and the thawing brings even more warmth.

gewusst: In Siberia, well-preserved mammoths from the Ice Age have been found in the permafrost.
Permafrost can even lie beneath the sea floor of the Arctic.

teile.einleitung: The ombú is a giant plant from South America. It looks like a mighty tree, but botanically it is a giant herb. In the almost treeless pampas it often stands completely alone and gives shade.
wichtigste: The ombú grows in the pampas, the grassland in Argentina and Uruguay.
It looks like a tree, but botanically it is a giant herb.
Its trunk becomes very thick, its wood is soft and stores a lot of water.
In the treeless pampas it gives people and animals shade.
It is regarded as a symbol of the Argentine pampas.

abschnitte.text: The ombú has the scientific name **Phytolacca dioica**. It belongs to the **pokeweed family**. It grows as big as a tree and has a very thick trunk. Its wood, however, is **soft** and **spongy** and stores a lot of water. That is why experts count it among the **giant herbs** and not among true trees. It grows quickly and can live to a great age.

The **pampas** are a wide, flat grassland in **Argentina** and **Uruguay**. By nature there are hardly any trees there. A single ombú therefore offers valuable **shade** for people and cattle. Its leaves and sap are **poisonous**, so animals do not eat it. In songs and stories of the **gauchos**, the cattle herders of the pampas, the ombú is a well-known **symbol**.

Because it grows so big and impressive, the ombú is also planted in other warm countries. In the Mediterranean region, for example in Spain and Portugal, it stands in parks and along streets. In Switzerland it is too cold for it in winter.

gewusst: Although the ombú grows as big as a tree, its soft wood is hardly suitable as timber or firewood.

teile.einleitung: Every river begins somewhere. The place where it starts is called its **source**. There the water comes out of the ground or out of a glacier and begins its long journey to the sea.
wichtigste: The source is the place where a river begins.
The water comes from the ground or from a glacier.
The Rhine rises in Switzerland, in the canton of the Grisons.
The Rhone comes from the Rhone Glacier in the Valais.
Water always flows downhill, so the source lies higher than the mouth.
A small stream often flows first from a spring.
Close to the source the water is usually at its coldest.

abschnitte.text: Rain and meltwater seep into the ground. Underground the water collects as **groundwater**. In some places it comes back up to the surface: this is a **spring**. Other rivers begin at a **glacier**, where ice melts. Close to the source the water is usually **very cold** and often very clean.

From a spring a small **stream** flows first. Several streams flow together and become a **river**. A river that flows into a bigger river is called a **tributary**. The **Aare**, for example, is a tributary of the Rhine. Water always flows **downhill**, so the source lies higher than the mouth, where the river ends.

In Switzerland some of Europe’s great rivers rise. The **Rhine** begins in the canton of the **Grisons** and flows to the **North Sea**. The **Rhone** comes from the **Rhone Glacier** in the Valais, close to the Furka Pass, and flows into the Mediterranean. The **Inn** also rises in the Grisons. Because so many rivers begin here, Switzerland is sometimes called the **“water tower of Europe”**.

Not all springs are cold. At **thermal springs** warm water comes up from deep underground. In Switzerland there are such springs, for example, in **Baden** in Aargau and in **Leukerbad** in the Valais, where you can bathe in warm water. Other springs contain many minerals, and **mineral water** is bottled from them.

Spring water is very important for us humans. A large part of the **drinking water** in Switzerland comes from springs and groundwater. To keep it clean, there are **protection zones** around many springs. There, for example, you may not dump rubbish or use poisonous substances.

gewusst: A single drop of water from the source of the Rhine can be on its way for many days until it reaches the North Sea.
Some springs bubble all year round, while others flow only after heavy rain or during the snowmelt.

teile.einleitung: Orientation means knowing where you are and which way you have to go. Maps and compasses help with this, but so do the Sun and the stars. If you know the points of the compass, you can find your way even without a phone.
wichtigste: At night the Pole Star points roughly north.
You find it by extending the back edge of the Plough about five times.
In Switzerland the Sun is in the south around midday.
At midday a shadow points north.
In the Southern Hemisphere the Southern Cross helps.
In orienteering you look for control points in the terrain with a map and compass.

abschnitte.text: The **Pole Star** stands almost exactly above the Earth's North Pole. That is why it shows the **direction of north** at night. To find it, you look for the **Plough** (the Big Dipper). You extend the line between the two rear stars of the bowl by about **five times**. There the Pole Star stands. In the Southern Hemisphere it is not visible, and there the constellation of the **Southern Cross** helps.

In the Northern Hemisphere outside the tropics, the Sun stands in the **south** at midday. In Switzerland, with summer time, that is at about 1.30 pm. A shadow always falls on the side turned away from the Sun. At midday it therefore points **north** and is at its shortest. The Sun rises exactly in the **east** only at the **equinox** in spring and autumn. In summer it rises in the north-east, in winter in the south-east.

A **compass** has a magnetic needle that points north. With it you can **orient** a map, that is, turn it so that its north points in the right direction. In Switzerland there are very precise **national maps** from swisstopo. On them paths, streams, woods and contour lines are marked. Striking points such as mountain peaks, church towers or lakes also help with orientation.

In **orienteering**, runners look for **control points** in the terrain as fast as possible. For this they have only a precise map and a compass. Each person chooses the route between the points. In Switzerland orienteering is very popular, and many schools and clubs take part. Swiss runners have already won many world championship titles.

gewusst: The word orientation comes from “Orient”, the east, where the Sun rises.
Moss does not reliably grow on the north side of trees and is therefore not a good signpost.

teile.einleitung: A pile dwelling is a house that stands on piles so that its floor is higher than the ground or the water. In Switzerland, people were building villages like this on lake shores more than 6,000 years ago. Pile dwellings also exist today in many parts of the world.
wichtigste: A pile dwelling is a house on wooden piles.
Piles protect the house from floods and damp.
In Switzerland the old pile-dwelling villages lay on lake shores and in bogs.
The first pile-dwelling villages appeared in the Neolithic period.
Under water and mud, wood and tools were preserved.
Since 2011 the pile dwellings around the Alps have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Venice, too, stands on many wooden piles.

abschnitte.text: To build a pile dwelling, long **piles** are driven into the ground. The house stands on top of them. This puts the floor of the house higher than its surroundings. If the water rises in a **flood**, the house stays dry. The old piles were made of **wood**, and the houses were made of wood, clay and reeds.

As early as the **Neolithic period**, more than 6,000 years ago, people in Switzerland built villages on the shores of lakes and in bogs. They were already **farmers**: they grew grain and kept animals. Many remains were found, for example, on **Lake Zurich**, **Lake Biel** and Lake Neuchâtel. In the later Bronze Age, too, people lived in villages like this.

Why do we know so much about these villages? The remains lay for a long time **under water and mud**. There is no air there, so wood, seeds, cloth and tools rotted only very slowly. That is why archaeologists still find piles, clay pots and even leftover food today. From the wood of the piles it is often possible to read off exactly which year a tree was felled.

In 2011 the **prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps** were added to the **UNESCO World Heritage** list. Prehistoric means: from the time before there were written records. The sites lie in six countries. Many of them, about half, are in Switzerland. Most cannot be seen from outside, because they lie under water or in the ground.

People still build on piles today. In the **tropics** many houses stand on **stilts**, because it often rains and the ground is wet. This keeps the house dry and makes it harder for animals to get in. The Italian city of **Venice** was built in a lagoon. Its houses stand on a very large number of wooden piles that are driven deep into the ground.

gewusst: In the winter of 1853/54 Lake Zurich had dropped especially low. At Meilen old piles came to light, and in Switzerland a great enthusiasm for the pile-dwellers began.
Wood that lies in water without air can last for thousands of years.

teile.einleitung: Pinatubo is a volcano on the island of Luzon in the Philippines. In June 1991 it erupted after about 500 years of rest. It was one of the largest volcanic eruptions of the 20th century, and it even cooled the climate of the whole Earth for a short time.
wichtigste: Pinatubo lies in the west of Luzon, about 90 km north-west of Manila.
Before 1991 it had rested for about 500 years.
The main eruption was on 15 June 1991, and the ash column rose about 35 km high.
The eruption reached 6 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index.
At the same time Typhoon Yunya passed over the area.
Afterwards the Earth’s temperature fell temporarily by about 0.5 degrees.
Timely evacuations saved thousands of lives.

abschnitte.text: **Pinatubo** lies in the west of the island of **Luzon**, about 90 km north-west of the capital Manila. Its last major eruption was about **500 years** earlier. The mountain was thickly forested, and many people hardly knew it was a volcano. In spring 1991 the ground began to shake, and steam and gases rose from the mountain.

After weeks of growing activity, the main eruption came on **15 June 1991**. The **eruption column** of ash and gas rose about 35 km high. The volcano threw out about 10 km³ of material and reached **VEI 6** on the **Volcanic Explosivity Index**. This scale measures how violent an eruption is. On the same day **Typhoon Yunya** passed over the area. Its rain soaked the ash and made it very heavy, so that many roofs collapsed.

Philippine and American experts watched the volcano closely. They analysed **earthquakes** and **gas measurements** and gave an early warning. **Tens of thousands** of people were brought to safety before the main eruption. The nearby **Clark Air Base**, a large base of the US Air Force, was also evacuated. Because of the heavy damage, the USA gave it up afterwards. The forecast is regarded as a great success for **volcanology**.

The volcano blew about 15 to 20 million tonnes of **sulphur dioxide** up into the **stratosphere**, a high layer of the atmosphere. From this, tiny floating particles formed, the **sulphate aerosols**. They spread around the Earth and reflected part of the sunlight back into space. In 1992 and 1993 it was about **0.5 degrees** cooler worldwide.

During the eruption the summit collapsed, and a **caldera** formed, a large basin about 2.5 km wide. The mountain became clearly lower as a result. Monsoon rains gradually filled the caldera with water. This created **Lake Pinatubo**, which today is also visited by tourists. For years after the eruption, rain washed ash down into the valley as mudflows called **lahars**.

gewusst: After the eruption of Pinatubo, strikingly coloured sunsets were also seen in Europe, because the fine particles high in the air scattered the light.
Pinatubo lost several hundred metres of height in the eruption.

teile.einleitung: The Pampas are a wide, flat grass plain in the south-east of South America. They lie mainly in Argentina and reach as far as Uruguay. Today they are one of the most important farming areas in the world.
wichtigste: The Pampas are a flat grass steppe with few trees.
The name comes from the Quechua language and means “plain”.
The soils are very fertile, and the climate is temperate.
Today wheat, maize and soya grow there.
Millions of cattle live on the pastures.
Typical wild animals are the rhea (“Nandu”) and the Patagonian mara.

abschnitte.text: The Pampas are so flat that you can see almost to the horizon. Originally there were hardly any trees, but tall grasses instead. The name comes from **Quechua**, an old language of the Andes, and means **“plain”**. Over the Pampas often blows the **pampero**, a cold, sometimes stormy wind from the south-west. It suddenly brings cool weather.

The Pampas have deep, **fertile soils**, enough rain and a temperate climate. That is why they are very well suited to **farming**. On huge fields wheat, maize and **soya** grow today. A large part of the harvest is sold to other countries. The original grass steppe has therefore disappeared in many places.

On the pastures of the Pampas live millions of **cattle**. That is why Argentina is known for its beef. The cattle herders are called **gauchos**. They like to drink **mate**, a tea made from the leaves of a plant, from a small cup with a metal straw. From about 1877, **refrigerated ships** carried fresh meat across the Atlantic to Europe. After that, cattle farming became big business.

The **rhea** (in German “Nandu”) is a big flightless bird that cannot fly, but can run very fast. It lives only in South America. The **Patagonian mara** (in German “Pampashase”, “Pampas hare”) has long legs and looks like a hare. But it is related to the guinea pig. The tall **pampas grass** also comes from this region.

gewusst: The capital of Argentina, Buenos Aires, lies on the edge of the Pampas.
The Patagonian mara is not a hare, but a relative of the guinea pig.

teile.einleitung: The Pantanal is the biggest inland wetland on Earth. It lies mainly in the west of Brazil and reaches as far as Bolivia and Paraguay. In the rainy season a large part of the plain is under water.
wichtigste: The Pantanal is the biggest inland wetland on Earth.
The largest part lies in Brazil, smaller parts in Bolivia and Paraguay.
From about November to March a large part is flooded.
Jaguars, caimans and capybaras live here.
Parts of the Pantanal are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

abschnitte.text: The Pantanal is a huge, flat **basin**. The name comes from the Portuguese word for swamp. In the **rainy season**, from about November to March, the rivers burst their banks, above all the **Rio Paraguay** and its tributaries. Then a large part of the plain is under water. In the **dry season** the water retreats, and lagoons, pools and lush pastures remain.

Because the water changes so much, the Pantanal offers a habitat to very many animals. Here live **jaguars**, the biggest big cats of America, and many **caimans**, a kind of crocodile. **Capybaras** are also common. They are the biggest rodents in the world. In addition there are hundreds of species of birds, such as storks, herons and the blue **hyacinth macaw**.

The Pantanal has long been used for **cattle farming**. Parts of it are protected and are **UNESCO World Heritage Sites**. Dangers are clearing at the edges, drought and big **fires**. Because wetlands store a lot of water and offer a habitat to many species, conservation organisations work to preserve them.

gewusst: The Pantanal is several times as big as Switzerland.
In the Pantanal you can often watch jaguars more easily than in the dense rainforest.

t663rq7.t: The New Seven Wonders of the World

teile.einleitung: The New Seven Wonders are seven famous buildings that were chosen in a worldwide vote in 2007. The idea came from the Swiss Bernard Weber. They recall the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
wichtigste: The New Seven Wonders of the World were announced in July 2007.
The idea came from the Swiss filmmaker Bernard Weber.
The winners were announced on 7 July 2007 in Lisbon.
The Colosseum in Rome is the only one of the new wonders in Europe.
Three of the new wonders lie in the Americas.
The Pyramids of Giza received an honorary place.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss filmmaker **Bernard Weber** founded the foundation **New7Wonders**, based in Zurich. It called on people all over the world to choose new wonders of the world. Millions voted by **internet** and **telephone**. **UNESCO** was not involved in the vote. That is why the list is not an official title, but it is very well known.

The winners were announced on **7 July 2007** in the football stadium of **Lisbon** in Portugal. The date 7.7.07 fitted the number seven well. The **Great Wall of China**, the rock city of **Petra** in Jordan and the **Taj Mahal** in India were chosen. Added to these were the statue of Christ, **Cristo Redentor**, in Brazil, **Machu Picchu** in Peru, **Chichén Itzá** in Mexico and the **Colosseum** in Rome.

The **Colosseum** is the only one of the new wonders in Europe. Emperor Vespasian began the building, and his son **Titus** opened it in AD 80 with games that lasted 100 days. It was the biggest **amphitheatre** of the Roman Empire and had room for about **50,000** spectators. There, **gladiator fights** and animal hunts took place, meant to entertain the people.

abschnitte.titel: Wonders in the Americas and Asia
abschnitte.text: Three of the new wonders lie in the **Americas**: Cristo Redentor, Machu Picchu and Chichén Itzá. Machu Picchu is a city of the **Inca** high in the Andes. Chichén Itzá was a big city of the **Maya**. Three more stand in **Asia**: the Great Wall of China, Petra and the Taj Mahal.

Even in antiquity there was a list of **seven wonders**, among them the Colossus of Rhodes and the Hanging Gardens of Babylon. Of these only the **Pyramids of Giza** in Egypt survive. That is why they were not up for election in 2007, but were given an **honorary title**.

gewusst: The Great Wall of China is the longest structure among the new wonders, stretching over thousands of kilometres.
The statue of Christ in Rio de Janeiro is the youngest of the new wonders, dedicated in 1931.

teile.einleitung: With a package holiday you buy several travel services at once and for a total price, for example flight, hotel and excursions. This way of travelling was invented in the 19th century in England.
wichtigste: A package holiday bundles several services for a total price.
Usually travel and accommodation are included.
Thomas Cook organised the first package tour in England in 1841.
He is regarded as the founder of modern package tourism.
In Switzerland a law of its own protects travellers.

abschnitte.text: In 1841 the Englishman **Thomas Cook** organised a train trip for about 500 people to a meeting. He took care of the tickets, and the participants paid a joint price. This is regarded as the first **package tour**. Later Cook offered ever bigger trips, also abroad. Already in the 1860s he led groups of travellers to **Switzerland**. He is regarded as the founder of modern **package tourism**.

In a package holiday, a **tour operator** puts together several services, for example flight, hotel, transfer and excursions. You pay a **total price** for it. This is convenient, because you do not have to book everything yourself. Because operators buy in large quantities, such holidays are often cheaper. A beach holiday by the sea is a typical example.

In Switzerland the **Federal Act on Package Travel** sets out the duties of the operator. He must carry out the trip as it was described. If something goes wrong, for example because the hotel is quite different from what was promised, travellers can demand **compensation**. In addition, amounts paid must be secured in case the operator gets into financial difficulty.

gewusst: The travel firm founded by Thomas Cook existed for almost 180 years, until it had to give up in 2019.
The first package tour was a short train trip within England.

teile.einleitung: Natural resources are everything that nature gives us and that we humans use: water, air, soil, wood, oil or metals. Without them there would be no food, houses, electricity or mobile phones. Because some resources are becoming scarce, it is important to treat them carefully and sustainably.
wichtigste: Natural resources are substances and goods from nature that we use.
Renewable resources such as wood or water grow back or form again.
Non-renewable resources such as natural gas, oil or coal will run out one day.
Earth Overshoot Day shows from what date humanity has used up the resources of one year.
Virtual water is the water needed to make a product.
Only about 3 per cent of the water on Earth is fresh water.
Switzerland is called the “water tower of Europe” because big rivers rise there.
The term sustainability originally comes from forestry.

abschnitte.text: **Resources** means everything from nature that people need to live and to do business. This includes raw materials such as metals and oil, but also water, fertile soil, clean air, forests and fish. Sunlight and wind are resources too, because we get energy from them. They are called natural because humans cannot make them themselves.

**Renewable** resources grow back or are constantly formed anew, for example wood, water, wind or solar energy. **Non-renewable** resources such as natural gas, oil, coal or ores formed over millions of years. When we use them up, they are gone for a very long time. But renewable resources too can become scarce if more is taken than grows back, for example with fish.

**Earth Overshoot Day** is the day in the year on which humanity has used as much as the Earth can renew in a whole year. Worldwide in recent years it has fallen at the end of July or the start of August. For the rest of the year we are, so to speak, living at the expense of the future. If all people used as much as the people in Switzerland, this day would already come in spring.

Of all the water on Earth only about 3 per cent is **fresh water**, and most of that is frozen in glaciers and polar ice caps. Switzerland is the **water tower of Europe**: the Rhine, Rhône, Inn and Ticino all rise in the Swiss Alps. We use a lot of water without seeing it, as virtual water. A cup of coffee takes about 130 litres of water from growing to the cup.

The term **sustainability** comes from forestry: you should fell only as many trees as grow back. The Saxon official Hans Carl von Carlowitz described this idea as early as 1713. In 1968 the researcher Garrett Hardin showed with the “tragedy of the commons” that jointly used goods are easily overused. It is like a pasture onto which every farmer drives more and more cows until no grass grows any more.

Everyone can help to save resources. You can use things for longer, repair them, swap them and **recycle** them, as is done in Switzerland, for example, with PET bottles, glass and paper. Throwing away less food saves water, land and energy. Electricity from hydropower, sun and wind instead of from oil or coal also helps.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something you can use to make something or to live.
Something that grows back by itself or forms anew again and again.
Acting in such a way that later generations still have enough to live on.
The invisible water that was used to make a product.
Land or goods used jointly by many people.

gewusst: It takes about 15,000 litres of water to produce one kilogram of beef.
In Switzerland there are still commons today that are used jointly by village communities.
By law, the area of Swiss forest may not be made smaller.

teile.einleitung: Niagara Falls are mighty waterfalls in North America, right on the border between the USA and Canada. They are not especially high, but very wide, and every year millions of visitors come.
wichtigste: Niagara Falls lie on the border between the USA and Canada.
They consist of three waterfalls.
The biggest is called Horseshoe Falls and is about 50 metres high.
The Niagara flows from Lake Erie to Lake Ontario.
A large part of the water is used for electricity.
In the evening the falls are lit up in colour.

abschnitte.text: Niagara Falls consist of three falls: **Horseshoe Falls**, **American Falls** and the small **Bridal Veil Falls**. Horseshoe Falls is the biggest and curved like a **horseshoe**. It is about **50 metres** high. That is not very high, but an enormous amount of water plunges over the wide edge. Most of Horseshoe Falls lies in Canada.

abschnitte.titel: Between two lakes and two countries
abschnitte.text: The **Niagara River** links **Lake Erie** with **Lake Ontario**, two of the Great Lakes. On the way it plunges over the falls. Here the river forms the border between **Canada** and the **USA**. The American side belongs to the state of **New York**, the Canadian to the province of Ontario. On both sides there is a city named **Niagara Falls**.

On **excursion boats**, tourists get very close to the roaring falls. They are given **raincoats**, because the spray makes everyone wet. From viewpoints and towers you can see the falls from above. In the evening big floodlights light them up in many **colours**. Often there are fireworks too.

A large part of the water flows, before the falls, through **tunnels** to **hydroelectric power stations**. Both the USA and Canada generate a lot of electricity here. At night and in winter more water is diverted, by day in summer less, so that the falls look beautiful for visitors. The water constantly gnaws at the rock, which is why the falls slowly move upstream.

gewusst: Niagara Falls formed after the last Ice Age, that is, about 12,000 years ago.
In very cold winters huge icebergs and icicles form at the falls, but they do not freeze completely.

teile.einleitung: The North Pole is the northernmost point on Earth, where all the lines of longitude meet. Unlike the South Pole, it does not lie on land, but in the middle of the Arctic Ocean on floating sea ice. All around live animals such as the polar bear, which cope with the great cold.
wichtigste: The North Pole is the northernmost point of the Earth's axis.
At the North Pole you stand on sea ice that floats on the Arctic Ocean.
Beneath the ice the sea there is over 4,000 metres deep.
Near the North Pole lives the polar bear, the biggest land predator.
The needle of a compass points north, more precisely to the magnetic North Pole.
At the North Pole, day and night each last about half a year.
The sea ice of the Arctic is shrinking because of climate change.

abschnitte.text: The **geographic North Pole** is the point where the imaginary axis of rotation of the Earth pierces the surface in the north. From there every direction points south. It lies in the middle of the Arctic Ocean, far from all coasts. The area around the North Pole is called the **Arctic**.

At the North Pole there is no land, only **sea ice**, which is a few metres thick. It is constantly drifting slowly on the water, so no fixed station can be built there. Beneath the ice the ocean is over 4,000 metres deep. In 2007 a Russian submarine even planted a flag on the sea floor beneath the pole.

The **polar bear** is the typical animal of the Arctic and hunts mainly seals on the ice. Its dense fur and a thick layer of fat protect it from the cold. In the Arctic there also live Arctic foxes, walruses, narwhals and many seabirds. When the sea ice melts, it becomes harder for polar bears to find prey.

Because the Earth's axis is tilted, at the North Pole the Sun does not set for about half a year in summer. This time is called **polar day**, and you can then see the midnight sun. In winter the polar night follows, in which it stays dark for months. Often the northern lights then glow in the sky.

A **compass needle** is a small magnet and aligns itself with the Earth's magnetic field. It does not point exactly to the geographic North Pole, but to the magnetic North Pole. This lies a few hundred kilometres away and moves a bit further each year. For hikes in Switzerland, though, the difference is very small.

For a long time explorers tried to reach the North Pole. The American Robert Peary claimed to have been there in 1909, but that is still disputed. The pole was certainly flown over in 1926 by the airship “Norge” with **Roald Amundsen** and Umberto Nobile on board. Today icebreakers even take tourists to the North Pole.

begriffe.erklaerung: The area around the North Pole.
Frozen seawater that floats on the ocean.
A time when, in polar regions, the Sun does not rise all day.
A device with a magnetic needle that shows the points of the compass.

gewusst: The North Pole has no time of its own, and you can pick any time zone.
Polar bears actually have black skin under their light fur.
There are no penguins at the North Pole, and they live in the Southern Hemisphere.

teile.einleitung: A spit, in German a “Nehrung”, is a long, narrow strip of sand that almost cuts off a bay from the open sea. Behind it lies a calm body of water, which on the Baltic Sea is called a “Haff”, or lagoon.
wichtigste: A spit is a narrow strip of sand between a bay and the open sea.
The sand is brought by waves and the longshore current.
The body of water behind a spit is called a “Haff” (lagoon) on the Baltic Sea.
The Curonian Spit is about 98 kilometres long and belongs to Lithuania and Russia.
Since 2000 the Curonian Spit has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Since 2022 a shipping canal has led through the Vistula Spit.

abschnitte.text: When waves hit a coast at an angle, they push the sand along the beach in a zigzag. This process is called **longshore drift**, and the current behind it the **longshore current**. The sand is deposited where the coast makes a bend. In this way a beach ridge grows bit by bit across a bay. Such coasts with spits are called **shoreline-straightening coasts**, because they gradually even out bays.

If a tongue of sand grows from the shore into the sea and ends freely in the water, it is called a **hook**. Its end is often curved towards the land. If the beach ridge becomes so long that it almost closes the bay, a **spit** has formed. The cut-off water behind it is a **“Haff”** or lagoon. A Haff is usually only slightly salty, because rivers bring a lot of fresh water into it.

The best-known spit is the **Curonian Spit** on the Baltic Sea. It is about 98 kilometres long and separates the **Curonian Lagoon** from the sea. The north belongs to **Lithuania**, the south to the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. It is famous for its high **moving dunes**, which are among the highest in Europe. Into the lagoon flows the **Neman**, called Nemunas in Lithuanian.

The **Vistula Spit** also lies on the Baltic Sea, between Poland and Russia. Poland had a canal built through it, which opened in 2022. Ships can thus go from the Vistula Lagoon directly into the Baltic Sea without passing through Russian waters. At the mouth of the Oder lies the **Szczecin Lagoon**. It is separated from the sea by the islands of Usedom and Wolin.

gewusst: Moving dunes can bury whole villages under sand, which is why forests were planted on the Curonian Spit to hold the sand in place.
From 1930 the writer Thomas Mann had a summer house on the Curonian Spit.

teile.einleitung: Patagonia is the southernmost part of South America. The region is divided between Argentina and Chile. It is known for wide steppes, mighty glaciers, steep mountains and very strong wind.
wichtigste: Patagonia belongs to Argentina and Chile, the bigger part to Argentina.
A fierce wind from the west often blows there.
The Perito Moreno Glacier lies in the Argentine part.
Torres del Paine National Park lies in the Chilean part.
Sheep are raised on big farms.
Right in the south lies the island group of Tierra del Fuego.

abschnitte.titel: At the end of South America
abschnitte.text: Patagonia stretches roughly from the Río Colorado in Argentina to the southern tip of the continent. The bigger part belongs to **Argentina**, the smaller to **Chile**. In the west lie the **Andes** with glaciers, lakes and fjords. In the east stretches a dry, wide **steppe**. Right in the south lies the island group of **Tierra del Fuego**, “Land of Fire”. Seafarers saw many fires of the inhabitants on the shore there and gave it this name.

The weather in Patagonia is known for **very strong wind**. It mostly comes from the **west**, off the Pacific. On the Chilean side of the Andes it rains out, so it is drier on the Argentine side. Trees there sometimes grow crooked, because the wind constantly pushes them in one direction.

In the Argentine part lies the **Perito Moreno Glacier**. It ends in a lake, and again and again big pieces of ice break off and crash into the water. In the Chilean part lies **Torres del Paine** National Park. “Torres” means “towers” in Spanish. Three steep **granite towers** are the park's landmark.

In Patagonia there are big farms with thousands of **sheep**. Their wool is sold all over the world. On the coasts the **Magellanic penguin** breeds. It digs its nests into the ground. In the steppe live **guanacos**, wild relatives of the llama, and the flightless bird called the rhea.

The name probably comes from the crew of the seafarer **Ferdinand Magellan**. In 1520 his men called the local people **“Patagones”**. From this came the name of the whole region. The **Strait of Magellan**, a strait between the mainland and Tierra del Fuego, and the Magellanic penguin are also named after him.

gewusst: The Perito Moreno Glacier is one of the few glaciers in the world that have hardly shrunk for decades.
Far fewer people per square kilometre live in Patagonia than in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Panama is a country in Central America. It lies on a narrow land bridge between Costa Rica and Colombia. It is famous above all for the Panama Canal, which connects the Atlantic and the Pacific.
wichtigste: Panama borders Costa Rica in the west and Colombia in the east.
It connects Central and South America.
The Panama Canal connects the Atlantic with the Pacific.
The currency is called the balboa, but in everyday life people mostly pay with US dollars.
The national bird is the harpy eagle.
The “Panama hat” actually comes from Ecuador.

abschnitte.text: Panama lies on the **Isthmus of Panama**, a narrow strip of land. In the west it borders **Costa Rica**, in the east **Colombia**. So Panama is the link between Central and South America. On one side lies the Caribbean Sea, which belongs to the Atlantic, on the other the Pacific. The capital is **Panama City**.

The **Panama Canal** was opened in 1914. With it, ships save the long detour round the southern tip of South America. With **locks** they are raised and lowered again. Near Panama City the **Bridge of the Americas** crosses the entrance of the canal on the Pacific side. It was opened in 1962.

The flag of Panama has four fields. In the two white fields there is a **star** each, one blue and one red. The country's own money is called the **balboa**, after the Spanish explorer Vasco Núñez de Balboa. In everyday life, though, people mostly pay with the **US dollar**, which is also official.

Panama has dense **rainforests** with many animals. The national bird is the **harpy eagle**, a very powerful bird of prey. The golden-yellow **Panamanian golden frog** is regarded as a lucky charm. It is very rare today and heavily threatened. In addition, sloths, monkeys and many colourful birds live in Panama.

The famous **Panama hat** actually comes from **Ecuador**. There it is woven from fine palm fibres. It got its name because it was sold via Panama. Workers building the canal also wore such hats against the sun.

gewusst: Because of the shape of the isthmus, in some places in Panama the Sun rises over the Pacific.
The Panama Canal is about 80 kilometres long and saves ships many thousands of kilometres of detour.

teile.einleitung: Tijuca National Park lies in the middle of the city of Rio de Janeiro in Brazil. Its Tijuca Forest is one of the biggest urban forests in the world. It was replanted by people in the 19th century.
wichtigste: The Tijuca Forest lies in the middle of the city of Rio de Janeiro.
It is one of the biggest urban forests in the world.
In the past the forest was cleared for coffee plantations.
In the 19th century it was replanted.
In the park, on Corcovado, stands the famous statue of Christ.

abschnitte.titel: A forest in the big city
abschnitte.text: **Tijuca National Park** lies in the mountains in the middle of **Rio de Janeiro**. Its **Tijuca Forest** belongs to the **Atlantic Forest**, which used to cover the whole coast of Brazil. There grow trees, ferns and orchids, and there are waterfalls. In the forest live monkeys, birds and many insects. For the people of the city it is an important recreation area.

In the 18th and 19th centuries a large part of the forest was cleared for **coffee plantations**. After that the city lacked clean water because the springs in the mountains dried up. That is why from 1861 the Brazilian emperor had the forest **replanted**. Over many years tens of thousands of trees were planted by hand. In this way one of the first big reforestations in the world came about.

The park also includes the mountain **Corcovado**. On its summit stands the famous **statue of Christ** with outstretched arms, a landmark of Rio. From there you can see over the city, the beaches and Sugarloaf Mountain. Another well-known mountain in the park is the Pedra da Gávea. The landscape of Rio de Janeiro is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

gewusst: The Tijuca Forest is an example of how people can let a destroyed forest grow back.

teile.einleitung: Precipitation is water that falls from the air to the Earth or settles on it. It includes rain, snow and hail. It is measured in millimetres, and one millimetre means one litre of water per square metre.
wichtigste: Precipitation is water from the air, liquid or frozen.
Rain, snow, hail, soft hail and drizzle are kinds of precipitation.
1 millimetre of precipitation means 1 litre of water per square metre.
In Zurich on average about 1,000 millimetres fall per year.
Precipitation is an important part of the water cycle.

abschnitte.text: When water falls from the clouds, this is called **falling precipitation**. This includes **rain**, **drizzle**, **snow**, **soft hail** and **hail**. Whether it rains or snows depends on the temperature. There is also precipitation that forms directly on the ground, for example **dew** and **hoar frost**. This is called **deposited precipitation**.

The Sun makes water from seas, lakes and plants **evaporate**. When the moist air rises, it cools and forms **clouds** made of tiny droplets or ice crystals. When these grow, they become too heavy and fall down. On Earth the water flows into streams and rivers and finally back into the sea. This path is called the **water cycle**.

Precipitation is measured with a **rain gauge**, a container with a known opening. You give how high the water would stand if nothing ran off or soaked away. **1 millimetre** on a square metre gives exactly **1 litre** of water. If 20 millimetres fall in a day, that is 20 litres on every square metre. In Switzerland, **MeteoSwiss** measures precipitation at many stations.

In **Zurich**, on long-term average about 1,000 to 1,100 millimetres fall per year. It rains especially much on the **northern slopes of the Alps** and in **Ticino**, because the mountains force the moist air to rise. The **Valais**, by contrast, is very dry, because high mountains keep the rain away. In Switzerland, precipitation is important for drinking water, farming and hydropower.

gewusst: A hailstone can grow as big as a tennis ball.
A large part of the precipitation in the Alps falls as snow and feeds the rivers in summer.

teile.einleitung: The polar front is the boundary zone between cold air from the polar regions and warm air from the subtropics. Many low-pressure areas form along it, and they also determine the weather in Switzerland. The model of the polar front was developed in Norway around 1920.
wichtigste: The polar front separates polar cold air from subtropical warm air.
It usually lies roughly between 40 and 60 degrees latitude.
The Bergen School developed the polar front model around 1920.
The term front comes from a comparison with the fronts of the First World War.
Low-pressure areas form on waves of the polar front.
When a cold front catches up with a warm front, an occlusion forms.
In winter the polar front shifts south.

abschnitte.text: On Earth there are large **air masses** with different temperatures. In the high latitudes lies cold **polar air**, in the subtropics warm air. The boundary zone between them is called the **polar front**. It usually lies in the middle latitudes, roughly between **40 and 60 degrees**, but varies a lot. It forms the boundary between the **Ferrel cell** and the **polar cell**, two large circulations of air.

Around 1920, meteorologists around **Vilhelm** and **Jacob Bjerknes** were working in **Bergen** in Norway. This **Bergen School** explained how fronts run and how lows form. They compared the meeting of the air masses with the front lines of the **First World War**. This is how the term **front** caught on. Their model is still taught today.

The polar front is not straight but bends into waves. At such a **wave**, the air begins to circle around the tip of the wave. This is how a **low-pressure area** forms. On its front side warm air pushes forward, which is the **warm front**. On the rear side cold air pushes in behind, which is the **cold front**. These travelling lows often move in from the Atlantic over Europe and Switzerland.

At a **warm front** warm air glides gently up over cold air. Far ahead of the front, high, wispy **cirrus clouds** appear first, and later longer-lasting rain often follows. At a **cold front** the cold air pushes under the warm air like a wedge and lifts it quickly. Towering clouds form with **showers** and **thunderstorms**, and afterwards it becomes clearly cooler.

Cold fronts usually move faster than warm fronts. When the cold front catches up with the warm front, the warm air is lifted off the ground. This is called an **occlusion**. In **winter** the Arctic cools down strongly, and the cold air spreads out. The polar front, and with it the tracks of the lows, then shift **south**, that is, towards the equator.

gewusst: On weather maps a cold front is drawn with blue triangles and a warm front with red semicircles.
High above the polar front there is often a particularly strong wind, the polar front jet stream.

teile.einleitung: Pikes Peak is a well-known mountain in the US state of Colorado. It belongs to the Front Range of the Rocky Mountains and towers above the city of Colorado Springs. It is famous for a song, a cog railway and a car race.
wichtigste: Pikes Peak lies in Colorado in the USA.
It is about 4,300 metres high and belongs to the Front Range of the Rocky Mountains.
It is named after the explorer Zebulon Pike.
Katharine Lee Bates wrote the poem “America the Beautiful” there in 1893.
A road and a cog railway lead to the summit.

abschnitte.text: **Pikes Peak** is about **4,300 metres** high, so only slightly lower than the highest peaks of the Swiss Alps. It belongs to the **Front Range**, the easternmost chain of the **Rocky Mountains**. Because it rises on its own above the flat prairie, it can be seen from far away. At the foot of the mountain lies the city of **Colorado Springs**.

The mountain is named after **Zebulon Pike**. This American officer explored the area in 1806. He did not reach the summit itself at that time. Later, during the Colorado gold rush, the mountain became a well-known landmark for settlers.

In 1893 the teacher and poet **Katharine Lee Bates** climbed Pikes Peak. The wide view over the land delighted her so much that she wrote the poem **“America the Beautiful”**. Later it was set to music. Today it is one of the best-known **patriotic songs** in the USA.

A **cog railway** leads to the summit, one of the highest in the world. Its railcars were built in **Switzerland**. There is also a road all the way to the top. Since 1916 the **Pikes Peak International Hill Climb** has been held on it, a famous mountain race for cars and motorcycles.

gewusst: At the summit of Pikes Peak the air is so thin that some visitors get a headache.
After the Indianapolis 500, the Pikes Peak hill climb is one of the oldest motor races in the USA.

teile.einleitung: Beijing, called Peking in German, is the capital of the People’s Republic of China and one of the largest cities in the world. The city is known for its old imperial palaces, temples and modern buildings.
wichtigste: Beijing is the capital of the People’s Republic of China.
“Beijing” means “northern capital”.
The Chinese emperors used to live in the Forbidden City.
The Summer Olympic Games took place in Beijing in 2008.
Beijing was the first city to host both the Summer and the Winter Games.
Also well known are the Temple of Heaven, the Summer Palace and the hutongs.

abschnitte.text: Beijing lies in the north of China. The Chinese name **Beijing** is made up of “bei”, meaning **north**, and “jing”, meaning **capital**. For many centuries Chinese emperors ruled from here. Today Beijing is the seat of the government of the **People’s Republic of China** and an important centre of culture and science.

In the centre lies the **Forbidden City**, a huge old **imperial palace**. The emperors once lived there with their court. Ordinary people were not allowed in, hence the name. Today it is a museum. In the north-west of the city lies the **Summer Palace** with Kunming Lake, hills and pavilions. The emperors spent the hot months there. It is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

At the **Temple of Heaven** the emperors prayed for a good **harvest**. The round hall with the blue roof is a landmark of the city. In the old town there are narrow, traditional alleys with courtyard houses. They are called **hutongs**. Many were pulled down, and some are now protected as part of the city’s history.

In 2008 the **Summer Olympic Games** took place in Beijing. The opening ceremony began on 8.8.2008, because eight is seen as a lucky number in China. The **National Stadium** was built for the Games. Because of its interwoven steel beams it is called the **“Bird’s Nest”**. In 2022 Beijing also hosted the Winter Games. This made it the first city in the world to have held both kinds of Olympic Games.

A famous dish is named after the city: **Peking duck**. The duck is roasted so that the skin becomes especially crisp. It is eaten cut into pieces with thin **pancakes**, cucumber, spring onions and a sweet sauce.

gewusst: Not far from Beijing runs the Great Wall of China, which you can visit from the city on a day trip.
The Forbidden City is one of the largest palace complexes in the world.

teile.einleitung: Parrots are colourful, clever birds with a strong, curved beak. They live mainly in warm regions of the Earth. Many of them can imitate voices and sounds.
wichtigste: Parrots have a strong, curved beak.
On the foot, two toes point forwards and two backwards.
Many parrots can imitate sounds and even words.
The macaws of South America are among the biggest parrots.
The grey parrot from Africa is regarded as an especially good talker.
Parrots often live in groups.

abschnitte.text: Parrots live mainly in the **tropics** and subtropics, for example in South America, Africa, Asia and Australia. Many have bright feathers in red, green, yellow or blue. The big **macaws** with their long tails live in the rainforests of Central and South America. Among them are the longest parrots in the world. **Budgerigars** and cockatoos are also parrots.

The beak of a parrot is **hard, strong and curved**. With it parrots crack hard **nuts** and seeds. They also need the beak for climbing: with it they hold on to branches as with a third hand. Many parrots also eat fruit and flowers.

In a parrot's foot **two toes point forwards** and **two backwards**. In this way parrots can grip branches firmly. They even take food in the foot and bring it to the beak, roughly as we do with a hand. Woodpeckers, too, have feet with this arrangement of toes.

Many parrots can **imitate voices and sounds**. In nature they communicate with loud calls within their group. If they live with people, some learn words or imitate ringtones. The **grey parrot** is regarded as an especially good talker. It has grey plumage and a red tail and lives in the rainforests of Africa, for example in the Congo.

Many species of parrots are **threatened** today. Their habitat, the rainforest, is being cut down, and some animals are caught and sold as pets. That is why trade in many species is strictly regulated. Anyone who keeps a parrot needs a lot of space and time, because the birds are sociable and often live to a great age.

gewusst: Some big parrots can live to over 50 years old.
Parrots are among the cleverest birds and can solve tasks to get at food.

teile.einleitung: Muskeg is a name for wide areas of bog and swamp in northern Canada and in Alaska. Muskeg is especially widespread on the Canadian Shield. For people who want to build roads or railways there, it is a big obstacle.
wichtigste: Muskeg consists of widespread areas of bog and swamp on the Canadian Shield.
It forms in hollows with poor drainage above impermeable rock.
The ground consists of wet peat and moss.
Muskeg makes the building of roads and railways very difficult.
