The word comes from a language of the Indigenous peoples of Canada.

abschnitte.text: The word **muskeg** comes from the language of the **Cree**, an Indigenous people of Canada. It describes wet boggy landscapes with mosses, shrubs and small trees such as black spruce. The ground consists of **peat**, that is, plant remains that hardly break down in water. On it grow mainly **peat mosses**. Anyone who walks on it feels the ground sway and give way.

The **Canadian Shield** is a huge area of very old, hard rock. Glaciers of the Ice Ages ground the rock down and left behind many hollows. Because the rock is **impermeable**, the water cannot soak away. In the hollows with poor drainage it stays put. In this way, over a long time, bogs and swamps form, which is muskeg.

Muskeg hardly bears any weight. Roads and railway tracks can **sink** into it, and vehicles get stuck. That is why building transport routes in northern Canada was very costly. In winter, when the ground is frozen, **winter roads** are often laid, which become impassable again in summer. Muskeg also stores a lot of **carbon** in its peat and is therefore important for the climate.

gewusst: Bogs like muskeg grow very slowly: a layer of peat often gets thicker by only about a millimetre a year.

teile.einleitung: Jellyfish are transparent, soft sea creatures that drift through the water. They have neither a brain nor bones, and yet they have existed for hundreds of millions of years. They catch their prey with tentacles full of stinging cells.
wichtigste: A jellyfish is about 98 per cent water.
Jellyfish have no brain, only a simple nerve net.
They catch small animals with stinging tentacles.
They swim by contracting their bell.
The immortal jellyfish can turn back into a young polyp.
The sea wasp is regarded as one of the most poisonous animals in the sea.
A small freshwater jellyfish also lives in some Swiss lakes.

abschnitte.text: A jellyfish is about **98 per cent water**. That is why it is so transparent and soft. It has **no brain**, no heart and no bones. Instead of a brain it has a simple **nerve net** that runs through the whole body. With this it senses, for example, light and touch. Jellyfish belong to the **cnidarians**, like corals and sea anemones.

The body of a jellyfish looks like an **umbrella** or a bell. To swim, it contracts the bell and so squeezes water out. This **recoil** pushes it forward. Then the bell opens again. Jellyfish can hardly make headway against strong currents, so they often drift with the water.

From the edge of the bell hang **tentacles**. On them sit tiny **stinging cells** with poison. If a small animal touches the tentacles, the stinging cells shoot out and paralyse it. Then the jellyfish brings the prey to its mouth. The **sea wasp**, which lives mainly off Australia, is regarded as one of the most poisonous animals in the sea. Its poison is very dangerous for humans.

Many jellyfish live in two forms. First the animal sits fixed to the bottom as a small **polyp**. Later young jellyfish detach from the polyp and swim away. When in danger or in old age, the **immortal jellyfish** can even turn back into a young polyp and grow up again. That is how it got its special name.

The **moon jellyfish** has four ring-shaped patterns in the middle that look like ears. It is common in the North Sea and the Baltic Sea and almost harmless to humans. The **lion’s mane jellyfish** is one of the largest jellyfish in the world. Its bell often measures about a metre, and its tentacles are very long. In some **Swiss lakes** a small **freshwater jellyfish** lives. It is only about 2 centimetres across and harmless to humans.

gewusst: Jellyfish have existed for more than 500 million years, much longer than the dinosaurs.
Even a dead jellyfish on the beach can still sting, so you should not touch it.
The freshwater jellyfish in Swiss lakes usually shows itself only in warm summers.

teile.einleitung: New York City is the city with the most inhabitants in the USA. It is famous for its skyscrapers, Central Park and the Statue of Liberty. The UN also has its headquarters here.
wichtigste: New York is the biggest city in the USA, with over 8 million inhabitants.
The city consists of five boroughs.
On the island of Manhattan stand most of the skyscrapers.
The Brooklyn Bridge links Manhattan with Brooklyn.
The United Nations has its headquarters in New York.
West of Manhattan flows the Hudson River.

abschnitte.text: New York City consists of five **boroughs**: **Manhattan**, **Brooklyn**, **Queens**, the **Bronx** and **Staten Island**. Over 8 million people live here, more than in any other city in the USA. Manhattan is a narrow island between the **Hudson River** in the west and the **East River** in the east. The Hudson separates New York from the state of New Jersey. The city lies on the east coast of the USA on the Atlantic.

abschnitte.titel: From New Amsterdam to New York
abschnitte.text: First the **Dutch** founded a settlement here with the name **New Amsterdam**. In 1664 the English took it over and called it New York. Later millions of immigrants arrived by ship. As a welcome they saw the **Statue of Liberty**, a gift from France of 1886. To this day, people from almost all the countries of the world live in New York.

On Manhattan stand a great many **skyscrapers**. The **Empire State Building** was finished in 1931 and for a long time was the tallest building in the world. The **Brooklyn Bridge** is an old, world-famous suspension bridge from 1883. It links Manhattan with Brooklyn. At **Times Square** huge screens light up day and night, and many people celebrate New Year's Eve there.

In the middle of Manhattan lies **Central Park**, a huge park with lakes, meadows and paths. Typical of New York are the yellow taxis, the **“Yellow Cabs”**. In the city the **United Nations** (UN) has its headquarters. The UN has another important seat in **Geneva**. New York is also a centre for banks, theatres and museums.

gewusst: The New York subway runs round the clock, every day of the year.
When it opened in 1883, the Brooklyn Bridge was the longest suspension bridge in the world.

teile.einleitung: A pipeline is a long pipe through which crude oil, natural gas, water or other substances flow over long distances. Pipelines connect production sites with ports, refineries and cities. An important gas pipeline also runs through Switzerland.
wichtigste: A pipeline is a long pipe for oil, gas or other substances.
The Druzhba pipeline brings Russian crude oil to central Europe; Druzhba means friendship.
The Trans-Alaska Pipeline runs about 1,300 km to the port of Valdez.
The Transitgas pipeline crosses Switzerland from Wallbach to the Gries Pass.
In September 2022 explosions damaged the Nord Stream pipelines in the Baltic Sea.
A pig is used to clean and inspect pipelines.

abschnitte.text: A **pipeline** is made up of many steel pipes welded together. Pumps or compressors push crude oil or natural gas through the line. Pipelines often lie underground, on supports above the ground or on the sea bed. They can be thousands of kilometres long. For large amounts over land this is usually cheaper than transport by lorry or train.

The **Transitgas pipeline** begins at **Wallbach** on the High Rhine in the canton of Aargau. It crosses the Alps partly in tunnels and is connected to the Italian network near the **Gries Pass**. In the past the gas flowed only from northern Europe to Italy. Since the **reverse-flow conversion**, completed in 2017, it can also flow from south to north. This increases security of supply.

The **Druzhba pipeline** was built in the 1960s, and its name is Russian for “friendship”. It supplied the Eastern Bloc states of the time with crude oil. The **Trans-Alaska Pipeline** runs about 1,300 km from the oil fields at Prudhoe Bay to the ice-free port of **Valdez**. Since 2019 the **“Power of Siberia”** pipeline has brought gas from eastern Siberia to **China**, and since 2020 the **Trans Adriatic Pipeline** has delivered gas from **Azerbaijan** to Italy.

Pipelines make countries dependent on one another: the supplying country on the buyer and the other way round. That is why they are often a topic in **politics**. In **September 2022** underwater explosions damaged three of the four strings of the **Nord Stream 1 and 2** pipelines in the Baltic Sea. Large amounts of gas escaped. New pipelines such as the TAP are meant to help reduce dependence on single suppliers.

To keep a pipeline safe, it has to be cleaned and inspected. For this a **pig** is sent through the line. This is a device that fits exactly into the pipe and is pushed forward by the oil or gas. Simple pigs push deposits out. **Smart pigs** measure the wall thickness on the way and find damage before a leak occurs.

gewusst: The Trans-Alaska Pipeline stands on supports in many places, so that the warm oil does not thaw the frozen ground.
In German the device is called a “Molch”, which means a newt: it slips through the pipe like one.

teile.einleitung: Peru is a country in the west of South America on the Pacific Ocean. It was once the centre of the Inca Empire. The country has deserts on the coast, high mountains in the Andes and rainforest in the east.
wichtigste: The capital of Peru is Lima, the largest city in the country.
Cusco used to be the capital of the Incas.
Quechua is an official language alongside Spanish.
The currency is called the sol.
The flag is red, white, red.
The famous Nazca Lines lie in the desert.

abschnitte.text: Peru has three very different landscapes. On the **coast** it is dry and there are deserts. The capital **Lima**, the largest city in the country, is also there. In the middle the high **Andes** run through the country. In the east the **Amazon rainforest** begins. Lake Titicaca on the border with Bolivia also belongs partly to Peru.

**Cusco** used to be the capital of the Inca Empire. The city lies high in the mountains at about 3,400 metres. Many walls from the Inca period still stand there today. Not far away lies the famous ruined city of **Machu Picchu**. The old Andean language **Quechua** has been spoken for centuries and is today an **official language** alongside Spanish. Millions of people still speak it.

In the desert in the south of Peru there are huge pictures in the ground: the **Nazca Lines**. They are more than 1,500 years old. They are best seen from the air. They show, for example, a monkey, a **hummingbird** and a spider. Why the people made them is still not fully understood.

The flag of Peru has three vertical stripes: **red, white, red**. Red and white are also the colours of the Swiss flag. In Peru people pay with the **sol**. In Spanish the word means “sun”. The sun was very important to the Incas, who worshipped the sun god Inti.

A famous dish is **ceviche**. For it, raw fish is marinated in **lime juice**. The juice firms up the fish, rather as cooking does. Many kinds of **potato** also come from Peru. People in the Andes had been growing them for a long time before the potato came to Europe and to Switzerland.

gewusst: In Peru there are thousands of different kinds of potato.
The Nazca Lines are so big that you cannot make out some of the figures from the ground at all.

teile.einleitung: The Ob is one of the great rivers of Siberia in Russia. It flows through the flat West Siberian Plain to the north into the Arctic Ocean. Together with its tributary the Irtysh, it forms one of the longest river systems on Earth.
wichtigste: The Ob flows in Siberia from south to north.
Its most important tributary is the Irtysh, which flows through Kazakhstan.
The Ob-Irtysh river system is about 5,400 kilometres long.
The Ob flows into the Gulf of Ob, a long bay of the Kara Sea.
On the Ob lies the big city of Novosibirsk.
In the area of the lower Ob, large amounts of oil and natural gas are produced.

abschnitte.text: The Ob forms in the **Altai Mountains** in the south of Siberia from two headwater rivers. Then it flows through the **West Siberian Plain**, one of the biggest lowlands on Earth. Because the land is so flat, the water drains slowly, and there are huge **swamps**. In winter the river is frozen for months.

The most important tributary is the **Irtysh**. It rises in China, flows through **Kazakhstan** and joins the Ob in Russia. Measured from the source of the Irtysh, the **Ob-Irtysh** river system is about 5,400 kilometres long. This makes it one of the longest river systems in Asia and the world.

The Ob flows into the **Gulf of Ob**, a sea bay over 700 kilometres long on the **Kara Sea**. The Kara Sea is part of the Arctic Ocean. The Gulf of Ob is one of the longest estuaries in the world. It too is frozen over for a long time in winter.

The biggest city on the Ob is **Novosibirsk**. It was founded in 1893 where the **Trans-Siberian Railway** crosses the river, and today it is the third biggest city in Russia. In the area of the lower Ob lie some of the biggest **oil** and **natural gas fields** in the world. A large part of Russian natural gas comes from there.

gewusst: Novosibirsk arose only because of a railway bridge over the Ob.
The Gulf of Ob is much longer than Switzerland from Geneva to Lake Constance.

teile.einleitung: A **pumped-storage power station** is a kind of giant battery made of water. It stores electricity by pumping water up into a reservoir at a higher level. When electricity is needed later, the water flows back down and drives turbines.
wichtigste: A pumped-storage power station has two reservoirs at different heights.
When there is a surplus of electricity, it pumps water into the upper lake.
When electricity is needed, the water flows down again through turbines.
In this way electricity can be stored until it is needed.
A well-known example is Nant de Drance in the Valais, opened in 2022.
Some of the energy is lost in pumping and in flowing back.

abschnitte.text: Electricity is hard to store in large amounts. A pumped-storage power station solves this with water and height. It has a **lower** and an **upper reservoir**. When there is more electricity than is needed, electric **pumps** drive water upwards. The water above then holds stored energy, like a ball that you lift onto a table.

abschnitte.titel: Electricity at the push of a button
abschnitte.text: When the demand for electricity rises, the pipes are opened. The water rushes down through pipes and drives **turbines**. These move **generators**, which produce electricity. Often the same machines serve both as a pump and as a turbine. A big advantage: a pumped-storage power station can deliver a great deal of electricity within a few minutes.

abschnitte.titel: Nant de Drance in the Valais
abschnitte.text: A particularly large pumped-storage power station is **Nant de Drance** in the Lower Valais, near the border with France. It uses the **Lac d’Emosson** and the higher reservoir **Vieux Emosson**. The machines stand in a huge cavern deep inside the mountain. The power station was opened in **2022**. In the canton of Glarus too there is a large pumped-storage power station, **Linth-Limmern**.

Solar and wind power stations do not always deliver the same amount of electricity. At midday the sun shines strongly, at night not at all. Pumped-storage power stations help to **even out** these swings. It cannot be done entirely without loss, however: of the energy used for pumping, about three quarters to four fifths is recovered.

Switzerland has many mountains and reservoirs. That is why it is well suited to pumped-storage power stations. They are also used for exchanging electricity with the neighbouring countries. Sometimes Switzerland is therefore called the **“battery of Europe”**. Pumped-storage power stations exist all over the world, though, for example in China, Japan and the USA.

gewusst: Nant de Drance can deliver about as much power as a large nuclear power station, but only until the upper lake is empty.
Pumped-storage power stations are the most common way in the world of storing large amounts of electricity.

teile.einleitung: Overtourism means that a place has too many tourists. The visitors then go beyond the limits of what the place can bear. The locals suffer from it, but so do the guests themselves.
wichtigste: Overtourism is tourism that goes beyond the limits of what a place can bear.
Typical consequences are overcrowding, rising rents and protests.
Since 2024 Venice has charged day visitors an entry fee on certain days.
Far fewer people live in the old town of Venice today than before.
Since 2021 big cruise ships have no longer been allowed to pass through the centre of Venice.
Barcelona wants to let all licences for tourist holiday flats run out by 2028.

abschnitte.text: The word **overtourism** means roughly “too much tourism”. If too many visitors come, the **quality of life** of the locals and the experience of the guests suffer. Typical are full lanes, noise, rubbish and **rising rents**. In 1975 the researcher **George Doxey** described in his **Irridex model** how the attitude of locals changes: from euphoria through apathy and annoyance to **antagonism**, that is, open rejection.

When flats become **holiday flats**, locals find it harder to find a home. Souvenir shops replace bakeries and neighbourhood shops. This displacement is called **touristification**, a term modelled on **gentrification**. In 2024 **Barcelona** announced that it would let all of the roughly 10,000 licences for tourist holiday flats run out by 2028. In the same year residents there protested against overtourism with water pistols.

**Venice** is visited every year by millions of day tourists. In the 1950s about 175,000 people lived in the old town, and in 2022 the number fell below **50,000**. Since 2021 big **cruise ships** have no longer been allowed to pass through the Giudecca Canal and the San Marco basin. Since April 2024 the city has charged day visitors an **entry fee** on peak days. In 2025 it cost 5 euros if booked early and 10 euros for late bookers.

Expert bodies of **UNESCO** saw Venice as threatened by mass tourism, climate change and building projects. In 2023 they recommended putting the city on the **List of World Heritage in Danger**. In September 2023, however, the World Heritage Committee decided against this listing. The discussion shows how hard it is to bring protection and tourism into balance.

Cities try to **steer the flows of visitors**: with fees, reservations, upper limits or rules for holiday flats. In Switzerland too, there is discussion about too many visitors at popular places, for example in **Lucerne** or in the **Lauterbrunnen Valley**. At the same time, tourism is an important source of income for many regions. Travellers can help by travelling outside the main season and visiting lesser-known places.

gewusst: Venice is the first big city in the world to charge day visitors an entry fee.
In the old town of Venice there are, on some days, more tourists than residents.

teile.einleitung: A rainforest is a dense forest in which it rains a great deal. The best-known rainforests lie in the tropics around the equator, where it is warm and wet all year round. More species of animals and plants live here than anywhere else on land.
wichtigste: The Amazon rainforest in South America is the largest rainforest in the world.
In the tropical rainforest it is warm and wet all year round.
Tropical rainforests lie in a belt around the equator.
Animals such as parrots, monkeys, jaguars and poison dart frogs live in the rainforest.
More than half of all species of animals and plants on Earth live in rainforests.
Rainforests are getting smaller because trees are being cut down.
Rainforests are important for the climate of the whole Earth.

abschnitte.text: A **tropical rainforest** grows where it rains almost every day and it is about 25 degrees all year round. Often more than 2,000 litres of rain per square metre fall in a year; in the Swiss Plateau it is about half as much. Because there are no winters, the trees are always green. There are also cooler rainforests, for example on the west coast of Canada.

The largest tropical rainforests lie in South America, in Central Africa and in South-East Asia. The **Amazon rainforest** extends over several countries, above all Brazil. The second largest rainforest lies in the Congo Basin in Africa. There are also large rainforests on islands such as Borneo and New Guinea.

The rainforest is built up like a house with several **storeys**. At the very top, single giant trees rise over 50 metres high. Beneath them the dense **canopy** forms a green roof in which most of the animals live. On the ground it is dark, damp and warm, because only little light gets through.

In the rainforest live colourful **parrots** such as macaws, monkeys, sloths, jaguars and poisonous frogs. There are countless insects, and many species have not even been discovered yet. Plants such as orchids and bromeliads grow high up on the branches of other trees. Many fruits and spices such as cocoa, bananas and vanilla originally come from tropical forests.

Every year large areas of rainforest are cut down or burnt. The space is used for cattle pastures, soya fields and plantations for **palm oil**, and the wood is used. With the forest, animals and plants disappear, and so does the living space of the people who live there. In addition, a lot of carbon dioxide gets into the air, which strengthens global warming.

Many **indigenous peoples** have lived in the rainforest for centuries and protect it. Bruno Manser from Basel lived in the 1980s with the Penan on Borneo and campaigned against the clearing of their forest. He has been missing since 2000, and his fund still carries on its work today. You can also help when shopping, for example with wood and paper from sustainable forestry.

begriffe.erklaerung: The warm region around the equator between the two tropics.
The dense, green layer made up of the treetops in the forest.
The felling of many trees so that the forest disappears.
Original inhabitants who have lived in an area for a very long time.

gewusst: A sloth moves so slowly that algae grow on its fur.
The Amazon carries more water than any other river in the world.
Many medicines have been developed from plants of the rainforest.

teile.einleitung: Pitch Lake is a lake of natural asphalt on the Caribbean island of Trinidad. It is regarded as the largest natural asphalt deposit in the world. Instead of water it contains a thick, black mass, which you can even walk on in many places.
wichtigste: Pitch Lake lies in the south of the island of Trinidad.
It is the largest natural asphalt deposit in the world.
Pitch is another word for tar.
The asphalt is formed from crude oil that rises from deep underground.
Asphalt has been mined there for a long time, for example for road building.

abschnitte.text: **Pitch Lake** lies near the village of La Brea in the south of **Trinidad**. It covers an area of about 40 hectares. The lake is filled with **asphalt**, a thick, black mass. At the surface it is so firm that you can walk on it in many places. Underneath it is softer and moves slowly. In hollows rainwater collects into small pools.

Beneath Trinidad lie large deposits of **crude oil** and **natural gas**. Some of the oil rises up through cracks in the rock. At the surface the light parts evaporate. What remains is a heavy, sticky mass, **natural asphalt**. Over a long time, a huge amount of it has gathered in Pitch Lake. The island is also known for its oil and gas production in other ways.

People used the asphalt early on. The English explorer **Walter Raleigh** is said to have used it in 1595 to seal his ships. Later the asphalt was mined in large amounts and sold to many countries, mainly for **road building**. Although a great deal is taken out, the lake slowly fills up again from below.

gewusst: Tiny microbes live in the thick asphalt of Pitch Lake, although there is hardly any water there.
Pitch Lake is a well-known sight, and guides show visitors where it is safe to walk.

teile.einleitung: The Orinoco crocodile is one of the rarest crocodiles in the world. It lives only in the area of the Orinoco in Venezuela and Colombia. In the past it was hunted so heavily for its skin that today it is critically endangered.
wichtigste: The Orinoco crocodile lives only in the Orinoco river system.
It occurs in Venezuela and Colombia.
It has a long, narrow snout.
In the 20th century it was hunted heavily for its skin.
Today it is critically endangered.

abschnitte.text: The Orinoco crocodile is called **Crocodylus intermedius** scientifically. It is one of the big crocodile species, and adult males can grow to about five metres long. Typical is its long, **narrow snout**. It eats mainly **fish**, but also other animals that come to the water. It lives in rivers and lagoons of the **Llanos**, the wide grass plains.

In the 20th century very many Orinoco crocodiles were hunted for their **skin**. It was made into leather for bags and shoes. As a result the populations almost completely collapsed. Today the species is regarded as **critically endangered**. New dangers are the destruction of its habitat and poaching.

In Venezuela and Colombia there are programmes to protect the species. In **breeding stations** young crocodiles are raised. When they are big enough, they are released in protected areas. In this way the population is meant to recover slowly.

gewusst: Young Orinoco crocodiles are raised in breeding stations until they are big enough for the wild.

teile.einleitung: The Peruvian anchovy is a small shoaling fish from the Pacific off Peru and Chile. It is caught in huge quantities, mainly for fishmeal and fish oil. It is also called anchoveta.
wichtigste: The Peruvian anchovy lives off the coasts of Peru and Chile.
It is also called anchoveta.
The cold Humboldt Current brings many nutrients and therefore plenty of food.
It is mainly processed into fishmeal and fish oil.
During the climate phenomenon El Niño, stocks often fall sharply.

abschnitte.titel: A small fish in huge shoals
abschnitte.text: The Peruvian anchovy is a slim, silvery fish and usually grows to barely 20 centimetres. It lives in large **shoals** near the surface of the water. Off the coast of Peru flows the cold **Humboldt Current**. It brings nutrient-rich water up from the depths. In it grows a lot of **plankton**, the food of the anchovies. This is how huge shoals come about.

abschnitte.titel: One of the biggest fisheries in the world
abschnitte.text: Hardly any other kind of fish is caught in such large amounts. Only a small part is eaten. Most of it is processed into **fishmeal** and **fish oil**. From these people make, for example, feed for farmed fish, pigs and chickens. Seabirds such as pelicans and cormorants also eat the anchovies. Their droppings, **guano**, used to be mined as a valuable fertiliser.

During **El Niño** the water off Peru becomes warmer, and fewer nutrients rise to the surface. Then the anchovies find less food, and stocks fall sharply. In the early 1970s the catch collapsed dramatically after overfishing and an El Niño. Since then Peru has set **catch limits** to protect the stocks.

gewusst: In some years more Peruvian anchovy was caught than any other kind of fish in the world.
Part of the fish feed used in fish farms around the world comes from these small fish from Peru.

teile.einleitung: The mouth is the place where a river ends. There it flows into a sea, a lake or another river. Mouths can look very different, for example as a delta with many arms.
wichtigste: At the mouth a river flows into a sea, a lake or another river.
In a delta, the river splits into many arms before the sea.
Delta is a letter of the Greek alphabet.
The Alpine Rhine flows into Lake Constance, the Rhône into Lake Geneva.
The Ticino flows into the Po near Pavia.
At the mouth into the sea the water is often slightly salty.

abschnitte.text: Every river has a beginning, the **source**, and an end, the **mouth**. At the mouth the water flows into a sea, a lake or another river. A river that flows into a bigger river is called a **tributary**. The place where two rivers come together is also called a confluence. After flowing into a lake, the river can leave the lake again and flow on.

A **delta** forms when a river brings a lot of sand and mud. At the mouth the water flows more slowly, and the material is deposited. The river then splits into many small **arms**. The name comes from the Greek letter **delta**, which looks like a triangle. Many river mouths have a similar shape. Well-known deltas are those of the Nile in Egypt and the Rhine in the Netherlands.

Not every river forms a delta. Some rivers flow into the sea in a wide funnel, which is called an **estuary**. There, ebb and flood tide push the seawater far up the river. An example is the Elbe at Hamburg. At every mouth into the sea, **fresh water** mixes with **salt water**. This slightly salty water is called **brackish water**.

The **Alpine Rhine** flows into **Lake Constance** at its eastern end. After that the Rhine flows on to Schaffhausen and finally all the way to the North Sea. The **Rhône** flows through the whole of the Valais and flows into **Lake Geneva** at **Le Bouveret**. The **Ticino** flows through Lake Maggiore into Italy and joins the **Po** near **Pavia**. The Aare joins the Rhine at Koblenz in the canton of Aargau.

Mouths and deltas are often very fertile because the river deposits nutrient-rich mud. Many **birds** rest there on their journey south. At river mouths into lakes, reed beds and floodplain forests form. On Lake Constance and Lake Geneva such areas are now nature reserves. In the past many mouths were straightened, and today some are being restored to a natural state.

gewusst: Where the Aare joins the Rhine, the Aare carries on average more water than the Rhine.
The Rhône delta on the Mediterranean is called the Camargue and is known for flamingos and white horses.

tg3chl1.t: Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries

teile.einleitung: OPEC is the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries. Its members are states that produce and sell a lot of crude oil. Together they try to influence the amount produced and so the oil price.
wichtigste: OPEC stands for “Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries”.
It was founded in Baghdad in September 1960.
Founding members were Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela.
Since 1965 OPEC has had its headquarters in Vienna.
With production quotas for its members it influences the oil price.
Since 2016 it has worked together with further countries such as Russia in the grouping “OPEC+”.

abschnitte.text: OPEC was founded in September 1960 at a conference in **Baghdad**. The five founding states **Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia** and **Venezuela** wanted more control over their oil. Until then, mainly big Western **oil companies** had set the prices. The Venezuelan minister **Juan Pablo Pérez Alfonzo** is regarded as one of the fathers of the organisation.

At first OPEC had its headquarters in **Geneva**. In 1965 it moved to **Vienna**. Austria, as a neutral country, offered favourable conditions. There the ministers of the member states meet regularly to decide on production levels.

OPEC sets **production quotas** for its members. If less is produced, supply becomes scarcer, and the price tends to rise. In economics, such an agreement among suppliers on quantities and prices is called a **cartel**. **Saudi Arabia** has a special role. It has big unused production capacities and can adjust its supply quickly. It is therefore called the “swing producer”.

Since 2016 the OPEC states have coordinated with further producing countries in the grouping **OPEC+**. The biggest partner is **Russia**. The members change again and again. **Qatar** left at the start of 2019 in order to concentrate more on natural gas. **Angola** left OPEC at the start of 2024 in a dispute over its production quota.

In 1973 Arab producing countries cut back their deliveries, and the oil price rose sharply. This **oil crisis** hit many countries, Switzerland too. Here in autumn 1973 there were three **car-free Sundays**, on which you were not allowed to drive. After that, many countries began to save more energy and to look for other sources of energy.

gewusst: On the car-free Sundays of 1973, people in Switzerland walked and cycled on empty roads and motorways.
Venezuela has some of the biggest known oil reserves in the world.

teile.einleitung: Fog is a cloud that lies right on the ground. It consists of tiny water droplets floating in the air. In the Swiss Plateau, fog is a frequent visitor in autumn and winter.
wichtigste: Fog consists of tiny water droplets in the air.
It is a cloud that lies right at the bottom, on the ground.
In dense fog you can see only a few metres.
In the Plateau there is especially often fog in autumn and winter.
From the mountains the layer of fog looks like a sea, the sea of fog.
In the morning fog is often at its densest.

abschnitte.text: **Fog** consists of countless tiny **water droplets** floating in the air. Fog is really a **cloud** that lies right at the bottom, on the ground. We speak of fog when you can see less than a kilometre. When you walk through fog, your skin and hair become **damp**. These are the little droplets that stick to you.

Air always contains some **water vapour**, which you cannot see. If the air cools down, it can hold less water vapour. Then small droplets form from the vapour, and fog arises. This often happens in clear nights, when the ground cools strongly. That is why fog is often densest in the **morning**. Later the Sun warms the air, and the fog clears.

In **autumn and winter** there is often a thick, grey layer of fog in the Swiss Plateau. Cold air is heavy and collects at the bottom between the Jura and the Alps. Above it lies warmer air like a lid. That is why the fog can sometimes stay for days. Often it lies a little above the ground, and then it is called **high fog** (“Hochnebel”).

The fog often lies only down in the valley. Further up **in the mountains** the Sun then shines, and it is sometimes even warmer than below. From a mountain the layer of fog looks like a white sea, which is why it is called a **sea of fog**. Only the tops of the hills stick out like islands. On such days many people go up high to escape the grey blanket.

In dense fog the droplets block your **view**. You can see only a few metres. That is why cars switch on their **lights** in fog, so that others can see them better. They drive slowly and keep more distance. Pedestrians and cyclists, too, should wear bright clothes or reflective strips to be easily visible.

gewusst: When fog freezes onto trees and fences in frost, hoar frost forms.
In some deserts, such as the Namib, fog is the most important source of water for plants and animals.

teile.einleitung: The **Pyramids of Giza** stand in Egypt, on the edge of the capital Cairo. They are more than 4,500 years old and are among the most famous buildings in the world. The ancient Egyptians built them as tombs for their kings, the pharaohs.
wichtigste: Three large pyramids stand at Giza.
They belong to the pharaohs Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure.
The largest is the Great Pyramid of Khufu, which was originally about 146 metres high.
The pyramids were built as tombs for pharaohs.
They are made of millions of blocks of stone, mainly limestone.
In front of the pyramids lies the Great Sphinx with a lion’s body and a human head.
The pyramids are more than 4,500 years old.

abschnitte.text: On a plateau near Cairo stand **three great pyramids**. They were built for the pharaohs **Khufu** (Cheops), **Khafre** (Chephren) and **Menkaure** (Mycerinus). Beside them there are several smaller pyramids, for example for queens. The pyramids were built more than **4,500 years ago**. Since 1979 they have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

The **Great Pyramid of Khufu** is the largest of all. It was originally about **146 metres** high. Today its tip is missing, so it is slightly lower. For almost 4,000 years it was the tallest building in the world. It is also the only one of the **Seven Wonders** of the ancient world that still stands today.

The ancient Egyptians believed in a **life after death**. The pyramids were huge **tombs** in which the pharaohs were to rest after their death. Inside, narrow passages lead to burial chambers. Beside the pyramids lay temples in which priests made offerings. Most of the grave treasures were already stolen in ancient times by tomb robbers.

The pyramids are made of **millions of blocks of stone**, mainly **limestone**. Some blocks weigh many tonnes. The workers cut the stones with tools of copper and stone and probably hauled them up on sledges and ramps. Researchers have found remains of settlements in which the builders lived. They were well-organised workers, not slaves, as people often used to think.

In front of the pyramids lies the **Great Sphinx**. It is a mythical creature with the **body of a lion** and the **head of a human**. The Sphinx was carved straight out of the **rock**. It is more than 70 metres long. Many researchers think that its face is meant to show the pharaoh Khafre.

gewusst: The sides of the Great Pyramid of Khufu are aligned almost exactly with the four points of the compass.
In the past the pyramids were covered with smooth, light limestone slabs and gleamed in the sun.

teile.einleitung: Lake Superior is the biggest of the five Great Lakes in North America. By area it is even the biggest freshwater lake on Earth. It lies on the border between Canada and the USA.
wichtigste: Lake Superior is called “Oberer See” in German.
By area it is the biggest freshwater lake in the world.
At about 82,000 km², it is roughly twice as big as Switzerland.
On its north shore lies the Canadian province of Ontario.
At its deepest point it is about 400 metres deep.
It drains via the St. Marys River into Lake Huron.

abschnitte.text: Lake Superior lies right at the top of the chain of the **Great Lakes**. That is where the name **Lake Superior** comes from, because “superior” means “the upper one”. The whole north shore belongs to the Canadian province of **Ontario**. On the south shore lie the US states of **Minnesota**, **Wisconsin** and **Michigan**.

Lake Superior covers about **82,000 km²**, while Switzerland covers about 41,000 km². So it is about **twice as big** as Switzerland. Its deepest point lies about **406 metres** below the water surface, which makes it the deepest of the five Great Lakes. On the lake there are high waves and dangerous storms, as on the sea.

The lake drains via the **St. Marys River** into **Lake Huron**. At the city of **Sault Ste. Marie**, big **locks** help ships over a difference in height of about 6 to 7 metres. Huge freighters carry iron ore and grain. In November 1975 the freighter **Edmund Fitzgerald** sank in a severe autumn storm, and all 29 crew members lost their lives.

The biggest island in the lake is **Isle Royale** in the north-west. It belongs to the state of Michigan and is a **national park** of the USA. The island is known for its **wolves** and **moose**. Researchers have been observing there for decades how predators and prey live together.

gewusst: Lake Superior contains more water than all the other Great Lakes together.
French explorers called it “Lac Supérieur”, which became the English name.

teile.einleitung: An oasis is a green place in the middle of the desert. There is water there, so plants grow and people can live. Oases used to be important resting places for caravans.
wichtigste: An oasis is a green place with water in the desert.
The water mostly comes from the ground, as a spring or from wells.
Typical of oases are date palms.
In the shade of the palms, people grow vegetables, grain and herbs.
Caravans stopped at oases to fetch water.
Well-known oases in Egypt are Siwa and the Fayum.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the water come from?
abschnitte.text: In some places under the desert there is **groundwater**. In an oasis it comes out as a **spring** or is drawn from **wells**. Some oases lie on a river, like the **Fayum** in Egypt. There an old canal, the **Bahr Yussuf**, brings water from the Nile. If the water in the ground runs out, the oasis dries up and becomes desert again.

The most important trees of the oasis are **date palms**. They like heat and need water at their roots. Their sweet fruits are an important food. In the **shade** of the palms it is cooler. There people plant **vegetables**, **grain** and herbs. In this way several storeys of plants arise one above the other.

A **caravan** is a group of travellers with many camels. In the past traders moved through the desert in long caravans. The camels carried salt, cloth and other goods. The journey was long and hot, so the caravans stopped at oases. There was water there for people and animals.

A **wadi** is a mostly dried-up river valley in the desert. It carries water only after rare heavy rainfall, and then dangerous **flash floods** can suddenly occur. A famous oasis is **Siwa** in the west of Egypt, with many springs and date palms. In the Sahara and on the Arabian Peninsula there are also many oases.

gewusst: Camels can go a long time without drinking and then drink a great deal of water at once.
The word oasis comes from Ancient Egyptian.

teile.einleitung: Palm oil is the most produced vegetable oil in the world. It is in many foods, cosmetics and cleaning products. Because a lot of rainforest has been cleared for plantations, palm oil is also highly controversial.
wichtigste: Palm oil is pressed from the flesh of the oil palm fruit.
The oil palm originally comes from West Africa.
Indonesia is the biggest producer, ahead of Malaysia.
Together the two countries supply about 85 per cent of palm oil.
No other oil plant yields as much oil per hectare.
Rainforests and peatlands were destroyed for plantations.
In 2021 Switzerland narrowly voted in favour of a free trade agreement with Indonesia.

abschnitte.text: The oil palm (Elaeis guineensis) is native to the west and centre of **Africa**. The name “guineensis” points to this too. It came to South-East Asia only in the colonial period. Its fruits grow in big bunches. **Palm oil** is pressed from the orange-red **flesh of the fruit**, whereas **palm kernel oil** comes from the kernel in the middle of the fruit. The two oils are made up differently.

The oil palm gives the **highest oil yield per hectare** of all oil plants, many times that of rape, soya or sunflowers. A palm bears fruit for about 25 years. Palm oil is semi-solid at room temperature and keeps for a long time. That is why it is often used, for example in margarine, chocolate spread, biscuits, soaps and candles. **Indonesia** also uses a large part of it as an additive to **biodiesel**.

Indonesia and Malaysia together make about 85 per cent of palm oil. For new plantations a lot of **rainforest** was cleared. Especially threatened are the **orangutans** on Borneo and Sumatra, whose habitat is being destroyed and cut up. For plantations, **peat swamp forests** were also drained. Peat stores huge amounts of carbon. When it is drained, it decomposes or burns, as in the big fires of 2015, and a lot of CO2 is released.

The **Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil**, **RSPO** for short, founded in 2004, certifies palm oil produced more sustainably. Producers, traders, banks and environmental organisations work together in it. The RSPO is registered as an **association under Swiss law**. Some environmental organisations find the rules too weak, others see in it an important step. Giving up palm oil is also controversial, because substitute oils need more land.

On 7 March 2021 Switzerland voted on the **free trade agreement** with Indonesia. At the centre of the discussion was palm oil. The agreement was narrowly accepted with **51.6 per cent** yes votes. Tariff concessions apply only to palm oil that meets certain **sustainability requirements**. Supporters saw in it opportunities for trade, and opponents feared further deforestation.

gewusst: Palm oil is the most produced vegetable oil on Earth.
One hectare of oil palms yields several tonnes of oil a year, much more than any other oil plant.

teile.einleitung: Outsourcing means that a company hands tasks over to another firm. Often this also involves work that is moved abroad. This has advantages and disadvantages and is much discussed in business and politics.
wichtigste: Outsourcing is the handing over of tasks to another firm.
If work is moved abroad, this is called offshoring.
Nearshoring means moving it to a nearby country.
Reshoring is the move back to the home country.
Bengaluru in India is an important centre for outsourced IT services.
Unit labour costs are central to decisions about moving work.

abschnitte.text: In **outsourcing**, an **external service provider** takes over tasks that were previously done within the company itself. This can be bookkeeping, cleaning, IT or a call centre. It makes no difference whether the provider is at home or abroad. If the work stays within the company's own group but is done by a **subsidiary** abroad, this is called **captive offshoring**.

If work is moved to a faraway country, this is called **offshoring**. In **nearshoring** the partner countries are close, for example from Switzerland to Eastern Europe. Shorter distances and similar time zones make working together easier. In **reshoring**, firms bring production back, for example because of rising wages abroad or uncertain supply chains. Since the 2020s people have also spoken of **friendshoring**, moving work to politically friendly countries.

**Bengaluru**, formerly Bangalore, is regarded as the “Silicon Valley of India”. Many IT firms and international groups have development centres there, because there are well-trained, English-speaking specialists. The **Philippines** have a big call centre industry, which mainly serves customers in the USA. In northern Mexico, **maquiladoras** assemble parts imported duty-free for export to the USA.

What matters are the **unit labour costs**. They show how much wage falls on one unit produced. Low wages are only worthwhile if **productivity** is not correspondingly lower. On top of that come costs for transport, supervision and coordination. In Switzerland wages are high, which is why Swiss firms, too, outsource some tasks.

Supporters say that outsourcing lowers costs and firms can concentrate on their **core tasks**. Critics point out that **jobs** can be lost at home. In addition, a firm becomes more dependent on its partners. For countries such as India or the Philippines, by contrast, new jobs are created. How you judge outsourcing often depends on your point of view.

gewusst: The word outsourcing is put together from the English words “outside”, “resource” and “using”.
Maquiladoras arose from the 1960s, mainly on the border with the USA.

teile.einleitung: Oil sands are a mixture of sand, clay, water and a thick crude oil mass called bitumen. The biggest deposits in the world lie in Canada. Extracting it is costly and puts a heavy strain on the environment.
wichtigste: The biggest oil sands deposits lie in the Canadian province of Alberta.
In oil sands the thick bitumen sticks to the grains of sand.
Deep bitumen is extracted with hot steam.
Fort McMurray is the centre of the oil sands industry.
Oil from oil sands usually causes more greenhouse gases than normal crude oil.
In Venezuela lies a huge heavy oil deposit, the Orinoco Belt.

abschnitte.text: **Oil sands** consist of sand, clay, water and **bitumen**. Bitumen is a thick, tar-like crude oil mass that sticks to the grains of sand. It is so viscous that it does not flow out of a borehole like normal crude oil. The biggest deposits in the world lie in the province of **Alberta** in Canada, in the areas of Athabasca, Cold Lake and Peace River. They are among the biggest known sources of crude oil of all.

If the oil sands lie near the surface, they are removed by **open-pit mining** with huge diggers. Then bitumen and sand are separated with hot water. If they lie too deep, in the **SAGD** process hot **steam** is pressed into a borehole. The heated bitumen becomes more fluid and flows to a deeper production well. For transport through **pipelines**, it is mixed with lighter substances so that it is thin enough. This mixture is called **“dilbit”**.

The town of **Fort McMurray** lies in the middle of the mining area on the Athabasca River. It is the centre of the oil sands industry. In May 2016 a huge **forest fire** reached the town. About 88,000 people had to flee, and production was temporarily cut back sharply. Many oil companies, by contrast, have their headquarters in **Calgary**, far from the oil sands.

Extraction needs **a great deal of energy**, because a lot of natural gas is burned for steam, mining and processing. That is why oil from oil sands usually causes more **greenhouse gases** than easily produced crude oil. What is left behind is polluted water with sand, clay and oil residues. It is stored in huge **tailings ponds**, which endanger migratory birds and groundwater. Also controversial was the **Keystone XL** pipeline to the USA, which was finally abandoned in 2021.

In **Venezuela** too there are huge amounts of very thick oil. They lie in the **Orinoco Belt**, north of the Orinoco River. This **extra-heavy oil** is about as hard to extract as bitumen. Because it is counted, Venezuela officially reports the **biggest oil reserves** in the world.

gewusst: The tailings ponds in Alberta are so big that you can see them from space.
Pure bitumen is almost solid at normal temperatures.

teile.einleitung: Kaliningrad Oblast is an area of Russia on the Baltic Sea. It has no land connection to the rest of Russia, which is called an exclave. In the past the capital was called Königsberg and belonged to East Prussia.
wichtigste: Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave between Poland and Lithuania.
Since 2004 the area has been surrounded by EU states.
At the Potsdam Conference in 1945, the north of East Prussia was placed under the Soviet Union.
In the port of Baltiysk the Baltic Fleet has its main base.
Near Yantarny lie the biggest known amber deposits in the world.
The philosopher Immanuel Kant was born in Königsberg in 1724.

abschnitte.titel: An exclave on the Baltic Sea
abschnitte.text: An **exclave** is a part of a state that is separated from the rest of the state's territory. On land Kaliningrad borders only **Poland** and **Lithuania**. Since their EU accession in 2004, the area has been surrounded by the **European Union**. Between Kaliningrad and **Belarus**, on the Polish-Lithuanian border, lies a narrow strip of land, the **Suwałki Gap**. It is about 65 kilometres long and the only land connection of the Baltic states to the other NATO countries.

The city used to be called **Königsberg** and was a centre of **East Prussia**. After the Second World War the victorious powers decided at the **Potsdam Conference** in 1945 to place the north of East Prussia under the **Soviet Union**. The German population was expelled in the following years. In 1946 the city was given the name Kaliningrad. Since the end of the Soviet Union the area has belonged to Russia.

In the port of **Baltiysk**, Russia's **Baltic Fleet** is stationed. The port is **ice-free** all year round. That is why it is strategically valuable to Russia. Because of its position between NATO states, the area is often mentioned in politics.

**Amber** is fossilised resin from ancient trees. In the open-cast mine at **Yantarny** lie the biggest known amber deposits in the world. Most of the amber mined worldwide comes from there. On the beaches of the Baltic Sea you can sometimes find small pieces.

The philosopher **Immanuel Kant** was born in Königsberg in 1724 and spent almost his whole life there. Today's university bears his name. Also famous is the **Königsberg bridge problem**: can you cross each of the seven bridges of the city exactly once? The Basel mathematician **Leonhard Euler** proved in 1736 that this is not possible. With this he founded **graph theory**.

gewusst: The solution to a walking puzzle in Königsberg became the start of a new field of mathematics.
Leonhard Euler from Basel was shown on the former ten-franc note.

teile.einleitung: The Northwest Passage is a sea route through the icy Arctic Ocean. It runs north of North America from the Atlantic to the Pacific. For centuries sailors looked for this route, and many expeditions failed because of the ice.
wichtigste: The Northwest Passage connects the Atlantic with the Pacific in the far north of America.
It runs through the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, the many islands in the north of Canada.
European traders looked here for a shorter sea route to Asia.
Roald Amundsen was the first to sail through the passage completely by ship, from 1903 to 1906.
Canada regards the waters as its own internal waters, while other states see an international strait.
Because the sea ice is receding, the passage is passable more often in summer than before.

abschnitte.text: Since the 16th century, sailors from Europe looked for a northern route to **China** and **India**. It was meant to spare the long voyage round Africa or South America. In 1610 **Henry Hudson** in doing so reached a huge bay in Canada, which is today called **Hudson Bay**. After a mutiny he was set adrift and was never seen again. Many other expeditions returned without success.

In 1845 the Briton **John Franklin** set off with the ships **Erebus** and **Terror**. The ships got stuck in the ice, and none of the men came back. Many search parties afterwards explored the islands. Only in the 21st century did Canadian teams find the wrecks: the Erebus in 2014 and the Terror in 2016.

**Robert McClure** came from the west from 1850 to 1854. His ship got stuck in the ice, but with his crew he reached a ship from the east on foot. Making it entirely by ship was achieved only by the Norwegian **Roald Amundsen** with the little **Gjøa**. He spent the winter in the ice several times. From 1940 to 1942 the **St. Roch** of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, under Henry Larsen, sailed as the first ship from west to east, and in 1944 it made the passage in a single season.

The passage runs through the **Canadian Arctic Archipelago**. Between the islands there are several possible routes, which are often blocked by ice. **Canada** regards these waterways as its own **internal waters**. Other states, for example the USA, see in them an **international strait** through which all ships may sail freely.

Because of **global warming**, more **sea ice** melts in summer. For some years now the passage has therefore been at times low in ice and has been used more often. Even so, the voyage remains dangerous, because drifting ice, fog and storms are common. The counterpart on the other side of the Arctic is the **Northeast Passage** along the coast of Russia.

gewusst: For the first complete voyage through the Northwest Passage, Amundsen needed about three years.
The wrecks of the Franklin expedition lay undiscovered in the Arctic sea for over 160 years.

teile.einleitung: Poison dart frogs are small, brightly coloured frogs from the rainforests of Central and South America. Their skin contains poison, and their colours warn enemies of it. Some species are among the most poisonous animals in the world.
wichtigste: Poison dart frogs live in the rainforests of Central and South America.
Most are only about 1.5 to 5 centimetres long.
Their poison is in the skin.
The bright colours warn enemies.
The poison comes from their food, for example from ants and mites.
In zoos they become harmless because they are given other food.
The golden poison frog is among the most poisonous animals in the world.

abschnitte.text: Most poison dart frogs are only **1.5 to 5 centimetres** long, and many are shorter than a thumb. They glow in yellow, red, blue, green or orange, often with black spots. These bright colours are called **warning colours**. They tell enemies: Watch out, I am poisonous! That is why many animals leave them alone. Unlike many frogs, they are often out and about during the day.

Poison dart frogs live in the damp **rainforests** of Central and South America, most species in **South America**. They stay on the forest floor, among leaves and on plants. There they eat tiny animals such as **ants**, mites and small beetles. The damp, warm air is important for their delicate skin.

The **poison** is in the frogs’ **skin**. Anyone who eats or licks them can become ill. The surprising thing is that the frogs do not make the poison entirely themselves. They take in certain substances with their food, above all from ants and mites, and make their poison from them. In a **zoo** they are given other food and so usually become **harmless**.

Indigenous peoples in South America rubbed the poison of some species onto their **hunting darts**. This let them bring down animals. That is where the name poison dart frog comes from. Especially dangerous is the **golden poison frog** from **Colombia**. It is often bright yellow, and even a very small amount of its poison is dangerous.

Many poison dart frogs lay their eggs on land, for example under leaves. When the **tadpoles** hatch, they stick themselves to the **back** of a parent. The parent carries them to a small pool of water, for example in a plant where rainwater has collected. There the tadpoles keep growing until they become small frogs.

gewusst: Some poison dart frogs carry their tadpoles right up into the treetops, where rainwater collects in plants.
Researchers study the frogs’ poison because new medicines might perhaps be made from it.

teile.einleitung: The oceans take up a large part of the carbon dioxide (CO2) that we humans give off. As a result the chemistry of sea water changes: it slowly becomes more acidic. This process is called ocean acidification.
wichtigste: The seas have taken up about a quarter of the human-made CO2.
Dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid in the water.
The pH value at the sea surface has fallen since industrialisation from about 8.2 to about 8.1.
The sea is still slightly alkaline, but is becoming more acidic.
Mussels, corals and sea urchins find it harder to build their shells of lime.
In cold polar seas acidification is advancing especially fast.

abschnitte.titel: How the sea becomes more acidic
abschnitte.text: Carbon dioxide from the air dissolves in sea water. There it reacts with water to form **carbonic acid** (H2CO3). The carbonic acid gives off **hydrogen ions**, and the more of them there are in the water, the lower the **pH value** falls. The pH value measures how acidic or alkaline a liquid is: 7 is neutral, below that is acidic, above that alkaline.

abschnitte.titel: A small number, a big effect
abschnitte.text: Since the start of industrialisation the average pH value of surface water has fallen from about 8.2 to about 8.1. That sounds like little. But the pH scale is **logarithmic**: if the value falls by 0.1, the amount of hydrogen ions rises by about 26 per cent. So even a small change in the number means clearly more acid in the water.

Many sea animals build shells and skeletons from **calcium carbonate**, that is, lime. For this they need **carbonate ions** from the water. The extra hydrogen ions, however, bind carbonate ions, so that fewer of them are available. Mussels, corals, sea urchins and sea butterflies (pteropods) then have to use more energy. Especially sensitive is **aragonite**, a form of lime that dissolves more easily than calcite.

Gases dissolve better in cold water than in warm. That is why the seas in the polar regions take up especially a lot of CO2. There aragonite becomes scarce first. This hits tiny sea butterflies, which serve many fish and whales as food. In this way acidification can change whole **food webs**.

Ocean acidification has the same cause as global warming, namely CO2. But it works chemically and not through temperature. That is why it is often called “the other CO2 problem”. In the “Planetary Health Check” of 2025, researchers at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research rated it as the seventh of nine **planetary boundaries** to be exceeded. The most important protection is to give off less CO2.

gewusst: Without the seas, global warming would be much stronger, because they swallow so much CO2.
A fall in pH of just 0.1 means about a quarter more hydrogen ions in the water.

teile.einleitung: Lake Poopó lies on the Altiplano, the great high plateau in the Andes of Bolivia. For a long time it was the second largest lake in the country after Lake Titicaca. Because it is very shallow, it almost completely dried up in 2015.
wichtigste: Lake Poopó lies on the Altiplano in Bolivia, at over 3,600 metres above sea level.
It was the second largest lake in Bolivia after Lake Titicaca.
The lake is very shallow and salty.
It is fed mainly by the Desaguadero River from Lake Titicaca.
In 2015 it almost completely dried up.
The reasons were drought, water extraction and strong evaporation.

abschnitte.titel: A lake on the high plateau
abschnitte.text: **Lake Poopó** lies in the department of **Oruro** in Bolivia, on the **Altiplano**. This is a huge high plateau in the Andes at over 3,600 metres. The lake is very **shallow**, usually only a few metres deep, and its water is **salty**. It has no outflow to the sea. It gets its water mainly from the **Desaguadero** River, which comes from **Lake Titicaca**.

Because the lake is so shallow, its size varies a lot. In dry years it shrinks, in wet years it grows again. In **2015**, however, it **almost completely dried up**. The reasons were a long **drought**, the **extraction of water** for farming and mining, and strong **evaporation** in the thin, sunny mountain air. Many experts also see a link with **climate change**.

Many **fishermen** lived at the lake, including members of the **Uru** people. When the water disappeared, they lost their livelihood, and many had to move away. The lake was also important for animals, such as **flamingos** and other waterbirds. In later years the lake partly filled again after rainy seasons, but it remains very vulnerable.

gewusst: After 2015 many fishing boats simply lay in the sand on the dry lake bed.
Lake Poopó is protected as a wetland of international importance.

teile.einleitung: Canada is the second largest country in the world. It is a federal state and is divided into **10 provinces** and **3 territories**. The provinces can be compared a little with the Swiss cantons, but they are much bigger.
wichtigste: Canada is made up of 10 provinces and 3 territories.
The territories of Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut lie in the thinly populated north.
Quebec is the largest province by area, and Nunavut is larger still overall.
In Ontario lives almost 40 per cent of the Canadian population.
Newfoundland joined Canada only in 1949, as the last province.
Prince Edward Island is the smallest province.
New Brunswick is the only officially bilingual province.

abschnitte.text: Canada came into being in 1867 as a federal state made up of four provinces: Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. More were added later. The **provinces** have many rights of their own, for example over schools and health. The three **territories** in the north have fewer powers of their own, and the federal government has more say there. They are **Yukon**, the **Northwest Territories** and **Nunavut**.

The largest province by area is **Quebec** with about 1.5 million square kilometres. Only the territory of Nunavut is larger. Most people live in **Ontario**: the largest city, **Toronto**, and the capital, **Ottawa**, are there. The smallest province is **Prince Edward Island** in the Gulf of St Lawrence. It is even smaller than the canton of the Grisons.

**Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba** are called the **Prairie Provinces**. They lie in the flat middle of Canada, where a lot of wheat and rapeseed is grown. Right in the west lies **British Columbia** on the Pacific. In the east lie the Atlantic provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and **Newfoundland and Labrador**. Newfoundland was for a long time a British colony of its own and joined only in **1949**, as the tenth province.

Canada has two official languages, English and French. In **Quebec** the majority speak French. **New Brunswick** is the only province in which English and French are official languages with equal status. Many French-speaking **Acadians** live there. The other provinces are mainly English-speaking.

The youngest territory is **Nunavut**. It was split off from the Northwest Territories in **1999** and is home to many **Inuit**. In the Inuktitut language the name means “our land”. Nunavut is huge, but only very thinly populated. Many places can be reached only by plane or, in summer, by ship.

gewusst: Since 2001 the province of Newfoundland has officially been called “Newfoundland and Labrador”.
Nunavut is larger by area than any province of Canada, but has very few inhabitants.
The capital Ottawa lies in Ontario, right on the border with Quebec.

teile.einleitung: The polar regions are the coldest places on Earth. There are two of them: the Arctic around the North Pole and the Antarctic around the South Pole. There is a lot of ice, long dark winters and bright summers.
wichtigste: The two polar regions are called the Arctic and the Antarctic.
At the North Pole there is no land; the ice floats on the sea.
Antarctica is a continent under a thick layer of ice.
In the polar regions the sun shines at a very low angle, which is why it is cold.
In winter the sun does not rise for a long time, which is called the polar night.
Icebergs are pieces broken off glaciers.
Polar lights are often seen in the sky.

abschnitte.text: The **Arctic** lies around the **North Pole**. There is no land there, but the **Arctic Ocean**, on which a layer of ice floats. The **Antarctic** lies around the **South Pole**. There is a whole continent there, Antarctica, which lies under a very thick sheet of ice. In both regions it is very cold and windy.

In the polar regions the **sun** stands low in the sky. Its rays hit the Earth at a very **slanting angle** and are spread over a large area. That is why they give little warmth. On top of this, snow and ice reflect a lot of sunlight. So it stays cool even in summer.

In **winter** the sun stays below the horizon in the polar regions for weeks or months. This is called the **polar night**. In summer it is the other way round: the sun does not set for days or weeks. This is the **polar day**. In the dark nights, **polar lights** often shine green, red or violet in the sky.

An **iceberg** is a large piece of ice that has broken off a **glacier** or an ice shelf and floats in the sea. It is made of fresh water. Most of an iceberg lies invisible **under the water**, and only about a tenth sticks out. That is why icebergs are dangerous for ships.

In the Arctic live **polar bears**, seals, walruses and Arctic foxes. In the Antarctic live **penguins**, seals and many seabirds. So penguins and polar bears never meet in the wild. The animals have thick fur, dense feathers or a thick layer of fat that keeps them warm. People also live in the Arctic, for example the **Inuit**.

gewusst: On average Antarctica is the coldest, driest and windiest continent on Earth.
Most of the Earth’s fresh water is locked in the ice of Antarctica.

teile.einleitung: A marginal sea is a part of an ocean that is partly surrounded by land. Examples are the North Sea, the Mediterranean and the Black Sea. From Switzerland, water flows into several of these seas.
wichtigste: Marginal seas are parts of the oceans that are partly enclosed by land.
A fringing sea lies at the edge of an ocean and is broadly connected to it, like the North Sea.
An inland sea is almost completely surrounded by land, like the Mediterranean or the Black Sea.
The Bosporus connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Marmara.
The water of the Inn flows via the Danube into the Black Sea.
Water from Ticino reaches the Adriatic Sea via the Po.

abschnitte.text: The big **oceans** of the Earth are the Pacific, the Atlantic and the Indian Ocean. Parts of them that are partly surrounded by land are called **marginal seas**. There are two kinds. A **fringing sea** lies at the edge of an ocean and is broadly connected to it, often separated only by islands or peninsulas. The **North Sea** is a fringing sea of the Atlantic. An **inland sea**, by contrast, is almost completely surrounded by land and connected to the ocean only by a narrow strait.

The **Mediterranean** is an inland sea between Europe, Africa and Asia. It is connected to the Atlantic only by the Strait of Gibraltar. It has many smaller seas of its own. Between Greece and Turkey lies the **Aegean Sea** with many islands such as Crete and the Cyclades. Between the Italian mainland and the islands of Corsica and Sardinia lies the **Tyrrhenian Sea**, bounded in the south by Sicily. East of Italy lies the **Adriatic Sea**.

The **Black Sea** lies between south-eastern Europe and Asia Minor. It is connected via the **Bosporus** to the Sea of Marmara and from there on to the Mediterranean. The Bosporus is a narrow strait that runs right through the city of **Istanbul**. It separates Europe from Asia. Many big rivers flow into the Black Sea, for example the Danube.

Although Switzerland lies far from the sea, its water flows into several seas. The **Rhine** carries water to the **North Sea**, the **Rhône** to the **Mediterranean**. The **Inn** from the Engadine joins the Danube at Passau, and the Danube flows all the way to the **Black Sea**. The **Ticino** flows through Lake Maggiore into the **Po**, and the Po reaches the **Adriatic Sea** south of Venice.

Marginal seas often differ greatly from the open ocean. In the **Baltic Sea**, another inland sea, the water is only slightly salty because many rivers bring fresh water. The Mediterranean, by contrast, is saltier than the Atlantic because a lot of water evaporates there. In marginal seas, ebb and flood tide are often weaker. In the Mediterranean the tides are hardly noticeable on many beaches.

gewusst: From Piz Lunghin near Maloja, water flows into three different seas: the North Sea, the Adriatic and the Black Sea.
The Black Sea is almost without oxygen in its depths, so there is hardly any life down there.

teile.einleitung: The oil palm is a palm whose fruit is used to make palm oil. It is the most important oil plant in the world. Palm oil is in many things we use every day.
wichtigste: The oil palm supplies the most vegetable oil in the world.
It originally comes from West Africa.
Today it is grown mainly in Indonesia and Malaysia.
Palm oil is in foods, soaps and cosmetics.
For new plantations a lot of rainforest has been cleared.

abschnitte.text: The **oil palm** originally comes from **West Africa**. It grows only in the warm and humid climate of the **tropics**. Its fruits grow in big, heavy **bunches**. From the flesh of the fruit people get **palm oil**, from the kernel **palm kernel oil**. Today the oil palm is grown mainly in **Indonesia** and **Malaysia** on huge plantations.

abschnitte.titel: What palm oil is used for
abschnitte.text: The oil palm yields **a great deal of oil** per area, more than other oil plants such as rape or soya. That is why it is the most important oil plant in the world. Palm oil is in many **foods** such as margarine, chocolate spread or biscuits. It is also used in **soaps**, detergents and **cosmetics**. Part of it is also used as fuel.

For new plantations, big areas of **rainforest** have been cleared. As a result, animals such as the **orangutan** lose their habitat. That is why there are labels for **sustainable palm oil**, for example from the RSPO. Giving it up is not easy, though, because other oil plants would need even more land for the same amount of oil. In Switzerland, food must state whether it contains palm oil.

gewusst: An oil palm can grow to over 20 metres tall.
A single bunch of fruit of the oil palm can weigh over 20 kilograms.

teile.einleitung: On cold, clear mornings meadows, plants and car windows are often covered with white ice crystals. This is **hoar frost**. It forms when water vapour in the air turns directly into ice in frosty conditions.
wichtigste: Hoar frost consists of ice crystals that form on cold objects.
It forms at temperatures below 0 °C.
In the process water vapour turns directly into ice, without first becoming liquid.
Hoar frost forms mainly on clear, windless nights.
In spring, frost with hoar frost can damage young blossoms.

abschnitte.text: In the air there is always some invisible **water vapour**. If an object cools to below **0 °C**, the water vapour can turn straight into **ice** on it. It does not first become water. Experts call this process **deposition**. This is how fine, white **ice crystals** grow on grass, leaves, fences and car windows. If it is above zero degrees, water drops form instead: **dew**.

Hoar frost forms mainly on **clear, windless nights**. Without clouds the ground gives off a lot of heat and cools down strongly. Objects close to the ground then become especially cold. That is why the meadow is often white, while the air a little higher up is not quite so cold. In the morning, when the sun shines, the hoar frost soon disappears again.

Similar, but not the same, is **rime**. It forms mainly in **fog and wind**: tiny, supercooled droplets of fog freeze on trees and fences and form long, feathery needles of ice. In **spring**, frost with hoar frost can cause problems. It damages young **blossoms** on fruit trees and vines. Some farmers then protect their plants with water or small fires.

gewusst: Every hoar frost crystal is a tiny work of art; under a magnifying glass you can see needles, plates and little stars.
Against frost on a car window a cover over the night helps, because then the ice cannot form directly on the glass.

teile.einleitung: Pack ice is sea ice that drifts on the water in floes and is pushed together by wind and currents. It covers large parts of the polar seas in the Arctic and around Antarctica.
wichtigste: Pack ice consists of drifting floes pushed together.
Sea ice forms from freezing sea water, not from glaciers.
When floes are pressed against each other, pressure ridges form.
Open stretches of water in the middle of the ice are called polynyas.
Ice that has survived a summer is called multi-year ice.
Since the end of the 1970s Arctic sea ice has been measured with satellites.

abschnitte.text: Because of the salt, sea water freezes only at about minus 1.8 degrees Celsius. First fine ice crystals form, then thin plates and finally thick **floes**. If many floes drift close together, it is called **pack ice**. Unlike **icebergs**, which break off glaciers, pack ice forms directly on the sea.

Wind and ocean currents move the ice constantly. If floes press against each other, they break and pile up into **pressure ridges**, which can be several metres high. In other places the ice tears apart. Bigger open stretches of water in the middle of the pack ice are called **polynyas**. They arise, for example, through strong winds or warmer water from below.

For many animals the pack ice is important. **Polar bears** hunt seals from the floes. Seals rest on the ice and raise their young there. In the polynyas whales surface to breathe, and seabirds find food. Under the ice grow tiny algae, which stand at the start of many food chains.

Since 1979 **satellites** have watched Arctic sea ice without a break. The measurements show that the area of ice in summer has become clearly smaller. Especially the **multi-year ice**, which has survived at least one summer, has become rare. It is thicker and firmer than young ice. More and more ice forms for only one winter and melts again in summer.

gewusst: The Norwegian Fridtjof Nansen had his ship “Fram” deliberately frozen into the pack ice from 1893 and drift across the Arctic.
When water freezes, most of the salt is pushed out of the ice, which is why old sea ice is almost fresh.

teile.einleitung: In an earthquake, waves spread out through the inside of the Earth. The fastest of them are the P waves. They arrive first at every measuring station, which is why they are called “primary waves”.
wichtigste: P waves are the fastest earthquake waves.
The rock vibrates back and forth in the direction of travel, much as with sound.
In the Earth's crust they travel at about 6 km per second.
P waves pass through solids and liquids.
With them the Moho and the inner core of the Earth were discovered.
Early warning systems use the P wave to warn of stronger waves.

abschnitte.text: P waves are **longitudinal waves** or **compression waves**. The rock is alternately squeezed together and stretched, and the particles vibrate in the direction in which the wave travels. **Sound** spreads through air in just the same way. The slower **S waves**, by contrast, vibrate across it and therefore arrive later.

In the Earth's crust P waves travel at about 5 to 7 km per second. In the mantle they become even faster with increasing depth. Because P waves also pass through liquids, they cross the whole planet. At boundaries between different layers of rock, though, they are **refracted** and **reflected**, much as light is at a water surface.

In 1909, after an earthquake in Croatia, **Andrija Mohorovičić** noticed two groups of P waves. He concluded from this that the speed at depth increases abruptly at a boundary surface: the boundary between crust and mantle, **Moho** for short. At the liquid outer core, P waves are strongly refracted. That is why, at a distance of between about 103 and 142 degrees from the epicentre, there is a **shadow zone**. In 1936 the Danish scientist **Inge Lehmann** interpreted weak signals in this zone as reflections from a solid inner core.

The P wave is the fastest, but usually does little damage. The destructive waves follow only afterwards. **Earthquake early warning systems**, for example in Japan, detect the P wave close to the source of the earthquake. Then there are sometimes a few seconds to slow trains and warn people. In Switzerland the **Swiss Seismological Service** at ETH Zurich records earthquake waves with many measuring stations.

gewusst: From the time gap between the P wave and the S wave you can work out how far away an earthquake was.
That the Earth has a solid inner core was discovered with P waves, not by drilling.

teile.einleitung: Photovoltaics means turning sunlight directly into electric current. This happens in solar cells, which are usually made of silicon. In Switzerland many new systems are built every year on roofs, façades and even dam walls.
wichtigste: A photovoltaic system turns sunlight directly into electricity.
Solar cells are usually made of silicon.
Many solar cells together make up a solar module.
An inverter turns the direct current into alternating current for the socket.
Photovoltaics produces no exhaust gases while operating.
In Switzerland many new systems are added every year.

abschnitte.text: The word **photovoltaics** is made up of the Greek word for light and the name of the unit **volt**.
