When light falls on a **solar cell**, tiny particles inside it, the electrons, are set in motion. This produces electric current. The cell needs no moving parts for this, and it works quietly and without exhaust gases.

Most solar cells are made of **silicon**. This is a material obtained from quartz sand. Many cells are put together to make a **solar module**, the familiar dark panels. Several modules form a **photovoltaic system**. The cells deliver **direct current**. A device called an **inverter** turns it into alternating current, as it comes out of the socket.

In Switzerland many new systems are built every year, mainly on **house roofs**, barns and factory halls. The electricity can be used by the owners or fed into the grid. Photovoltaics is an important part of the Confederation’s **Energy Strategy 2050**. With it, Switzerland wants to get more of its electricity from renewable sources. Systems are also being built in the mountains, for example on the dam wall of the **Muttsee** in the canton of Glarus.

Sunlight is free and never runs out. A system produces no CO2 while operating. However, it only delivers electricity when it is light: not at all at night, and less in winter. That is why **storage**, for example batteries, and other power stations are also needed. In the mountains the sun often shines above the fog in winter, and snow reflects extra light back.

gewusst: The French physicist Alexandre Edmond Becquerel discovered as early as 1839 that light can produce an electric voltage in certain materials.
Space probes and satellites in space also often get their electricity from solar cells.

teile.einleitung: Pampas grass is a tall ornamental grass with big, feathery flower heads. It comes from South America and is also liked in Swiss gardens and in bunches of flowers.
wichtigste: Pampas grass comes from the Pampas and the neighbouring regions of South America.
It belongs to the grass family.
The feathery flower heads can grow up to three metres tall.
The leaves have sharp edges.
Dried flower heads are often used for decoration.

abschnitte.text: Pampas grass (Cortaderia selloana) forms dense, big tussocks. From these, long stalks with white or slightly pink, **feathery flower heads** grow in late summer. They can reach up to three metres tall. The narrow leaves have **sharp edges** that you can cut yourself on. The scientific name points to this too: “cortar” means to cut in Spanish.

Because of its striking feathery plumes, pampas grass is a popular **ornamental plant**. It likes sunny spots. In winter the leaves are often tied together so that no water runs into the heart of the plant. Dried flower heads keep for a long time and are used for **dried bouquets**. When cutting it, it is better to wear gloves.

A single plant forms very many light seeds, which the wind carries far. In some warm regions, for example in parts of Spain, pampas grass spreads outside gardens and crowds out native plants. Such plants from foreign regions are called **neophytes**. Anyone who plants pampas grass should make sure that it does not run wild.

gewusst: The flower heads of pampas grass can grow taller than an adult person.
The grass is named after the Pampas, a wide grass plain in Argentina and Uruguay.

teile.einleitung: The **prairie** is a wide grassland in the interior of North America. It stretches from Canada to the south of the USA. Huge herds of bison used to roam here, and today the prairie is one of the most important grain-growing regions in the world.
wichtigste: The prairie is a grassland in the middle of North America, and a large part of it lies in the Great Plains.
In the dry west short-grass prairie grows, in the damper east tall-grass prairie.
The west lies in the rain shadow of the Rocky Mountains.
The bison shaped the prairie until it was almost wiped out in the 19th century.
In the 1930s, in the Dust Bowl, dust storms blew away the farmland soil.
Today the prairie is used mainly as farmland for wheat and maize.
Prairie grasses have a very deep and dense root system.

abschnitte.text: The prairie is an almost treeless landscape, flat to gently rolling. Instead of forests, mainly grasses and flowers grow there. Similar grasslands exist elsewhere too: in eastern Europe and Asia they are called **steppe**, in South America **pampas**. In North America a large part of the prairie lies in the **Great Plains**, the great plains east of the Rocky Mountains.

The **Rocky Mountains** keep damp air from the Pacific away. In the west of the Great Plains, in the **rain shadow** of the mountains, little rain therefore falls. Only short grasses grow there: the **short-grass prairie**. From west to east the rainfall increases. In the damper east, grasses grow that can get as tall as a person: the **tall-grass prairie**. In between lies the mixed-grass prairie.

Once many millions of **bison** lived on the prairie. For many indigenous peoples they were the most important basis of life: they provided meat, hides and material for tools. In the 19th century the animals were hunted in huge numbers. By the end of the century only a few hundred were left. Thanks to protective measures there are clearly more bison again today, but only a small part live free. Also typical of the prairie are **prairie dogs**, sociable rodents that live in underground burrows.

Prairie grasses are adapted to drought and fire. A large part of the plant lies underground, in a **deep, dense root system**. When the stalks dry out or burn, the grasses sprout again from the roots. The roots also hold the soil in place and make it very fertile.

Settlers ploughed up most of the prairie in the 19th and 20th centuries. Today the **wheat belt** and the **corn belt** of the USA are among the most important grain regions in the world. But the deep ploughing destroyed the protective cover of grass. When a drought came in the **1930s**, the wind blew the dry soil away. This disaster is called the **Dust Bowl**, and many farming families had to leave their land.

gewusst: Of the original tall-grass prairie only a very small part is left.
Prairie fires, often started by lightning, are part of the nature of the prairie and stop trees from growing up there.

teile.einleitung: The **Puerto Rico Trench** is a long, very deep channel in the floor of the Atlantic Ocean. It lies north of the island of Puerto Rico. Here, at about 8,400 metres, is the deepest point of the whole Atlantic Ocean.
wichtigste: The Puerto Rico Trench is a deep-sea trench in the Atlantic.
It lies north of Puerto Rico.
Its deepest point is about 8,400 metres deep, the deepest in the Atlantic.
The trench lies on the boundary between the Caribbean and North American plates.
In the region there is a risk of earthquakes and tsunamis.

abschnitte.titel: The deepest point of the Atlantic
abschnitte.text: The Puerto Rico Trench is several hundred kilometres long. At its deepest point it goes down about **8,400 metres**. That is almost as deep as Mount Everest is high. No other place in the **Atlantic** is as deep. At the bottom there is complete darkness, icy cold and enormous water pressure.

The Earth’s surface is made up of large **plates** that move slowly. At the Puerto Rico Trench the **Caribbean Plate** and the **North American Plate** meet. The two plates slide past each other at an angle, and part of one plate dives under the other. This creates a **deep-sea trench**, a long channel in the sea floor.

Where plates catch on each other and suddenly move with a jerk, **earthquakes** occur. A strong quake under the sea can set off a huge wave, a **tsunami**. That is why experts watch the region closely. In **1918** an earthquake off the west coast of Puerto Rico set off a tsunami that caused great damage on the coast.

gewusst: In 2018 the American Victor Vescovo dived in a submersible to the deepest point of the Puerto Rico Trench.
The trench is so deep that a mountain like the Matterhorn would vanish in it almost twice over, one on top of the other.

teile.einleitung: In many warm countries there is no summer and winter as there is with us. Instead the **rainy season** and the **dry season** take turns. In the rainy season it often rains heavily over several months.
wichtigste: The rainy season consists of months with a lot of rain.
It occurs mainly in warm countries near the equator.
There the year is divided by the rain, not by the temperature.
In the tropics there are often heavy thunderstorms in the afternoon in the rainy season.
The rivers carry a lot of water, and the grass becomes green and fresh.
In Africa the waterholes fill up again in the rainy season.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland we tell the seasons apart mainly by **temperature**. In many warm regions near the **equator**, however, it stays warm all year round. There the year is divided by the rain: into the **rainy season** and the **dry season**. When the rainy season comes depends on the place. The rain belt moves north and south through the year with the position of the sun.

In the rainy season a day in the tropics often runs in a similar way. In the morning it is sunny, and the sun heats the **damp air** strongly. The warm air rises, and huge clouds form. In the afternoon they discharge in **heavy thunderstorms** with lightning, thunder and downpours. In the evening it is often calm again.

Because of the heavy rain, the **rivers** fill up. They then carry a great deal of water and sometimes even burst their banks. In **India** and other countries of South Asia the **monsoon** brings the rainy season. Many farmers urgently need this rain for their fields, for example for rice. But too much rain can also cause floods.

In the African **savannah** the landscape is brown and dusty in the dry season. With the rain the **grass** grows quickly, and everything turns **green and fresh**. Water collects in hollows and pools, and the **waterholes** fill up again. Large herds of wildebeest and zebras move to where there is fresh grass.

gewusst: In some tropical regions there are two rainy seasons a year, a big one and a small one.
Many animals in the savannah have their young in the rainy season, when there is enough food.

teile.einleitung: In some countries there is a single city that towers far above all the others. Experts call it a **primate city**. It is much bigger than the second largest city and brings together politics, business and culture.
wichtigste: The geographer Mark Jefferson formulated the “law of the primate city” in 1939.
As a rule of thumb, a primate city is at least twice as big as the second largest city.
Bangkok in Thailand and Lima in Peru are well-known examples.
In Austria, Vienna is often called a “Wasserkopf”, an oversized head.
Many primate cities in former colonies arose because administration and trade were focused on one port.
Primate cities often lead to large differences between regions.
Switzerland, by contrast, has a polycentric system of cities.

abschnitte.text: In 1939 the American geographer **Mark Jefferson** noticed that in many countries the largest city is many times bigger than the second largest. He called it a “primate city”, meaning roughly “first city”. A **primate city** is not just big. It is usually also the capital, the most important business centre and the cultural centre. As a rule of thumb it counts as at least twice as big as number two.

The comparison used is the **rank-size rule** of George Zipf. It describes a balanced hierarchy of cities: the second largest city has about half as many inhabitants as the largest, the third largest about a third, and so on. Primate cities differ clearly from this rule. In their case the gap between rank one and rank two is much bigger.

A particularly marked example is **Bangkok**. The urban area is many times bigger than any other city in Thailand. In South America **Lima** is regarded as a classic primate city: about a third of the population of Peru lives in the greater area. In Austria **Vienna** is often called a “Wasserkopf”, which literally means “water head”, an oversized head. Vienna used to be the capital of a large empire, but the country afterwards was much smaller.

In many former colonies the colonial powers concentrated administration, ports and transport routes in a single place. This concentration remained after independence. A strong primate city attracts investment, jobs and universities. Other regions are left behind, and large **regional disparities**, that is, inequalities, arise. This increases migration into the metropolis even further.

Switzerland is a counter-example. Here **Zurich, Geneva, Basel, Bern and Lausanne** share important roles. Bern is the federal city, Zurich the largest business centre, Geneva the seat of many international organisations. A system of cities like this is called **polycentric**. Federalism with strong cantons encourages this distribution.

gewusst: Paris is also often seen as a primate city: no other city in France comes close to it in size.
In Germany, by contrast, there are several large cities such as Berlin, Hamburg and Munich, similar to Switzerland with its several centres.

teile.einleitung: Rice terraces are rice fields that lie like giant steps on steep slopes. They were built by hand over many generations and are among the most impressive landscapes of Asia.
wichtigste: Rice terraces create level fields on steep slopes that hold water.
The rice terraces of Banaue on the island of Luzon in the Philippines are famous.
On Bali the Subak irrigation system is part of the UNESCO World Heritage.
Near Ubud on Bali lie the well-known rice terraces of Tegallalang.
In Vietnam there are well-known rice terraces in the mountains in the north around Sa Pa.
A wet rice field is called “sawah” in Indonesian.
In a warm, damp climate up to three harvests a year are possible in good places.

abschnitte.text: Many kinds of rice grow in fields that stand under water. For this you need **level areas**. On a steep slope the water would simply run downhill. That is why farmers dig flat steps into the mountain and support them with **earth banks** or **stone walls**. The water flows from step to step downwards. In this way every terrace is irrigated, and the soil is not washed away by the rain.

The **rice terraces of Banaue** on the island of **Luzon** are very famous. They were built by the **Ifugao** people and are very old. The terraces climb high up the mountains. The rice terraces in the mountains of the Philippines are part of the **UNESCO World Heritage**. They are looked after to this day so that they do not fall into ruin.

On the Indonesian island of **Bali** there is an old irrigation system called **Subak**. The farmers of an area share the water together and fairly. Temples and religious festivals also play an important part in this. The Subak is part of the **UNESCO World Heritage**. A wet rice field is called **sawah** in Indonesian. Well-known rice terraces lie at **Tegallalang** near **Ubud**.

In **Vietnam** too there are impressive rice terraces, above all in the **mountains in the north** around the town of **Sa Pa**. Different mountain peoples live there and grow the rice. In the Chinese province of **Yunnan** lie the rice terraces of the Hani, which are likewise part of the World Heritage. In the warm, damp climate of South-East Asia **up to three harvests** a year are possible in good places.

gewusst: Many rice terraces are hundreds of years old and were built entirely without machines.
Today rice terraces are also a popular subject for photographs among travellers from all over the world.

teile.einleitung: For more than half of all people, rice is the most important staple food. The plant grows mainly in warm, damp regions, often in fields that stand under water.
wichtigste: Rice is a grass, like wheat, barley or maize.
The grains we eat are the seeds of the rice plant.
Around nine tenths of the world’s rice grows in Asia.
China and India together harvest more than half of the world’s rice.
Many rice fields are flooded with water, which keeps weeds away.
On steep slopes farmers build rice terraces.
Rice is also grown in the canton of Ticino.

abschnitte.text: Rice belongs to the family of the **true grasses**, just like wheat and barley. The plant grows to about one metre tall and carries a **panicle** with many grains at the top. Each grain is a seed of the plant. After the harvest the hard husk is removed. If the brown **silverskin** stays on the grain, it is called **wholegrain rice**. If this is removed too, white rice is the result.

Many rice fields are flooded with water while the rice grows. They are called **paddy fields**. Rice copes well with the water, but many weeds do not. That is why the water helps to keep the field clean. For the water to stay put, you need flat fields with small banks. There is also **upland rice**, which grows without flooding.

In mountainous regions there is little flat land. That is why farmers build **rice terraces** on steep slopes. These are flat fields that lie on top of one another like the steps of a staircase. On each step the water stays put and then flows slowly down to the next step. Famous rice terraces are found in the Philippines, in China, in Vietnam and on Bali.

By far the greatest part of the rice grows in **Asia**. The two biggest rice countries are **China** and **India**. Bangladesh, Indonesia, Vietnam and Thailand also harvest a great deal. In many Asian countries rice is part of almost every meal. The warm, damp climate with a lot of rain is ideal for growing it there.

Rice grows in Switzerland too. Near **Ascona** in the canton of **Ticino**, rice is grown in the fields along the Maggia. It is one of the most northerly places in Europe where rice grows. People like to cook **risotto** with this rice. That is a creamy rice dish from Italy, which is also very popular in Ticino.

gewusst: People have grown rice for many thousands of years, very early on in China, for example.
There are thousands of different kinds of rice, for example long grain rice, round grain rice and fragrant rice.

teile.einleitung: Rain is water that falls in drops from the clouds to the Earth. It is sometimes a nuisance, but it is very important: without rain there would be no plants, no streams and no drinking water.
wichtigste: Rain falls from clouds to the Earth.
Plants need the water from the rain to grow.
Drizzle has very fine drops, a downpour is sudden and very heavy.
Part of the rain seeps away, and the rest flows into streams and rivers.
After heavy rain puddles often form on the road.
Rain is part of the water cycle.

abschnitte.text: The sun warms water in seas, lakes and rivers. Part of it **evaporates** and rises into the air as invisible water vapour. Higher up it is colder. There tiny droplets form, which together make a **cloud**. When the droplets grow into big drops, they become too heavy and fall to the Earth as **rain**.

Water is always on the move. It evaporates, forms clouds, falls down as rain and flows back into streams, rivers and lakes. Then everything starts again. This journey is called the **water cycle**. Part of the rain **seeps** into the ground and becomes groundwater. The rest flows into **streams and rivers** and finally into the sea.

Rain is not always the same. In **drizzle** very small, fine drops fall. It is light, but can last a long time. A **downpour**, on the other hand, is sudden and very heavy: a great deal of water falls in a short time, often in **thunderstorms**. Then the water collects in hollows, and **puddles** form. By the way, a raindrop is not teardrop-shaped as in drawings, but rather round, or slightly flat underneath.

Rain brings water into the ground. **Plants** take it up with their roots and can grow as a result. Animals drink from streams and puddles. Our **drinking water** too ultimately comes from rain and snow. In Switzerland it does not rain equally much everywhere: on the edge of the Alps and in Ticino a lot of rain falls, in the Valais rather little.

To stay dry in the rain, you take an **umbrella**. A **raincoat** and **wellies** also help, so that you can even jump through puddles. After the rain it often smells especially fresh outside. And if the sun then shines, you may be able to see a **rainbow**.

gewusst: Big raindrops fall to the Earth at up to about 30 km/h, roughly as fast as a bicycle going downhill.
The water that falls as rain today has been travelling in the water cycle for millions of years.

teile.einleitung: A **rainbow** is a coloured arc in the sky. It appears when sunlight hits raindrops. The white light is split into its colours as this happens.
wichtigste: You can only see a rainbow with the sun behind you and the rain in front of you.
Usually seven colours are counted, which blend smoothly into one another.
It forms when sunlight is refracted in raindrops.
In the morning or in the late afternoon you see it especially often.
Sometimes you see a double rainbow.
With a garden hose in the sun you can make one yourself.

abschnitte.text: Sunlight looks white, but is made up of many **colours**. When the light hits a raindrop, it is deflected, which is called **refracted**. Inside the drop it is reflected at the back and leaves again. As this happens, the colours are deflected by different amounts and fanned out. Millions of drops together make up the coloured **arc**.

Usually **seven colours** are listed: red, orange, yellow, green, light blue, dark blue and violet. Red is always on the outside, violet on the inside. In reality, though, the colours blend into one another **smoothly**, and there are no sharp boundaries. The number seven goes back to the scientist **Isaac Newton**, who studied light with a glass prism.

You only see a rainbow when the **sun is behind you** and the **rain is in front of you**. The sun must not be too high. That is why a rainbow appears especially often **in the morning** or **in the late afternoon**. At midday in summer the sun is usually too high. Everyone sees their own rainbow, by the way, because it depends on where you stand.

Sometimes a second, weaker rainbow appears above the first. This is a **double rainbow**. In the second arc the light is reflected twice inside the drop. That is why its colours are **reversed**: red is on the inside, violet on the outside. Between the two arcs the sky is slightly darker.

You can make a small rainbow yourself in the garden. Stand with your **back to the sun** and spray fine drops into the air with the **garden hose**. A coloured arc appears at once. You often also see rainbows at waterfalls or fountains when the sun is shining.

gewusst: From an aeroplane you can sometimes see a whole, round rainbow, because the ground does not hide the circle.
There are rainbows at night too, when the bright moon is shining. But they are very pale.

teile.einleitung: Sometimes cyclones become dramatically stronger within a short time. Experts call this **rapid intensification**. It is especially dangerous, because people on the coast then have little time to get to safety.
wichtigste: Rapid intensification means: the wind speed of a hurricane rises by at least about 55 km/h within 24 hours.
It often occurs over very warm seawater.
Little wind shear also favours it.
Rapid intensification is hard to predict.
Because a storm suddenly becomes much stronger, there is little time for evacuations.

abschnitte.text: A **hurricane** is a huge tropical cyclone. Usually it becomes stronger bit by bit. In **rapid intensification**, however, this happens very fast: the highest wind speed increases by at least about **55 km/h** within **24 hours**. A moderate storm can in this way become a very dangerous hurricane in a day.

Hurricanes get their energy from **warm seawater**. The warm water evaporates, the damp air rises and gives off heat as clouds form. If the water is very warm, also at depth, the storm gets especially much energy. Little **wind shear** is also important: that means the wind blows at similar strength and from a similar direction at different heights, so the vortex can build up undisturbed.

Rapid intensification is hard for weather services to **predict**. If a storm suddenly becomes much stronger just before the coast, there is little time for **evacuations**. A well-known example is Hurricane **Otis**, which in 2023 became a very strong storm within a short time and hit the Mexican city of Acapulco hard. Researchers are studying whether rapid intensification is becoming more common because of warmer seas.

gewusst: Hurricane Patricia off Mexico strengthened in 2015 as fast as hardly any other storm ever measured.

teile.einleitung: The Okavango Delta is a huge wetland in the north of Botswana. Here a big river spreads out in the middle of a dry region. Many wild animals come to the water.
wichtigste: The Okavango Delta lies in the north of Botswana in southern Africa.
The Okavango does not flow into the sea, its water seeps away and evaporates in the delta.
The delta lies in the area of the Kalahari.
It consists of many channels, islands, swamps and grasslands.
Since 2014 it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The delta has the most water, oddly enough, in the dry season.

abschnitte.text: Most rivers flow into the sea. The **Okavango** does not: it flows into Botswana and spreads out there in a big **inland delta**. Its water **seeps away** into the sand or **evaporates** in the heat. In the delta the river splits into many small **channels**. In between lie islands, swamps and grasslands.

The delta lies in the middle of the **Kalahari**, a big dry savannah. The plentiful water in the dry region attracts animals from far away. The water comes from the rain in the highlands of **Angola**. It takes months to reach the delta. That is why the delta is fullest, oddly enough, in the **dry season**.

In the north of Botswana live very many **elephants**. They like coming to the water in the delta. There are also hippos, crocodiles, lions, buffalo and many antelopes. Countless species of birds live here too. The delta is world famous for watching animals.

The people of the delta often travel in narrow **dugout canoes**. These boats are called **mokoro**. In the past they were carved from a single tree trunk. You move them with a long **pole** that you push into the bottom. In 2014 the delta was added to the UNESCO list as the **1,000th World Heritage Site**.

gewusst: The Okavango Delta is one of the biggest inland deltas on Earth.
Many islands in the delta arose from termite mounds.

teile.einleitung: New Delhi is the capital of India. The city was planned by the British as a seat of government and is today a part of the huge metropolis of Delhi on the River Yamuna.
wichtigste: New Delhi is the capital of India.
The city lies on the River Yamuna, a tributary of the Ganges.
The British architect Edwin Lutyens planned large parts of the city.
In the Rashtrapati Bhavan lives the President of India.
The India Gate commemorates Indian soldiers who fell in the First World War.
The Red Fort was built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan.

abschnitte.text: In the past **Calcutta** was the capital of British India. In 1911 the British decided to move the capital to **Delhi**. Next to it a completely new city arose: **New Delhi**. The architect **Edwin Lutyens**, with Herbert Baker, designed wide avenues, gardens and big government buildings. That is why people speak of **“Lutyens' Delhi”**. Since independence in 1947, New Delhi has been the capital of free India.

The biggest building is the **Rashtrapati Bhavan**. It was finished in 1929 and was first the palace of the British viceroy. Since 1950 the **President of India** has lived there. At the other end of the grand avenue stands the **India Gate**, a big archway. It commemorates Indian soldiers who fell in the First World War.

Delhi is much older than New Delhi. In the 17th century the Mughal emperor **Shah Jahan** had the **Red Fort** built of red sandstone. He also had the famous Taj Mahal built in Agra. On Indian Independence Day, 15 August, the prime minister gives a speech at the Red Fort every year. In the old town there are narrow lanes, markets and big mosques.

A special building is the **Lotus Temple**. It looks like an opening **lotus flower** and consists of 27 petals clad in marble. It opened in 1986 and is a house of worship of the **Baháʼí faith**. People of all religions may go in to pray quietly or reflect.

Delhi lies on the **Yamuna**, one of the most important tributaries of the **Ganges**. The metropolis is growing very fast and is one of the biggest urban areas in the world. Many people, a lot of traffic and industry put heavy strain on the air and the river. In winter there is often dense smog over the city.

gewusst: In Delhi stands the Qutb Minar, a medieval tower over 70 metres high.
The Delhi Metro is one of the longest underground networks in the world.

teile.einleitung: A plantation is a large farm that usually grows only a single crop. Typical plantation crops are coffee, tea, cocoa, bananas, sugar cane or oil palms. Many products from plantations also end up in Swiss shops.
wichtigste: A plantation is a large farm that usually grows only one crop.
This way of farming is called monoculture.
Plantations lie mainly in the warm countries of the tropics and subtropics.
Typical crops are coffee, tea, bananas, cocoa and oil palms.
The harvest is often sold to other countries.

abschnitte.text: On a **plantation** usually only one kind of plant grows over very large areas. This is called **monoculture**. Many plantation crops are **perennial crops**: coffee bushes, tea bushes or oil palms are planted once and then harvested for many years. Plantations are found mainly in warm regions, that is, in the **tropics** and **subtropics**.

On plantations grow, for example, **coffee**, **tea**, **cocoa**, **bananas**, **sugar cane**, **oil palms** and rubber trees. The harvest is often processed right on the spot, for example dried or pressed. After that it is sold to other countries. Switzerland also buys a lot of it, for example cocoa for chocolate, or coffee.

Plantations can produce large amounts cheaply. But monocultures also have disadvantages: pests and diseases spread easily, and the soil can be drained of nutrients on one side only. For new plantations, **rainforest** was and sometimes still is cleared. Fair wages for the workers are also important. Labels such as **Fairtrade** are meant to show that certain rules are being followed.

Many plantations were set up in the time of the **colonies**, when European countries ruled territories in America, Africa and Asia. On the sugar cane plantations of the Caribbean and the Americas, millions of **enslaved people** from Africa had to work. This history still shapes many countries today.

gewusst: A cocoa tree bears its fruit directly on the trunk and on thick branches.
Bananas from plantations are picked green and ripen only on the long journey to the customers.

teile.einleitung: A political map shows how the Earth or a country is divided into states and administrative areas. On it you can see borders, capitals and often other cities. The colours serve mainly to keep neighbouring areas apart.
wichtigste: A political map shows mainly states, borders and capitals.
Neighbouring countries have different colours so that they are easy to tell apart.
The colours usually have no further meaning.
Capitals are often marked with a special symbol.
Switzerland has 5 neighbouring states.
A political map of Switzerland also shows the borders of the 26 cantons.

abschnitte.text: A **political map** shows how an area is divided into **states** or **administrative areas**. What matters are the **borders**, the **capitals** and often other large cities. Mountains and heights, by contrast, appear on a **physical map**. Many atlases contain both kinds so that you can compare nature and states.

On political maps neighbouring countries have **different colours**. The colours usually have no further meaning. They only help to **tell the areas apart** clearly. A country in pink is not warmer or bigger than a country in yellow. Mathematicians have proved that for any such map **four colours** are enough so that no two neighbours are ever coloured the same.

**Capitals** often get a symbol of their own, for example a circle with a dot or a star. Sometimes they are also written in particularly eye-catching lettering. Other cities are marked with smaller dots. What each symbol means is explained in the **key**. This is the box of explanations at the edge of the map.

On a political map of Europe you can see that Switzerland borders **5 states**: **Germany**, **France**, **Italy**, **Austria** and **Liechtenstein**. A political map of Switzerland usually shows, besides the national border, the borders of the **26 cantons**. The cantons are often coloured differently, and their capitals are marked. Bern is specially marked as the federal city.

gewusst: Borders can change. That is why political maps have to be redrawn again and again, whereas physical maps need it much more rarely.
Liechtenstein is one of the smallest states in the world and often appears on world maps as just a tiny dot.

teile.einleitung: Nimbostratus is a thick, dark grey layer cloud. It often covers the whole sky and brings long-lasting rain or snow. This steady rain is also called “Landregen” in German.
wichtigste: Nimbostratus is a thick, dark rain cloud.
It usually covers the whole sky.
Rain or snow falls from it for hours.
“Nimbus” means rain cloud, and “stratus” means layer.
It often forms ahead of a warm front.

abschnitte.text: **Nimbostratus** is one of the ten main kinds of cloud. It is a thick, dark grey layer without clear shapes. It often covers the **whole sky**, so that you cannot see the Sun at all. Its underside usually hangs low and is often hidden by rain or scraps of fog. It can be several kilometres thick.

The name comes from **Latin**. **“Nimbus”** means rain cloud, and **“stratus”** means spread out or layer. Together, nimbostratus means roughly **“rain layer cloud”**. The abbreviation used by weather services is **Ns**.

From nimbostratus, rain falls evenly and often for **hours**, called **steady rain**. In winter it can **snow** from it for a long time. It does not bring thunderstorms, lightning and thunder, though, which is the job of the thundercloud cumulonimbus. A nimbostratus often forms ahead of a **warm front**, when warm air slowly slides over cold air. In Switzerland it brings the typical grey rainy days.

gewusst: A nimbostratus often forms when an altostratus cloud becomes thicker and lower.

teile.einleitung: Peak oil is the point at which oil production reaches its maximum and then begins to fall. The idea comes from the geologist M. King Hubbert. People still debate whether supplies will run short first or whether demand will fall before that happens.
wichtigste: Peak oil is the maximum of oil production, after which output declines.
In 1956 M. King Hubbert predicted that US production would peak around 1970.
The Hubbert curve is bell-shaped.
Reserves are deposits that can be extracted profitably with today’s technology.
Britain reached its production peak in the North Sea in 1999.
Thanks to fracking, US production passed its 1970 record in 2018.
With “peak demand”, demand falls before oil becomes scarce.

abschnitte.text: The geologist **Marion King Hubbert** worked for the oil company Shell. In 1956 he presented a model: production from an oil field first rises, reaches a **maximum** and then falls again at a similar speed. This produces a **bell-shaped curve**. Hubbert predicted that the USA would reach its production peak around 1970. Conventional US production did in fact peak in 1970.

Experts distinguish between two terms. **Reserves** are proven deposits that can be extracted profitably at today’s prices and with today’s technology. **Resources** also include amounts that are only suspected or that are not currently economic. The **static range** is reserves divided by annual production. For example: 1,750 billion barrels divided by 35 billion barrels a year gives 50 years. New discoveries and changes in consumption are not taken into account.

British oil production in the **North Sea** reached its maximum in **1999** and has fallen sharply since then. Norway followed in 2001. If the output of an oil field falls by 5 per cent every year, after two years it is not 90 but 0.95 × 0.95 = **90.25 per cent** of the original. Percentage declines are multiplied, not added. In the USA things turned out differently from what was expected: **fracking** made it possible to extract oil from shale rock, and in 2018 production passed the 1970 record for the first time.

Extracting oil takes energy in itself. The figure **EROI** (Energy Return on Investment) compares the energy gained with the energy used. The harder the oil is to reach, for example from **oil sands** or the deep sea, the smaller this ratio becomes. As early as 1972, the report **“The Limits to Growth”** by the Club of Rome made the finite nature of raw materials a worldwide topic. It used computer models to study population, production and the use of raw materials.

With **peak oil**, geology limits production. With **peak demand**, on the other hand, need falls first, even though there would still be enough oil. Reasons can be **electric cars**, more economical appliances and climate policy. Experts do not agree on when, or which, of the two peaks will arrive worldwide. Switzerland also wants to reduce its use of fossil energy, for example with heat pumps instead of oil heating.

gewusst: A barrel holds about 159 litres.
Switzerland produces no crude oil of its own and has to import all of it.

teile.einleitung: A **pyroclastic flow** is a glowing hot avalanche of gas, ash and lumps of rock. In some volcanic eruptions it races down the slopes at enormous speed. Pyroclastic flows are among the most dangerous things that happen at volcanoes.
wichtigste: A pyroclastic flow is a hot mixture of gas and particles of rock.
It can reach speeds of several hundred km/h.
Gravity drives it down the flanks of the volcano.
It often forms when an eruption column collapses in on itself.
The rock ignimbrite forms from its deposits.
A thinner, gas-rich form is called a pyroclastic surge.
After the eruption of Mont Pelée in 1902 the term “nuée ardente” was coined.

abschnitte.text: The word **pyroclastic** comes from Greek and means roughly “broken by fire”. A pyroclastic flow is made up of hot **gas**, **ash** and **lumps of rock**. It is often several hundred degrees hot. Because the mixture is much denser than air, it flows downhill like an avalanche, following **gravity**. It often reaches more than 100 km/h, in extreme cases up to about 700 km/h.

In an explosive eruption a huge **eruption column** of ash and gas shoots upwards. If it draws in too little hot air, it becomes too heavy and **collapses in on itself**. The material then flows down the flanks as an avalanche of embers. Pyroclastic flows can also form when a **lava dome**, a thick dome of lava, collapses.

A thinned-out, strongly swirling form is called a **pyroclastic surge**. It contains more gas and less rock and can therefore even spread over hills. When the deposits of large pyroclastic flows cool down, ash and pumice often weld together. This produces the rock **ignimbrite**. The name comes from the Latin ignis, fire, and imber, rain.

In AD **79** Vesuvius in Italy erupted. In the ancient town of **Herculaneum** many people sought shelter on the beach in **boathouses**. Pyroclastic flows reached them there, and researchers found hundreds of skeletons. In **1902** a pyroclastic flow from **Mont Pelée** on the Caribbean island of Martinique destroyed the town of **Saint-Pierre** almost completely. One of the very few survivors was **Ludger Sylbaris**: he was sitting in a thick-walled prison cell and survived with severe burns. The geologist **Alfred Lacroix** afterwards called the glowing clouds **“nuée ardente”**, burning cloud.

Pyroclastic flows are so fast that it is almost impossible to escape them. That is why it is important to evacuate endangered areas early when an eruption threatens. On **3 June 1991**, at the volcano **Unzen** in Japan, 43 people died in a pyroclastic flow. Among them were the famous Alsatian volcanologists **Katia and Maurice Krafft**, who filmed eruptions from very close up, and the American Harry Glicken.

gewusst: Pyroclastic flows can even glide over water and so reach islands or coasts some distance away.
The Kraffts’ films still help today to warn people in volcanic areas about the dangers.

teile.einleitung: Potosí is a mining city in the highlands of Bolivia. Above the city rises the **Cerro Rico**, the “rich mountain”. Its silver made Potosí one of the richest cities in the world in the 16th and 17th centuries.
wichtigste: Potosí lies in Bolivia on the edge of the Altiplano highlands, at about 4,000 metres above sea level.
This makes Potosí one of the highest cities in the world.
In colonial times the Cerro Rico was famous for its huge silver deposits.
The Spaniards took enormous amounts of silver out of the mountain.
Many indigenous forced labourers died in the mines.
The old town is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: In 1545 the Spaniards discovered rich veins of silver at the **Cerro Rico**. Soon afterwards Potosí was founded. The mountain rises like a cone above the city. Countless tunnels and shafts were dug into it. To this day the mountain is riddled with passages.

The silver from Potosí was made into coins and bars and shipped to Spain. It paid for large parts of the **Spanish colonial empire**. The city grew quickly and for a time was one of the largest cities in the world. In the Spanish language the expression “vale un Potosí” arose, which means roughly “that is worth a fortune”. In the **Casa de la Moneda**, the old mint, there is now a museum.

The wealth had a dark side. The Spanish rulers forced many indigenous people to work in the mines. This system was called the **mita**. The work underground was dangerous, and many workers died from accidents, exhaustion and poisonous substances. Miners still work at the Cerro Rico today, often in difficult conditions.

The silver reserves are now largely exhausted. Tin and other metals are also mined. The old town with its churches and colonial buildings was added to the **UNESCO World Heritage** list in **1987**. Because of the great height the air is thin, and visitors quickly notice this when climbing stairs.

gewusst: Potosí lies higher than most of the peaks of the Swiss Pre-Alps, and it is a city.
Because of the many tunnels, the top of the Cerro Rico is sinking in some places.
